Resolved, That it is expedient to make provision for payment of annual salaries to judges to he appointed to the Court of Appeal in the province of British Columbia, as follows:-
The Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal,

Three Justices of Appeal, each, $7,000.
Why does the Prime Minister not go on with the Exchequer Court Bill ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We shall.
Are we to have no explanation of this resolution ?

The object of this resolution is simnly to found on it a Bill for the provision of salaries in furtherance of the legislation of the provincial legislature passed at the session which concluded about a year ago. An Act was then passed by the British Columbia legislature to establish a court of appeal for the province : the court to consist of a chief justice with three justices of appeal. The Act contains provision that it is not to come into force until proclamation be issued by the lieutenant-governor in council, and so far as I am aware no such proclamation has as yet been issued. But there have been official com-1
munications between the Attorney General of the province and the Department of Justice on the subject, and with the object of providing the salaries in order that the court may be properly constituted when it pleases the lieutenant governor of the province to bring the provincial legislation into force, the legislation which I propose, if this resolution is adopted, has been prepared.

I did not hear the hon. gentleman very distinctly. I understand there has been provincial legislation establishing a court of appeal which has to be brought into force by proclamation by the lieutenant governor in council of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
And that they intend passing the necessary order in council some time in the early future, and therefore it is necessary to make provision for the salary of these judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Act passed by the legislature of British Columbia establishing a court of appeal for the province, contains a clause that the legislation is not to come into effect until it shall be proclaimed. Of (purse no court can be ae- [DOT] tually constituted until there is provision for the salaries of its judges, and that is the legislation which we will propose.

That is all right.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. AYLESWORTH moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 105) respecting the Court of Appeal of British Columbia. He said : Perhaps I may explain the purpose of the Bill. It contains not only a clause providing for the salaries at the figures just adopted, hut also two or three sections amending the Criminal Code, the Winding-Up Act and the Disfranchising Act. to confer upon the court when constituted the appellate powers which the Supreme Court of the province setting en banc now exercises.
In this connection I would ask the government if there has been legislation on similar lines providing for the appointment of three new judges for the district of Montreal ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No such legislation has yet been introduced into this House. Legislation of similar character, I understand, has been passed by the legislature of Quebec, and the question of passing in this House legislation for the province of Quebec of similar character to that which I am now proposing for British Columbia is under consideration.

It was in that connection that I put the question, because there is a congestion of judicial business in the district of Montreal, and the provincial legis-

lation has provided for the nomination of new judges. I suppose that during the present session the salaries of those additional judges will be provided for ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is under consideration.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. FRANK OLIVER moved second reading of Bill (No. 163) to authorize the exchange of certain school lands for other Dominion lands. He said : Sections 11 and 29 in every surveyed township in the three prairie provinces are dedicated to school purposes for the use and benefit of the province, and are administered as a trust by this government. The procedure of utilizing these lands for the benefit of the province is laid down in the statute as being by auction sale only. There is, however, a provision that where the lands are settled upon before survey, an exchange may be made by order of the Governor in Council ; but where they have not been settled upon before survey, they must be disposed of by auction sale. Therefore when and where an occasion arises to make it necessary to deal with any of these lands otherwise than by auction sale, a special Act of parliament is required. In regard to the lands with which this Bill is concerned, I will take the liberty of reading to the House the explanation that has been furnished by the officers of the Interior Department:
Ottawa, February 21, 1908.
Memorandum.
With reference to the Bill which it is proposed to submit to parliament to authorize the sale of section 11-20-2-5, west fifth meridian, to Mr. Joseph Fisher, of Millarville, Alberta, and to set apart another section of equal value in lieu thereof as school lands, I beg to submit the following explanation:
On July 17, 1901, Messrs. Joseph Fisher, Henry H. Barnes, George Stagg, E. Stagg, W. G. Hanna and J. S. Hanna applied for permission to divert water from the south fork of Sheep creek for the irrigation of certain lands in township 20, ranges 1 and 2, west of the fifth meridian. These gentlemen had entered into an agreement for the joint construction by them of the necessary works for the irrigation of lands in that vicinity which they individually held under homestead entry or had applied to purchase under the terms of the Irrigation Act, each of them to bear the expense of constructing parts of the said works in proportion to the acreage of land held by him which could be served by the works. Authorization for the construction of the works was issued on November 18, 1901.	.	.
As the works were not completed within the allotted time, investigations were made by the department from which it appears that:
1st. Messrs. J. S. Hanna, W. G. Hanna and Mr. MONK.
Edwin Stagg held under homestead entry the north half and southwest quarter of section 10-20-2-5. The Messrs. Hanna practically repudiated the agreement and did no work on the ditch. Mr. Edwin Stagg left his homestead without making any improvements and did no work on the ditch.
2nd. Mr. George Stagg purchased the southeast quarter of section 10 of the same township, did work to the value of $10, which amount Mr. Fisher paid him, and assigned his interest in his homestead to Mr. Fisher, having paid $160 thereon.
3rd. Messrs. Fisher and Barnes proceeded with the construction of the ditch, but the latter has not appeared to be very actively interested in the work and has left it largely to Mr. Fisher to construct and to finance. Mr. Fisher's lands lie nearest the point of intake for the ditch and his portion of the work has been the most costly and the most difficult to construct. A recent inspection shows that the cost of the works constructed has been paid as follows by Messrs Fisher
and Barnes:
Paid by Mr. Barnes	$1,107 70
Paid by Mr. Fisher	 6,382 82

whereas, if the cost had been borne by them in proportion to the lands held by each, in accordance with the original agreement, the
account should stand:
Expended by Mr. Barnes	$2,931 07
Expended by Mr. Fisher	 4,559 45
7,490 52
thus leaving Barnes indebted to Fisher in the sum of $1,823.37, plus such interest as may be subsequently agreed upon, or judicially determined.
Mr. Barnes was permitted to purchase under the terms of the Irrigation Act the east half of section 18-20-1-5 and the south half of section 24-20-2-5, but the sale of the northeast quarter-section 18 was subsequently cancelled. He has paid $480 thereon. Mr. Fisher was permitted, by order in council dated January 10, 1902, to purchase the south half-section 14, north half-section 2 and the southeast quarter-section 12-20-2-5. Mr. Fisher was under the impression that the southwest quarter of section 12 had been sold to him and he later applied to have the error rectified, but, although the southwest quarter of section 12, has been reserved for sale to him, it does not appear that authority for the sale has been obtained. He has paid $600 on account of these lands. The abandoned homestead of Mr. Edwin Stagg on southwest quarter-section 10-20-2-5 is also now reserved for sale to Mr. Fisher.	'
From the nature of the tract which it is proposed to irrigate it appears that section 11-20-2-5 is the central and most essential portion of the scheme. Mr. Fisher desired to purchase it but, owing to its being a school section, he could not be permitted to do so. He was, however, permitted to lease it for grazing purposes and still holds it on such lease. He was informed repeatedly that no sale of this section could be made to him, but he does not appear to have clearly understood the situation and has expended a large sum of money in the construction of irrigation works, which would involve a consider-

able loss to him if the section were disposed of to any other person.
The fact that authorization was granted for the construction of works to irrigate lands which included this school section has, to some extent at least, committed the department to the sale of the land, if the necessary authority can be obtained, and in consideration of this and of the difficulties which Mr. Fisher has encountered in completing this irrigation scheme, the minister has decided to submit a Bill to parliament for authority to sell section 11-20-2-5 to Mr. Fisher, under the terms of the Irrigation Act, and to set apart another section of equal value in lieu thereof for school purposes. The commissioner of irrigation recommends this sale.
That is -with regard to section one of the Act. With regard to section 2, the memorandum of the department Is as follows :
The application for homestead entry is based on the grounds that by the Acts 56 Victoria, chapter 18, and 58-59 Victoria, chapter 31, the granting of homestead entry is authorized to the persons mentioned in the said Acts on their proving that they were in bona fide residence on, and occupation of the school land applied for prior to January 1, 1880, and that they had continued to reside upon and cultivate the land in accordance with the homestead .provisions of the Dominion Lands Act.
The first application on behalf of Martin Aitken was for the southwest quarter of this section and was filed in the department in March, 1895, with his declaration and that of George Spencer, to the effect that Spencer had settled on the southwest quarter of section 29, in township 10, range 6, east, in 1878, and had cultivated it at intervals until 1880 when he sold it to Aitken, who began to reside on it in 1881, and has continued to do so from that time.
It was, however, impossible to grant Ait-ken's application as the land had already been sold at public auction, and the patent issued.
In any case, however, the application would not have been granted at that time, as the meaning of the Acts 56 Victoria, chapter 18, and 58-59 Victoria, chapter 34, was so interpreted that only actual residence in person by the applicant prior to January 1, 1880, was recognized, while in this case Aitken was hot in residence prior to that date, but claimed through the purchase from Spencer, who had settled prior to January 1, 1880. His name is therefore not included in the Act 5859 Victoria, chapter 34, nor in 56 Victoria, chapter 18, which was passed prior to his application.
It will be observed that the application at that time was for the southwest quarter.
In September, 1900. however, the application of Martin Aitken was again filed here, but this time for the northwest quarter, but as his name was not included in either of the Acts before-mentioned, and as the said Acts were still interpreted so as to exclude any claim through the purchase from one who had settled on the land prior to January 1, 1880. his application was refused.
Since that date, however, this interpretation has been reversed, and in the cases of William and Jackson Holmes their claim through their purchase from one Huggard, who settled on the east half of section 29, in township 10, range 6, east, prior to January 1, 1880, was recognized, and homestead entry was granted them for tl^e southwest and northeast quarters respectively of section 29, in township 10, range 6, east.
In view of the ruling in these cases, application was again made on behalf of Martin Aitken, and it was pointed out that the original application for the southwest quarter was clearly a clerical error on his part, as he was perfectly aware at the time that that quarter-section had already been sold and patented, and that it was his intention to have applied for the northwest quarter, for which land application has since been made.
It is claimed that in view of the action taken in the cases of William and Jackson Holmes that Martin Aitken is entitled on the same grounds to homestead entry for the northwest quarter of section 29, which is part of the same section on which homestead entry has been granted to the Messrs. Holmes, it being pointed out that in his case, as well as in that of the Messrs. Holmes the claim through purchase from the person who settled on the land prior to January 1, 1880, should be recognized, and as Aitken's name was not included in either of the Acts before mentioned that the authority of parliament should be sought to place him in the same position as those who have already obtained entry on the same grounds.
It is urged that had his aplication been originally made as intended for the northwest quarter of this section and had the present ruling as to the right of homestead entry of those persons who purchased the claim of one who settled prior to January 1, 1880, been then in force, his name would have been included in the Act, 58-59 Vic., chap. 34, and that under all the circumstances he is equitably entitled to homestead entry for the northwest quarter of section 29, in township 10, range 6 east, and that entry for that land should now be authorized by legislation.

Were all the parties interested notified ?
iMr. OLIVER. The only parties concerned are Barnes and Fisher, and the statement I have already given sets out the agreement between them and the carrying out of that agreement by them. It shows that Mr. Fisher is entitled to land in proportion to the amount of money he has paid towards the irrigation of the total area irrigated. He would not get his proper share of the total area which the joint money of Fisher and Barnes irrigated unless this land is sold to him.

How does the hon. gentleman determine that the land he has set apart for school purposes in lieu of this land, is of equal value ? The land will be enhanced in value by this irrigation ditch, if we are to credit the prospectuses sent out by irrigation companies. According to these prospectuses, the irrigated land is worth $25 an acre whereas formerly it was worth only $3 to $5 an acre. That irrigation would enhance the value of the school land, and if some other lands, which are at a re-

mote distance from the irrigation ditch, he taken in exchange, the school fund would lose to the extent of the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have pointed out that the irrigation involved in this scheme has cost the two parties $7,490.
But are not the school lands more valuable than the lands to be given in exchange ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say the school section that is involved is part of the area that is irrigated as a result of the expenditure of this amount of money. Unless the parties who have expended this money, receive the benefit of this particular school section they will lose the return on a large proportion of the money they have expended.

That may be, but it appears to be one of the accidents of life. Is there any provision in the land law which allows the levying of a rate on school lands for irrigation purposes where other parties irrigate the section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly not. And there is no question of levying a rate in this case. Two private individuals undertake an irrigation scheme
In a certain section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In a certain locality. And this scheme involves certain sections of land. The parties go on and expend their money and bring their scheme to completion. Now, the expenditure of their money gives, unquestionably, a largely enhanced value to the land on which they have spent their money-otherwise, they would not spend it. Part of the land affected by the expenditure of the money is this particular school question, which was included in their original application, and which they believed they would be able to acquire. But, as the fact is, they cannot acquire it under the law except by auction sale; which would, of course, put the man who had spent his money in making the section valuable at the mercy of any buyer who chose to pay for the land up to the amount that Mr. Fisher had spent in order to irrigate it, and who would, in that case, still be better off than Mr. Fisher if he got it for nothing. It would seem to me eminently unfair to put Mr. Fisher in that position. Of course, it is because there is no law to cover the case that 1 ask parliament to sanction the sale of this section to Mr. Fisher and the authority to take a section of equal value elsewhere-that is, of value equal to that of this land before Mr. Fisher's money was spent upon irrigation to make it valuable, not of value equal to it after Mr. Fisher's money had been spent upon it.

That is where I think the whole thing is wrong. It was contem-Mr. SPROULE.
plated that the land would increase in value by virtue of settlement and other things and that the school fund would have the increased value. This irrigation is one means by which the school land is enhanced in value, and, if you give other land in lieu of it which is not enhanced in value, the school fund must lose the amount of money to which it is entitled. Therefore, this seems an injustice to the school fund.

Suppose John Smith held these sections of land, how could he be dealt with under the irrigation scheme? He would have an absolute right to his sections, and he would gain by the expenditure of other people's money without having to make compensation to them. Was there any guarantee to these gentlemen that they would have all the lands within that area?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Then, why should not the government have its chance of increased value owing to the labours of these irriga-tionists as well as private individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, that is the question that is before parliament at the moment. If parliament should' see fit to hold that view, it is within the right of parliament to do so.
Does not the minister think it fair?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, my view is that it is desirable to facilitate the bringing under irrigation of land that requires irrigation and is susceptible of it; and that it is not well for the government, having the general interests of the country in view, because it owns a certain piece of land, to use its ownership of that piece of land as a means of preventing the completion of a scheme of irrigation that would be to the general benefit of the country at large and to the special benefit of that particular locality. But let me emphasize the point brought out in this report, that this particular section is the central point of the tract irrigated and that without the benefit of that particular section the rest of the scheme would not be undertaken-that is to say there would not be sufficient other land irrigable to warrant the expenditure of the $7,000 or $8,000 necessary to make the scheme complete.
Is that absolutely so?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is the fact, and that is set out in the report.

May I ask the minster -what effect this will have upon large irrigation schemes like that of the Canadian Pacific Railway ? What has been the practice [DOT]with regard to school sections contained in the tracts covered by such schemes? Will this cause claims to be put in by these

companies for the purchase at cheap rates of school sections within their irrigation districts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Each case stands upon its own merits, as, of course, must be the case when we come to parliament for authority.
But you are creating a precedent in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but it is only a precedent for the consideration of parliament, which is no precedent, for the right of parliament to give or withhold is absolute. In regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway irrigation scheme, the lands which they have been authorized to take as an irrigation proposition are in the country lying east of Calgary. In that case they were allowed the school sections, and school sections are to be taken elsewhere.
Done by act of this House?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able to answer off hand how it was done, but that is how it is. The Canadian Pacific Railway, when they were allowed to take the odd-numbered sections which they were entitled to select in other parts of the country and to select for them even-numbered sections within the tract, in order to get as solid a block as possible, to facilitate and advantage the irrigation scheme, at the same time, were given the privilege of taking school sections, and school sections in lieu of these have been selected and set aside elsewhere. I think the same thing was done in regard to the Alberta Railway and Coal Company's tract-that is, the part of their irrigation tract that they acquired as a railway land grant, which stands on all fours with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am not able to answer as to the additional tracts that they acquired by purchase under irrigation conditions, but lam under the impression that there the same conditions prevailed. In regard to the tract acquired by the Roblins Irrigation Company the school sections are not disposed of, they remain the property of the school fund within that tract, without any claim from the company.

Does the minister think that we can properly take away land that was set apart by Act of parliament in trust for the benefit of the provincial school fund, and exchange it at any time? We have exchanged land before, but by what authority ? From the arguments I have heard in this House many years ago I think it was held that we could not do it. Would it not be a great injustice to the province and to the school fund if, by settlement, or by the making of an irrigation ditch, school lands that were set apart in trust for the benefit of the educational fund of the province were enhanced in value, and that then
we disposed of these lands and took other lands in lieu thereof where there was no development, lands which were comparatively in a primeval state ? If these lands are worth $12 to-day, and are exchanged for lands in some remote parts worth only $3 or $5, the province has a just right to claim the difference in value, in the interests of their school fund.
In what province is this land ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In Alberta.

I think my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) has made a strong appeal. This land does not belong to this government, this government holds it in trust for the school fund of the province of Alberta. Is it right for one party, while the other party for whom it is held in trust is living, to dispose of that land and thereby diminish its value to the party for whom it is held in trust, without the consent of the latter ? This land has appreciated in value until it is worth $12 an acre. The Alberta government says that this increase in value belongs to their school fund. You take laud in some other place, it may be of equal fertility, but which is worth only $3 or $5 : and there is no certainty that it ever will come up to $12, but if it does, it will be many years.

It is hard to get any other land of equal value to this land owing to its being peculiarly fit for irrigation. For that reason there is scarcely any other land that is as valuable. I have no particular objection to this Bill, I have no instructions from any party concerning it. It may be all right to make the exchange. But I suppose the minister has a report from some of his own officers which justifies him in making the exchange. I have known cases where people have bought half and quarter-sections under the irrigation law in that country, bought at a low rate, about $3 an acre, with a rebate when they had constructed a ditch. I know some cases where the value put upon the construction of the ditch was five times more than its actual value ; in fact I think in one case the patent was put through and the sale was completed without there having been any water on the land, and I do not think any water was ever put on the land, nevertheless they got the patent and the rebate.
At what figure does the department propose to sell this land ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The regulations under which the land is disposed of for irrigation purposes are as stated by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Herron) that is to say, we sell the land at $3 an acre subject to a reduction for work done on the ditch to the amount of $2 per acre, so the land may stand the purchaser only $1 an acre. This

policy is adopted with the view of encouraging enterprises to bring the land under irrigation. It is a policy which has been in force for a number of years, and I think has proved generally acceptable. Where any part of the country requires irrigation, where the land is capable of being irrigated, and where there is water that can be used for the purpose, it is considered desirable in the interest of everybody that the water should be brought to the land. In order to encourage the employment of capital for that purpose the system of sale which has been alluded to was adopted. It has been generally acceptable, and fairly successful in bringing into operation a considerable number of irrigation propositions, and very useful ones. My hon. friend from Alberta has suggested that in the past there have been cases where work done on the ditch was credited at too high a figure, and where sales were made although actual irrigation had not taken place. Possibly that has been the case in the past. When the irrigation law was administered by the deputy Minister of Public Works for the territories and when he was also Commissioner of Irrigation, he had a great deal more to do than he could attend to. At that time there may have been cases such as the hon. gentleman has mentioned. But when the provinces were divided and it was impossible to continue the previous system, a Commissioner of Irrigation was appointed with residence at Calgary ; and I think I am safe in saying that since then there has been no case such as the hon. gentleman has alluded to. We have been very particular as to the merits of any scheme that is proposed. When an irrigation scheme is proposed to us, we have the locality surveyed by our own officers to see whether the scheme is practicable before we accede to it. After the work is completed, we have it inspected and reported upon before any transfer of the land is made. I think if the hon. gentleman wTill inquire he will find that any recent transactions -which have taken place since the appointment of a Commissioner of Irrigation with residence at Calgary, have not been of the class he has mentioned.
The case I have reference to was over four years ago.

There is an important principle involved in this question of the exchange of school lands. The proceeds of the sale of school lands are to be put aside and invested in a fund for the purpose of advancing education in the northwestern provinces. A Bill was introduced a couple of sessions ago in regard to the exchange of certain school lands ; one of the pieces of land which had to be exchanged was very valuable, close to the town of Indian Head, and was being used as a nursery for trees by the government. I pointed out at that Mr OLIVER.
time that it was a valuable piece of land and it would probably be difficult to find an equally valuable plot to place at the disposal of the school funds. Can the minister state the actual facts in connection -with that exchange?
With regard to the question immediately at issue here I would not like to see discrimination against any particular Individuals. Whatever the general plan which we decide upon is it appears from the statements of the Minister that in the case of some of the larger companies the acquisition of school lands has been permitted, other lands of supposedly equal value being given to the school fund. I would suggest that it might be better if some arrangement could be made by which when application is made for purchases of land for irrigation purposes, if it was found that school lands would be involved in the irrigation scheme, these lands should be disposed of in advance by public auction and their full value in their natural state obtained.
Has the minister had any communication with the province, which is of course deeply interested in this and what position do they take on it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have had no communication with the province on this matter. As my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) has said, the precedent has been established and no objection has been taken to that position, because I am satisfied that the authorities of the province feel practically quite as much interested in the dedevelopment of irrigation in that country as the authorities here because by the development of an irrigation scheme the taxable value of the land of course increases very greatly. Therefore, from a provincial point of view, there is no objection to the exchange which is suggested here for such a purpose as this. The very fact that there is no general provision for the exchange of the lands which have once been surveyed shows how carefullysthe trust is guarded. In each particular case we have to lay the facts before parliament and it is within the judgment of parliament whether the permission is granted or not. Irrigation propositions such as this one, it will be agreed in fact by every one who understands the question, are on a very different footing from any other cases. My friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) hardly appreciates the position in this case. This is not the case of the mere enhancement of value of the land by reason of conditions surrounding it or near it.
That is one important element.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, not in this case. That was the case in the instance alluded to by the hon. member from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) but this case is entirely different. In
this case the completion of the scheme de-

pends upon the acquisition of this very land by the projectors of the scheme. Suppose that parliament should not permit this exchange to be made ; if the projectors had known that such permission would not be granted at the beginning they never would have undertaken the scheme.
Were they ignorant of the land law ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They assume, I presume, that the same consideration that had been granted to others would be granted to them. The scheme would not have been undertaken if this section could not have been made part of it: then none of the land involved in the scheme would have had the advantage of irrigation and none of it would have been increased in value by the expenditure of this large amount of money upon it. It is not an ordinary case of land which has increased in value by reason of surrounding conditions.
As to the question raised by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) I am not able to give any information directly on that point. The land was required for the purposes of the forestry farm at Indian Head and it did not seem to be advisable or in the public interest or necessary or fair, as it seemed to us, that the government in order to apply that land to a different purpose, which was essential for the benefit of the province in which it was situated as well as in the other provinces, should be required to pay a price for that land because of the surrounding conditions having increased in value, when it was possible to set aside elsewhere land which had an equal intrinsic value. However, that question is a fair subject for consideration and it has been before me for consideration. I have done what I think my friend will admit was fair. Where we find that land has been held under reservation for some particular reason for a considerable length of time, and during that time has come into value, instead of opening that to homestead entry, we have, in certain cases, set aside these quarter-sections of the school lands so that the school fund would have the same advantage in these cases of increased value by reason of surrounding conditions as occurred in the case of the Indian Head farm, and as may occur in numerous cases in which it would be desirable to secure an exchange of school lands.

To what kind of reserves does the minister refer?
Mr. OLIVER, I can hardly give any general statement of the classes and I would not say that it was done in cases where there is no special value to consider. But where there was special value in the land, for instance, where there is a preemption taken 15 or 20 years ago which has been held possibly in the centre
of a well settled piece of country, and which has been cancelled, instead of opening that up for homestead entry we may set aside that for the school fund so that the school fund will get the increased value of that land by reason of the surrounding settlement. Another instance is this:	In
the opening of the Doukhobor reserves, right adjoining the town of Langham was a quarter-section of land which was entered for as a Doukhobor by a man who was afterwards proven not to be a Doukhobor, and therefore had not the right of prior entry on this land. It was necessary to cancel his entry. This land was immediately adjoining the town of Langham and of course if it were opened up for ordinary homestead entry it would have been a snap for whoever got it. Instead of opening it for homestead entry or selling it by auction for the benefit of the treasury at large, we thought it right to take that quarter-section in exchange for some of the school lands that we have secured exchange for. My hon. friend may consider if he pleases that we exchanged a quarter-section at the Indian Head farm for a quarter-section adjoining the town of Langham. At any rate we have adopted this principle and I think have thus evened up with the provinces for such eases as he mentions.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,

If I understand it correctly, parliament formerly reached the conclusion that we cannot divest ourselves of a trust once it is created nor can we divert these school lands for any other purpose than that provided for in the law creating the trust. In view of that, I would like to ask the Minister of the Interior if he has secured the advice of the Department of Justice as to the authority of this House to deal with these school lands in such a way as Is proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I imagine this Bill has been referred to the Department of Justice, but I cannot answer for it specifically. I may say, however, that the trust of which my hon. friend speaks is a trust existing by Act of Parliament, and inasmuch as any Act of Parliament can be amended so that Act can be amended as it is being amended by this Bill. This Bill is only one of several that have been passed to meet such cases as these now before the House. The Acts hitherto passed have not been questioned as to their legality, and the only question for consideration is as to their wisdom in dealing with the circumstances of each case.

At one time Manitoba wanted her school lands given up and it was strongly contended by eminent lawyers in this House that we could not divest

ourselves of the trust. Have we any better authority for divesting ourselves of this trust? On that point the opinion of the Department of Justice should have been secured.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are not divesting ourselves of the trust in this case. We are making a certain exchange of lands in accordance with precedents established during all the years since the trust was created. In the general operation of settlement in the country it has been found necessary from time to time to make such exchanges as are contemplated in this Bill. I think there can be no doubt that the precedent has been established for cause, that it has the sanction of law, and that there can, therefore, be no objection to this Bill.
Mr. SPIiOULE. It is of no importance to me personally, and I do not want to object to the Bill, but I would point out that many bad precedents are established and we should not follow them. The impression left on my mind from the discussion in this House was that we could only dispossess ourselves of such land in accordance with the terms of the trust.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not recall the debate to which my h'on. friend refers and while no doubt some expressed the view he has presented, others possibly took the contrary view.

I believe it was generally conceded that we could not do>
it with respect to the Manitoba school lands, and I would like to know what authority we have for doing it in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I still think there must be a very radical difference between handing over the ownership of lands to some organization or person and merely exchanging one piece of land for another, which is rendered necessary in the administration of the lands by the settlement of the country.

When the progress of settlement enhances the value of certain land to $10 or $20 an acre, and you exchange that for some other land worth only $2 an acre, surely the school fund must lose the difference. Could not the province demand from us an accounting for that difference, and claim, equitably if not legally, that we should pay to the province the $18 an acre that was lost as a result of the exchange?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is quite possible that in a close scrutiny of the case that might be done. But, on the other hand, there have been instances in which an exchange has been made of lands less valuable for lands more valuable; for instance, the two sections in the Canadian Pacific Railway irrigation tract, which undoubtedly were of less value, aside from the question of irrigation, then the land for which they were exchanged, which was in a part of the Mr. SPROULE.
country where irrigation was not necessary. In that case the school fund benefited by the exchange; so that, while it is perhaps a matter for discussion, it does not at all follow that by this proposed exchange the school fund will ultimately suffer.

Section agreed to.
On the preamble,

It would have been interesting to see the correspondence in connection with this exchange. I do not assume that there is anything wrong in it, but there are so many crooked kinks in these land transactions that one becomes a little suspicious about them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was not contemplated to bring the papers down; but if the hon. gentleman wishes them, I will see that they are brought down.

I do not wish to go into the matter.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. FRANK OLIVER Minister of the Interior) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That the Minister of Finance may, under the authority of the Governor in Council, pay the proper authorities of each of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, out of the Assurance Fund formed under the Territories Real Property Act, chapter 26, of the statutes of 1886, and continued under The Land Titles Act, 1894, chapter 28, of the statutes of the year, so much' thereof as has arisen from transactions relating to lands now within such province.
He said :	This resolution is practically
to complete the Autonomy Bills. It is to provide for handing over to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta certain moneys which have accumulated in the Assurance Fund in the hands of this government under the operation of the Land Titles Act. Under the provisions of that Act, which gives absolute title to lands, and takes the responsibility of mistakes made in the administration of the Act, a certain tax is levied on each transaction, which tax goes to form an assurance fund out of which to pay claims arising as the result of these mistakes. When the two new provinces were organized, they were given control of the registration of titles, and the administration of the Land Titles Act passed to them. They have been operating the Act in those provinces since, but the assurance fund, which had accumulated to the Dominion treasury during the period when the Dominion operated the Act, has not yet been handed over to the new provinces.
Did the money go into the consolidated revenue ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 3STo, it was a separate fund created for the sole purpose of meeting claims that might be made upon it, arising out of mistakes which might occur in the operation of the Land Titles Act. But the transactions against which that fund stands as an assurance are now in the jurisdiction of the provinces, and as the provinces have assumed the responsibility of administering the Act and consequently any liability for mistakes that may occur, it is only reasonable that this fund should be transferred to them.
What is the amount of the fund now?
How does the government divest itself of the responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: By the provisions of the Autonomy Acts. The fund amounts at present to $118,912.62.
Has the assent of the Governor General been given ? That was not announced when the hon. minister gave notice of the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I neglected to give that announcement but the requisite authority has been received.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolution.
Could the hon. minister state the amount for each province ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. the Bill is for the purpose of handing over the money and providing for its division between the two provinces in proportion to the transactions within each province.
How does the Dominion government divest itself of liability to the parties assured ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The government cannot divest itself absolutely of liability, but the two provinces have given an undertaking that they will assume that liability.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.
Mr. OLIVER moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 168) to authorize payment to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta of a part of the Assurance Fund under the Land Titles Act of 1894.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.	.
