Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill 270
(No. 150) to amend the Yukon Placer Mining Act. He said :	Until last session the
placer mining in the Yukon was regulated by order in council. That system was necessary under the circumstances prevailing in the Yukon for so many years. But, as time went on, and the conditions in regard to mining there became better known, not only did that condition of the law become less necessary, but it became less and less to the liking of the people who were affected by it. The very facility which the administration of the mining law by regulation gave to meet changed conditions, or conditions which had been misunderstood, grew objectionable under conditions which had become to a great extent fixed and when people wished to know, from time to time and from year to year, just what their rights were without any question of alteration. In accepting the view that the time had come for regulation to be succeeded by enactment, the Yukon Placer Mining Bill was introduced and accepted by the House. We were aware that, at this distance from the Yukon, and even with the advantages we have of being in touch with conditions in that country, there were difficulties in placing on the statute-book a law that would be in actual accord with those conditions unless there was close consultation with the people of the Yukon, T'he Yukon has a partially representative council or local government, and the representations of a committee of this council were accepted by the government and by the House last year in the terms of the Act which was passed. As I said, the intention of that Act, its very purpose, the desire which it was intended to meet, was that there should be stability in the placer mining law of the Yukon. Therefore, when we come forward at this, the next succeeding session, with a series of amendments, it may seem that either the people who were interested in the passage of the law last year did not know their own minds at the time or that they had changed their minds. The fact is, however, that there are serious difficulties in meeting the conditions, as they are found to exist And, as all legislation is necessarily imperfect and has to be amended from time to time -otherwise there would be no necessity for parliament-so in the case of the Yukon Placer Mining Act, which might be said to have been an experiment in legislation of that character for this parliament, it has been found in operation during the past year that there are faults and failings in it which require to be remedied, instances or conditions that were not foreseen that require to be met, or expressions used that were not sufficiently definite. There is no change in the princinle of the Yukon Placer Mining Act in the amendments now before the House. These amendments are simply to give fuller effect to the principles contained in the Act of last session. These

amendments, as the Act itself was, were prepared by a committee of the Yukon council in the light of such experience as they have had under the Act and presented to the government here, endorsed by the Commissioner of the Yukon, who is an officer of this government, as being in the interest of mining in that country. The Bill, then is offered to the House under these circumstances.
In the preparation of the Bill for presentation to the House, there has been some little departure from the ordinary form. We have given the amendment in the ordinary wording; beneath that we have printed the section as it is and the section as it is proposed to be amended, with the amendments in italics and with an explanation following. It is hoped that by this arrangement a full understanding of the wording and the meaning of the various changes will be given. However, I may say that since the Bill was put in type there have been certain representations made as to the protection of certain interests in the Yukon which may be said to be an embodiment of a new principle. These I will place before the House as we reach them in the progress of the Bill, and will give the necessary explanations. But the Bill as it stands in print contains and continues only the principles contained in the original Bill.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
1. Paragraph (c) of section 2 of The Yukon Placer Mining Act is amended by adding the following words thereto:-but does not include streams which may be considered rivers under the provisions of the Dredging regulations, that is, sti'eams having an average width of one hundred and fifty feet.
Mr. SrilOULE. What do you mean by the average width ? I presume most streams are wider in some places than in others.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is because they are wider in some places and narrower in others -that we use the word average. There has to be some way of defining a stream to which dredging regulations may apply, as distinguished from a stream to which placer mining regulations may apply. We have to make some division, and the wording is the best we can make. We give a definition as to the measurement, and in the last resort the decision as to the average width is left to the gold commissioner.
On section 3,
I thought you only had one gold commissioner, but this seems to contemplate the appointment of several.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It may be that more than one would be necessary, and thijs permits Mr. OLIVER
the appointment of more than one. But at present there is only one gold commissioner in the Yukon.
Do you mean mining commissioner or commissioner of the Yukon ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The gold commissioner, an officer whose business it is to administer the law in regard to mining, and to bear appeals from the decisions of the mining recorder.

What is meant by 'Governor in Council ' ?	1 did not know there
was a Governor so-called in the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Governor in Council is the Governor of the Dominion Council. This is a law of the Dominion parliament, and the Governor in Council appoints a gold commissioner. This law is not administered by the local council of the Yukon ; that council merely administers the ordinary business of the territory, and has nothing to do with the administration of gold mining.
What is the salary of those gold commissioners, and what are their duties ? Is it necessary to have more than one ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The section provides for the division of the territory into mining districts, in each of which there shall be a head office for recording mineral claims. That division is made by the commissioner in council at the present time. Now the commissioner in council at the present time means the commissioner of the Yukon territory sitting in council. As the council only sits once a year it follows that this division could only he made at a time when the council was in session. In case there is a stampede to any particular part of the country it may become desirable to constitute that part of the country a mining district with a mining recorder, and it should not be necessary to wait until the council sat in order to make that division. It is thought proper that the commissioner should have
84S5

power to declare any part of the country a mining district. Mr. Alexander Henderson is the Yukon commissioner now, he was formerly Judge Henderson, at Vancouver.

In section 4 the word ' commissioner ' means the commissioner of the Yukon ; in section 3, in the 18th line, the word ' commissioner,' according to the minister's explanation, means the gold commissioner. There is likely to be confusion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In section 3 the word used is gold commissioner. According to the Bill the Governor in Council may appoint gold commissioners and assistant gold commissioners for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this Act. But mining recorders, mining inspectors and deputies thereto, shall be appointed by the commissioner subject to the annroval of the Governor in Council, and in this case the commissioner means the commissioner of the Yukon.
On section 12-Extension of boundaries of claim.
Mr. OLIVER moved to amend the section by adding the words :
Or which may he subject to the terms of any agreement with the Crown.
He said : This is to provide for a certain condition which was overlooked in the original Bill. There are cases in which there are certain rights which are not the rights of ownership but which are rights under agreement with the Crown. These rights will be ignored by the provisions of the Bill as it is printed, but, with the addition of the words which I have moved, will be protected.
I should think the more responsible officer would be the gold commissioner, and yet you include the mining recorder with him in this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The mining recorder is the officer most nearly acquainted with the actual circumstances and as the distances are great and the means of communication limited it is thought well that in such a case as this where it is really a question of fact, it might fairly be left to the mining recorder with an appeal always to the gold commissioner.
On section 13,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purpose of this amendment is to allow a period to intervene between the abandonment and relocation so that the world will have notice that the claim is available for relocation and so that the person who abandons will not have priority of right in relocating as he would were he allowed to abandon to-day and relocate to-morrow.
Is any official document filed establishing the abandonment ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. A man must abandon one claim before he can take another and under this amendment he cannot abandon for the purpose of relocating and thereby avoid paying his renewal fee or doing his assessment work.
On section 16,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I move that after the word ' following ' in the second line, the words be inserted :
Subject to any right granted by the terms of any existing agreement with the Crown.
This is in order to protect certain rights which are not rights of ownership and yet are rights under agreement with the Crown and therefore entitled to be respected.
What is the effect of that amendment ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are certain rights to what are called reverted claims, which rights are held under an agreement with the Crown at the present time and this amendment will preserve these rights.
Is that reserving to the Crown the right overlapping claims ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Are not these claims in many instances already granted to other parties in the event that they should lapse into the hands of the government. How would the amendment affect a position of that kind ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This condition exists ; there are certain lease holders who have a lease of a large area of territory within which area there are situated individual claims. It is a condition of the lease that whenever any of these individual claims Situated within the leasehold revert to the Crown or when the conditions upon them are not fulfilled, instead of reverting to the Crown they fall into the lease. It is to preserve that right of reversion of the claims within a lease to the leasehold that these words are inserted.

I notice in one of these sections, and perhaps it is the case in some others, that the word ' Commissioner ' where it refers to the Commissioner of the Yukon is printed with a capital C, while in other sections it js not printed with a capital C. If the word ' Commissioner,' where it refers to the Commissioner of the Yukon, were printed with a capital C all through this Act it would be better in every way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A very good idea.
On section 21-Performance of work by owners of adjoining claims.
It seems to me that this is a means of enabling a few parties to get control of the whole district.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is a means whereby a number of men may group their interests in order to a more economical working of the properties. This is a principle which was admitted in the Act of last year as well as under the previous regulations. It is, of course, a principle which is subject to abuse-something that must be carefully guarded against. The difference between the provision in the amendment and the provision in the Act of last year is that the number of claims was not defined in the provision of last year, and it was believed that abuses might readily arise under it; any number of claims might be grouped. The new provision is that ten claims may be grouped freely, but the grouping of a greater number shall be subject to the approval of the Commissioner of the Yukon on the report of the mining engineer. It is believed tha,t mo great harm can be done by the grouping of ten claims or less, while the grouping of more than ten might be subject to great abuse. At the same time, there may bo occasions when it would be desirable that a larger number of claims should be grouped.
On section 22,
Section 52 of the said Act is amended by adding thereto the following subsection :
2. In granting the privilege allowed under this section the mining recorder shall charge the applicant two dollars and fifty cents for every three months or portion thereof for each claim during that portion of the year it is necessary to renew it to make all the claims renewable on the same day; and the representation work required for the fractional portion of the year for which each claim is renewed shall be allowed at the rate of fifty dollars for each three months or fraction thereof, and the said representation work shall be performed and recorded on or before the date from which all the claims are first made renewable.
At present a man must pay a full fee if he renews a claim for a portion of a year. Under this amendment he need only pay for a fraction of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is necessary perhaps to read the section as it stands in the present Act to catch the full meaning of the amendment :
Grants of claims in respect of which such permission has been granted, and grants of any claims within a mining district, owned by one person, may be made renewable by the mining recorder on the same day.
This provision is to permit broken periods to be brought together without requiring the miner to pay a full year's fee.
On section 23,
Section 54 of the said Act is amended by striking out the word ' ground ' in the ninth line and inserting the word r property ' in lieu thereof.
Mr. SPROULE

My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) sets a remarkably good example in the fullness of the printed explanations which he brings down to the House when he makes these amendments. It is a course I have advocated in respect of all Bills for several years. I am bound to say that any minister who does this will always succeed in getting his legislation through in one quarter of the time and with about one-tenth of the trouble it would otherwise involve. I congratulate the minister most heartily.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I desire to add a proviso as follows :
Provided that before entering upon or constructing or repairing works upon the mining property of another person, such applicant shall give adequate security by bond or otherwise, to the satisfaction of the mining recorder, to secure payment to the owner of such mining property of all damage caused by such entry.
Who is to be the judge of that damage?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We necessarily give the right to one person to go upon the property of another, but the person who receives this right may not be a man of any substance, and should he, in the carrying out of his work, damage the property upon which he has been permitted to enter, the owner, though he may have legal recourse, may have no valuable recourse against him. This provision requires that before any one enteres on the property of another, he shall satisfy the mining recorder as to his being good for the damage. The owner will then have security should he require to take legal action.	.

What is the general effect of this section ?-not the portion of it which is amended but the portion which remains as it was before. I will read the section omitting the immaterial words :
A mining recorder may .	. .grant . .
the right to divert or take and use or sell the water from any stream or lake . . . and the right of way through, and entry upon any mining property, for the purpose of constructing and repairing ditches and flumes to convey such water.
Then follows the proviso which has been read by the minister as to security. Thus it will be seen that power is given to grant the right to divert water

 '

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not the material point that is being amended.

I know that; but the whole section is before us and we should consider what it means. The reason I mention it now is to understand exactly the effect of the amendment. You provide for the right of way through and entry upon mining property for the purpose of constructing or repairing ditches or flumes, and

then you provide that tlie person who exercises this right should give adequate security.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To the owner of the claim through which he is permitted to carry the water.

Yes, security for payment to the owner of such mining property of all damages caused by such entry. Well, is that enough-' damage caused by such entry '. You do not say anything about the damage which may be occasioned by the construction and repair of ditches and flumes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The security demanded is at the discretion of the mining recorder.

No. If it were that,
I would not raise any objection. But you are to give security for ' damage caused by such entry,' thus the ' entry ' is distinguished from ' the construction and repair of ditches and flumes.' You speak of ' entry ' as one thing, of ' construction, and repair of ditches and flumes ' as another thing, and of the diversion of water as still another thing, but you provide damages only for the entry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no connection between the diversion of the water and the subsequent part of the section.
Perhaps not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is, of course, a direct connection between the construction or repair of works and the entry. Of course, my belief was that when you gave a person permission to enter upon the property you thereby took chances on whar he was going to do when he got there, and you exacted beforehand security adequate to cover what he was likely to do after he got entry. If that is not ciear, I would like it to be made clear.

I think the minister had better ask his legal adviser about that. If I were asked to draft a section to cover what the minister obviously intends, I would make it a little wider than this. As I have mentioned the point, the minister can deal with it as he sees fit. When you give power to divert and take or use' and sell water, does that mean power to go on any man's property and divert the water from it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. the water cannot be diverted except by the order of the mining recorder.
All the water that runs in that country is subject to the order of the mining recorder ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely.

In mining in British Columbia, we sometimes meet that difficulty. I think that the case in mind is this :
You grant a man permission to divert water from a certain stream. If it is not necessary for him to take that water across another man's property in order to make it available for his own use, the latter part of this section does not apply. But, if he must bring the water across another man's property, he must receive permission to cross that man's property, but you protect the owner of that property under the latter part of the clause. You give the right of entry and right of way upon the property for a certain purpose, that of constructing and repairing ditches and flumes, and all this is taken into consideration in fixing the security. That is, the entry is directly connected with the construction and repair of ditches and flumes.
I do not agree that that view is right. But the minister will look into the matter.
I mention it, not merely as a lawyer, but because we encounter the same thing in our own province and have had cases of it.

I dare say. But where you specify the entry and also specify something besides the entry, and when your damages are allowed for the entry alone, it seems to me it would be well to make the matter clear.
But the entry is for a certain purpose and you provide for damages in respect of such entry for such purposes.
I understand. But where you specify several things in one place, it seems to me they should be covered in the other place also.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I desire to have the provision clear and adequate, and so I would like to make a suggestion. If it does not seem sufficient, I will reserve the section for further consideration of the law clerk of the department. Suppose the section were made to provide that ' before entering for the purpose of constructing or repairing works upon the mining property of any other person ' security shall be given for ' all damage caused by such entry for such purpose.'

I think it would be better to repeat the words at the commencement of the clause and provide that before entry the applicant shall give security to secure payment to the owner of such mining property ' for all damage caused by such entry, or construction, or repairing.' We want it to be placed beyond doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We will sacrifice elegance for certainty; and I move in amendment that these words be introduced :

By such entry, or construction, or repairing.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 25,-amending section 1 of the old Act.
The change proposed here is rather important, and the minister might explain the reason for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amendment .consists in inserting the word 'first' in two places. The case which it is intended to meet arises where there has been a diversion of water from any stream for the purpose of working claims which are either not on the stream or are at some considerable distance down the stream from where the water is taken out, and where there are claims discovered upon the creek below the ditch-head and above the return of the water to the creek. These claims are not workable, and this clause is intended to restore to those claims the inherent right which they are in mining custom supposed to have, to some reasonable measure of the natural flow of the water of that creek.
The water is diverted from the creek into a ditch?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is intended to meet such a case.
Then there is a claim situated above the place where the water returns to the creek from the ditch-cannot that person be served by the ditch in the ordinary course ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No.
,^r- k. BORDEN. You intend to pro vide that a certain portion of the watei must come down the creek to that man's claim, aud that only the balance of it shal go into the ditch for the purpose of serving the parties for whose use the ditch wa< created ?
RF^VER. Yes. The insertion of the word first' is rendered necessary by an interpretation that it seems has been placed upon the section as it now stands in the Act, that the right of the miner upon the creek to a share of the water only accrued after the owner of the ditch had satisfied his own requirements. Of course that in most cases would mean no relief at all would mean that the conditions intended to be met would not be met. Therefore it is proposed to meet the conditions which the Bill as passed last year were intended to meet, by inserting the word ' first,' so that the first 40 inches or 20 inches of water as the case might be, will be available'on these streams to which that water naturally belongs.	J
I do not understand how it came to pass that the authorities deprived the person of forty inches under the law as at present.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. OLI \ ER. Because he was not there when the first grant of water was given.
The statute is only intended to apply to persons who were there at the time the ditch was constructed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the statute is intended to apply to people who were not there when the ditch was constructed. If they were there when the ditch was constructed, then the water could not be diverted. They were not there when the right to the ditch was granted, and this is to maintain the natural right of the gold-bearing gravel along the stream to some reasonable portion of the water of that stream for the purpose of production.

There may be a case or cases that require some remedy. It seems to me that the language of this amendment goes beyond any case of that kind. The minister's explanation is this, that under the Act as it now stands a person who acquired property on a creek below the ditch-head is entitled to 20 per cent of the water diverted. Under the amendment the claim owner is entitled to the first forty or sixty inches of water, as the case may be, whether the owner of the ditch obtains his quantity or not. Now you are making a general amendment to the law which means this : At the present time the owner of the ditch can only be called upon to give up twenty per cent of his water; according to the amendment he can be called upon to give up the first 40 or 60 inches, as the case may be, and whether he gets any water or not. The case I have in mind is this, the case of companies that have acquired rights there now, who are operating on those creeks, and who have vested rights to the extent of whatever those rights may be. Those people can now be called upon to give up 20 per cent of the water. That is correct, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, provided they are workable claims to which that water would be applied, aud not otherwise, bona fide claims, subject always to the decision of the mining recorder or gold commissioner that they are entitled to the water by reason of having workable claims.

That is assumed. But assuming that, and assuming that these claims are bona fide, these newcomers are down below the ditch-head, and at the present time they can only call upon a man to give up 20 per cent, of his water, whether that be great or small, whether the season be dry or wet; he can only be asked to give up 20 per cent of his supply, whatever it is. Now, by the amendment, an old established company who have rights there might be called upon in a dry season to give up to the newcomer the entire flow

of water that goes through the ditch. That certainly seems to me to be going a little too far. You are interfering with the rights which have been acquired and in a dry season the company above might be compelled to give up their entire supply of water. Surely it was not intended to pass legislation as far-reaching as that. The water might be shared proportionately if the flow is small or great, but do not provide that the newcomer or any one may be entitled to take the whole flow.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The proposed provision is exactly the same as the previous provision except that the new provision contemplates that the claim holder on the original stream shall have the first 40 or 60 inches, as the case may be, even if that is all. There was no provision for a division of water in the first instance and there is no such provision intended now ; unless there is enough water to work a claim there is no use in any water being taken, and it is considered that less than 40 inches is not sufficient to do any goodS-i Suppose there were just 40 inches of water in the stream, the percentage basis which my hon. friend suggests of giving 20 per cent to the holder of the claim on the original stream and 80 per cent to the holder on the ditch would not give enough to either to be of any use. It is better, therefore, that one man or the other should have enough if there was only sufficient water for one.
My hon. friend argues on the principle that there is an inherent right to the water resting in the capital employed to divert that water. That is not the principle which obtains in the distribution of water in a placer mining country any more than in an irrigation country. There Is an inherent public right in the water in its natural flow and it is in maintenance of that inherent public right that this provision was made and that this amendment is being introduced. The public interest demands that if there is gold and if there is water by which that gold may be produced, the water shall be applied to produce the gold, and it is not in accordance with sound public policy that the water which is in its natural course available to produce the gold lying along that course should be diverted from that use or purpose to some other use or purpose, even although there should be an expenditure of capital.' The water will flow for ever, the gold will ultimately be exhausted. There is in the long last enough water to produce gold and if there is water by which that is that, for the time being and for the immediate purpose, the water shall be first available to that gold which is most ready of access to it. It is in strict accordance with this principle that this legislation was introduced last year and is being amended this year. There is no change in principle between this year's amendment and last year's legislation, the amendment of this
year is merely to make as definite as possible the intent of the legislation of last year.

I do not quite understand the wording of the section. The intention of the section, I understand, is that the person who establishes works below the ditch shall be entitled to the first 40 inches of water. The section says he shall be entitled to that if 200 inches are diverted. I do not understand this diversion very well but it looks as if he does not get the first 40 inches unless 200 inches are diverted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That might be the meaning that is taken out of the section. The English languige is peculiar and it is difficult to so frame it that two meanings cannot be taken. When the committee of the Yukon council drafted the section which appeared last year they fully believed that they had met the case, but under the criticism of legal gentlemen they found they had not met the case. They have made another attempt, perhaps they have failed again. I understand this is the way they have presented the Bill.

What was fix-law prior to last session ? Last year the Act was amended so that the man who had the ditch was obliged to give up 20 per cent of it in a certain event, scarcity of water. You have given the man who builds this ditch certain rights; I presume you have, because they have proceeded and constructed this ditch and watercourse and, after having done that and invested their money and capital you curtail their powers. Last session apparently these rights were curtailed so as to oblige them to give up a certain percentage of that water. You come again this session and say you want that further amended by obliging them to give up what might be the whole flow of water, thereby rendering their works entirely useless, unless there be water sufficient to supply the owners of claims on the creek below the ditch-head. Am I correct in that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

So it practically means confiscation of the works and property of the people who invested their money under the laws that existed which permitted this to be done, and under which they acquired these rights. It is a very important matter. The minister seems to have satisfied himself as to the desirability of a change in the law but it certainly looks as if the result would be to inflict hardship. For instance, there is a creek and there is a ditch-head and water is diverted from that creek. The law is known to be that a man who has a ditch has the right to divert the water of the stream for his own use and possibly for the use of those below him. Under that condition rights have been acquired and under

that condition rights have been abandoned. Rights have been acquired on the ditch and with the knowledge of the law rights have been abandoned on the creek, because those who took up claims on the creek below the ditch-head knew they were doing so subject to the prior right of the man who owned the ditch, if they located below the ditch-head. There would be no hardship in asking the gentlemen to abide by the law as it stood, because whatever rights they have acquired on the creek below the ditch-head were acquired with the full knowledge that the owner of the ditch had the right to divert the stream. If you are going to give one man what may be in certain seasons all of the water and the other man none, it would seem to me that it would be in the interests of justice and according to the faith of the contract entered into with the government that the man who has the ditch and who has previously acquired the right to the flow of water front it by legislation of this parliament, should be preserved in his rights, or if there is not sufficient water for both there should be a division or partition of whatever water is available. They may both have to abate their works to a certain extent, but do not give it all to one man and let the other man's works go dry. It does seem to me that if there be a partition of this water it should be on a percentage basis so as to give them both an opportunity to continue their works. If there is not enough water for both they must both abate their operation, and if there is abundance of water they have both full rights. It seems to me the matter is well worthy the consideration of the government and that the parties interested should be heard. This is a public Bill discussed in Committee of the House and the parties have no right to appear here and make known their claims as they would if it were a private Bill considered in a special committee. There should be an opportunity given to the parties to be heard. I hope the minister has'informed himself well and wisely as to the effect of this legislation and as to its desirability. I am informed that there are companies who have invested large sums of money in these ditches and in the undertakings and works and they should be reasonably accorded a hearing or some means of informing the minister of their position. Let me ask the minister if he has had any representations made to him along these lines, and if so, how lie is considering them ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have had representations such as my hon. friend has made and they have been carefully considered. In fact the Commissioner of the Yukon came here specially for the purpose of considering, amongst other things, this particular question. He has considered it, I have consulted with him on it, and he is of opinion that the legislation proposed is in the public interest and Mr. MACDONELL
is necessary. I am of the same opinion for the reasons which I have already given to the House. I might add further-I have already said that the gold is there in limited quantities, and that by continuous working the gold will eventually be exhausted in the one claim or in the other, but the water will continue to flow from year to year for all eternity. The application of the water to the claims containing the gold is an absolute necessity to the production of the gold. Therefore, the man who has acquired the right to the water, to all intents and purposes practically owns all the gold, that is subject to the application of that water in order to secure its production. Therefore unless some provision such as this is inserted, the man who has been fortunate in the early days to acquire the right to the water of a small stream and has for reasons of his own diverted that water and carried it we will say down the stream a mile or two or three miles ; unless there is some intervention of this kind, that mail to all intents and purposes has locked up in his strong box and owns against all the world all the gold along the banks of that stream between the ditch-head and where his water is returned to the creek. That is a condition which, of course, cannot be maintained as being in the public interest. This provision is inserted for the purpose of meeting that condition. Of course the right under this section can only be exercised bona fide on the approval of the mining recorder or the gold commissioner or on appeal to the territorial court of the Yukon. But the point is that it is necessary that the inherent right ol' the people at large to the use of that water shall be asserted and shall be maintained and established by legislation. We cannot afford to have the gold of the Yukon locked up by the locking up of the water.

I have not even suggested any such thing. The minister has spoken about those who acquire rights to the water. Now, the man who has acquired the right to the water is the man to whom this government has given the right to divert the stream. No one is suggesting that this man who has acquired this right should be allowed to divert the whole flow of the water or that either party should, but that there should be a partition of the water. The minister speaks about the gold being taken out in a certain time and lie says that the water flows on for ever. That is quite true, but that is no reason why a man should be postponed in his right to take out his gold, to the advantage of another man who is to have the use of the water immediately. Surely the minister would be facilitating the getting out of the gold of that country by extending the area over which the water rights shall be acquired rather than by confining these water rights either to a particular channel or to a ditch. It surely is more in the inter-

ests of the production of gold in that country that the water should be spread over as large an area as possible. Give the ditch owner what water will serve him, if there is water to serve him, and give the owner of the creek claim the same right. If there is a dearth of water, then do the best you can with what there is : give each man a portion. It seems to me that in that way you would be best serving the gold-mining industry of that country. Parliament has, wisely or unwisely, given the owners of these' ditches certain vested rights in the waters of these creeks and streams, and it seems to me to be a great hardship to deprive them of those rights. Curtail those rights if they have too much water ; but it seems to me to be a pretty high-handed proceeding to take them away altogether, so that in a dry season they will get no jwater.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I must repeat that the Act as it now stands is identical with the Act as it is proposed, except that the first right shall be to the claim-holder on the original creek. That was the intention in the original Act, and to my mind it is so expressed, but it seems that it is not so held by some authorities. The proposal before the House is the proposal of practical men best acquainted with the conditions and anxious to conserve the water for the production of gold, and I think the House is warranted in accepting their judgment.

My hon. friend is speaking just as if this were a virgin country and as if no rights had been granted. I quite understand ali that he has said, but he is overlooking the fact that rights have been granted on these streams
to certain persons to divert these waters, and they have made their investments on the faith of those rights. Conditions have changed because of the intervening rights that have been thus acquired. I think the effect of this amendment would simply be to encourage people working claims or pretending to work claims to exact from people who are affected by this legislation certain payments in order that they may be protected in their mining rights. That is not new in mining countries, and I think that you will find history repeating itself here.
That diversion does not do away with the basic principle that the people having gold-bearing grounds on a stream, even after the wTater is diverted, are entitled to the flow of that water.
I would like to inquire how much water any bona fide worker would be entitled to if there were 150 inches diverted, and how much if there were 250 inches diverted?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would be entitled to 40 inches if 250 inches were diverted, or to 00 inches if 300 indies or over were diverted. What my hon. friend from Toronto says is correct, that if there were only 40 inches in the stream and the owner of the ditch had a right to divert 40 inches, and a claim were established below the ditch-head, and the mining recorder gave permission, the owner of the claim would be entitled to that 40 inches as against the owner of the ditch. Forty inches is the amount of water which is considered sufficient for the efficient working of a placer claim ; less than that is not considered to be sufficient.
Would it not be better to say that he shall be entitled to the first forty inches of water if not more than 200 are diverted?
I think that would be a good amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He will be entitled to forty inches if not more than three hundred are diverted and to sixty inches if more than three hundred are diverted. How would that do?
That would be plainer to the ordinary layman.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would then move in amendment that he shall be entitled to the first forty inches of water, if not more than three hundred are diverted, and to the first sixty inches if more than three hundred are diverted.

Then he would be entitled to forty inches if two hundred and ninety-nine inches were diverted, but as soon as three hundred inches are diverted the sixty inches would start and that is ail he can get.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unless he pays for more.
They will ask for two hundred and ninety-nine and then he will get only forty.

Suppose two hundred inches are diverted, do you mean that there shall be two hundred and forty inches altogether in the original channel of which forty shall be retained by the person working below, or does it mean that there are two hundred altogether in the channel and one hundred and sixty to go into the ditch?
Mr. OLIVER One hundred and sixty in the ditch and forty in the channel.
I do not think it says that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am under the impression that the Act, as it stood last year, really conveyed the idea desired.
The trouble about the Act last year was that it did not give a prior right to the man to have the forty or the sixty inches.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it did. They did not allow it that way, but I think it did.
The difficulty arises in the use of the word 'diverted.' You speak of the forty inches as part of that diverted.

It does not say the water was diverted, but the stream :
If after a grant has been made, any one locates bona fide works on any claim below the ditch-head on any stream so diverted, he shall be entitled to the first forty inches of water if not mdre than 200 inches are diverted.
BORDEN Perhaps under the new form of expression the diffieutly does not arise so much. I do not think it does.
It means absolutely not the water in the river, but the water in the ditch.
I do not think the difficulty would arise very much under the form of expression now selected.

,1 do not know about that, because the man does not get his forty inches out of the water diverted into that ditch, as I understand it.

Bill (No. 116) to amend the Exchequer Court Act.-Mr. Aylesworth-was read the second time, House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
Mr. AYLESWORTH It will be observed that this clause is substituted for the present sections 8 and 0 of the statute. The two clauses 8 and 9 are recast, are repeated in a slightly different form, and are made wider in application. At present, section 8 deals with the appointment of a substitute or temporary judge in case of the illness of the judge of the court or his absence from Canada. It will be observed that the section now under consideration widens that slightly, making it apply to the ease, not onlv of illness or absence from Canada, but to leave of absence. Then section 9 as it now stands provides for cases in which an ad hoc judge may be appointed for some particular cause or matter. Those cases, according to the present clause 9, are covered simply by the phrase ' any case In which the judge is interested.' The clause as drafted in the printed Bill applies to the case, first, of the judge being interested in any cause or matter, and then is added ' or disqualified by kinship to any of the parties.' That ground of disqualification is not expressly mentioned in the statute as it now stands; it is practically covered by the general expression of the present Act that the judge should not adjudicate upon any case in which he is interested. But it was thought better that it should be expressly mentioned, and also a similar provision as to the judge having been professionally engaged in any cause or matter as counsel or solicitor before his appointment to the bench. In the present Act that reason of disqualification is not expressly mentioned, but is simply covered by the general expression referring to the judge's possible interest. Then the present statute says that the judge ad hoc for a particular cause may be appointed upon the application of the judge of the court, and the word ' written ' is now inserted, so that there will be a record preserved of the application for the appointment of a judge for some particular cause. The provision as to taking the oath of office in each of these cases is at present in the law as it stands, and is not changed.
Then as regards the present fourth subsection, that is a provision the necessity for which appeared in the events which happened a few days before this Bill was drafted. The death of Air. Justice Bur-bidge necessarily worked an immediate cessation of the jurisdiction of his substitute, Sir Thomas Taylor. There were some cases standing for judgment, and in a few of them judgment was in fact delivered on the very morning of the death of Air. Justice Burbidge. Sir Thomas Taylor was not aware at the time he was sitting in the court and delivering these judgments of what had taken place a few hours earlier in the day, a circumstance which had ended his jurisdiction under the statute. A question has been raised as to the validity of the judgments so pronounced, and whether those cases will have to be tried again or argued again before the judge who has now been appointed to the court. The view has been taken by some of the counsel interested that those judgments would not be affected by the circumstance of the death of Air. Justice Burbidge earlier in the day on which they were delivered, in the view that the law takes no account of fractions of a day, that the delivery of the judgments being a step in legal proceedings, must have reference to the earliest hour of the day, and that at the earliest hour of the day had begun Air. Justice Burbidge was still alive. But it was thought that such a thing ought not to be left to any possible uncertainty. This clause was on that account drafted, and that there might be no possible question about it, I have drafted an amendment which I move to add to this subsection 4 in the shape of a fifth subsection, in these words :
This section shall be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of January, 1908.
That amendment has application, it will be seen, in terms, to the whole of section 1. But to the first and second and third subsections of the section as here printed there can never be any practical application of it, because the time having gone by since the 1st of January until the present time without there having been in fact any action under these subparagraphs of the clause, it would have application simply to the giving of the judgments under subsection 4, and would prevent any doubt as to the validity of these judgments.
Then reference was made this afternoon to the judicial duties of the judge of the court which might interfere with his transacting the pending business of the court with such expedition as was desirable. I propose to meet that case by the insertion of subparagraph (c) in the second subsection, which is the subsection providing for the appointment of a judge ad hoc in a particular case or matter with regard to which there is such necessity. I propose to insert this subclause (c) in the following words:
Or if the other judicial duties of the judge make it impossible for him to hear without undue delay any cause or matter.
Then will follow the concluding words of the section :
The Governor in Council may in that event, upon the written application of the judge, appoint any other person having the qualifications mentioned in the statute, to act as judge for that particular cause.

As far as the proposed amendment to section 1 by the addition of subsection 5 is concerned, there could, I think, be no reasonable objection provided the persons interested in the litigation iii question have been consulted, and have expressed their consent to have the judgments, already pronounced, confirmed bj this amendment. It would, I presume, be a matter of course that they would be consulted and be given an opportunity for being heard before the legislation shall be passed. I presume that they have been consulted by the Justice Department.
It is perfectly apparent that this Bill had no relation whatever, wiien introduced, to the additional duties which have been imposed upon Mr. Justice Cassels. It was framed by reason of certain questions arising during the illness of Mr. Justice Bur-bidge, and the Minister of Justice very properly preoared the Bill and brought it Mr. AYLESWORTH.
to the House in order that the inconveniences of which he has spoken might not be experienced again. It had no relation whatever to anything that has occurred in connection with the appointment of Mr. Justice Cassels to be commissioner for the purpose of investigating certain matters in connection with the Department of Marine and Fisheries ; and, indeed, the remarkably fresh appearance of the amendments which have been submitted by the Minister of Justice indicate that those amendments have been prepared not many hours ago.
So far as the proposed subsection (c) is concerned, I entirely agree in the necessity for some such amendment. I do not know that I would have selected exactly the phrasing which has commended itself to tlie Minister of Justice. His amendment reads :
If the other judicial duties make it impossible for him to hear without undue delay any cause or matter.
I am unable to appreciate the use of the word ' other,' in that connection. What is intended to be distinguished by the use of the word 'other'? I would also invite the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to the expression ' judicial duties.'
I am not prepared to say at the moment that the expression ' judicial duties ' would not include duties imposed by the chapter of the revised statutes which enables the government to appoint Mr. Justice Cassels; but it is fairly open to question whether some broader and more comprehensive expression ought not to be used. It is not precisely a judicial proceeding in the ordinary sense of the word ; you do not have two parties before that commissioner, the one attacking and the other resisting some particular judgment or decree which that learned judge will be invited to pronounce as such commissioner. Whether you can properly apply the term 'judicial ' woul !. I think, be open to a great deal of doubt. It should be made absolutely and perfectly plain. I concur entirely in the object aimed at by this section, but without any present consideration of the exact words of the statute providing for the investigation, I am not perfectly clear that the best form of words has been selected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The history of this Bill is simply that the clause which is here given as No. 2 was suggested by the late Mr. Justice Burbidge in December last as a measure of relief to his work in empowering the registrar of the court to do routine work in chambers and other work of that character. The learned judge wrote me very fully on the subject at that time, making a suggestion with regard to clause 9 of the Act, the appointing of a judge for a particular cause. What is now the second section of this Bill was then drafted. The

first section was not then thought of because it was not then apprehended that any such difficulty would arise as afterwards did take place. After the appointment of Sir Thomas Taylor as substitute judge, and at or about the time of the death of Mr. Justice Burbidge, that which is now the first clause of this Bill was drawn and the Bill was introduced in the House on March 9. I do not remember at the moment whether Mr. Justice Cassels had yet been appointed at that date, hut certainly there was no thought at that time of the new judicial duty which since then has been put on the learned judge with reference to the investigation lie is now engaged in. The report of the Civil Service Commission had not then been made and there was in nobody's mind any thought of what has since taken place.
The amendment which I first read, that is the amendment to cover the case of the two judgments which were in effect delivered after Mr. Justice Burbidge had actually passed away, was prepared some weeks ago. The possibility of difficulty was imminent and whether the question should arise or not, legislation would be necessary to place beyond question the validity of the decisions which had so been pronounced. I am not in a position to say whether the unsuccessful litigants, the parties against whom the judgments have been pronounced, have been consulted or not. The successful litigant, the party in whose favour the judgments have been given, will of course be interested in having these judgments validated if they need any validation, and it does not seem necessary to consult that party with reference to this clause. I fully concede the great impropriety, ordinarily speaking, and except in the most extraordinary circumstances, of any legislation which is to be of ex post facto operation. This is legislation of that character and I would never propose it to this House if it did not seem plainly in the interests of justice that it should in this particular instance be enacted, and if it did not seem that no possible harm could ensue from it.

I am not maintaining that the legislation should not be passed even when an unsuccessful litigant should object, but I do think it is only right that notice of the proposed legislation should be given to the unsuccessful litigant in order that he might place, either before a committee of the House or before the government, his contention, if he has any, against its enactment. Before any legislation of an ex post facto character is passed, the person who is to be affected thereby ought surely to have the right to be heard. Whether we concur in the view he may put forward is another consideration. I am contending merely that he has the right to be heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection whatever to the party being notified.
1 think in one instance the Crown is the party. There is no objection to that. With regard to the second amendment I may state with absolute candour that the surmise of my hon. friend is entirely correct that the amendment was not prepared many hours ago. The reason for that is very simple. I had no expectation until a few hours ago that this Bill would come up for consideration to-day. Having knowledge of the correspondence which passed between Mr. Justice Cassels and members of the government in relation to his duties, and having had personal conference with the learned judge on the subject, I had it always in mind that when the proper time arrived the insertion of a very brief amendment in this Bill would meet the difficulties which the learned judge had pointed out. But I had not done the actual work of draftsmanship until as I sat here this afternoon I was told by a friend that the suggestion was made in the House that the clause had not yet been drafted. That occurred to me as more or less amusing and the original draft I penned then and there in a couple of lines upon the margin of the copy of the Bill which now lies before me. I do not know that it is any better or any worse for that. Now as to the wording of it-the phrase ' judicial duties ' is a statutory one and is the phrase in the section of the statute to which the learned judge referred in his communication which has-been read in the House. Section 33 of the Judges' Act, chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes, is the section which provides that a judge is not to engage ' in any occupation or business other than his judicial duties.' A question was put in the House some time ago by some hon. gentleman asking for an interpretation of these words. In answering that question I disclaimed any right to pronounce ex cathedra the interpretation of any statute, but I stated that I had no objection, whatever my opinion was worth, to say what I thought the phrase 'judicial duties' meant, and in response to the question I proceeded to say that in my opinion any duty of judicial character which a judge undertook, thereby became a part of his judicial duties. This investigation is certainly work of a judicial character, and being of that nature -though it may perfectly well be thought it does not fall within the scope of the judge's ordinary duties-it is work of a judicial nature which he has been willing to assume the responsibility of, and once he has so assumed that responsibility it becomes part of his duty to carry it out; and part of his judicial duty, and the full scope and meaning of the phrase it would appear to me in either section 33 of the Judges' Act or in this amendment I am proposing would simply be that if the other

judicial work of the judge makes it impossible for him within a reasonable time to overtake the work of hearing and disposing of any particular cause, then he is empowered to make application to the government to appoint some substitute for that cause that he is unable so to try. It meets the exact objection which the learned judge has put before the government in the present instance, and leaves the appointment of a substitute judge for a particular cause to be made on his application if the circumstances seem to call for it. I am of course not wedded to the particular words I have adopted. I have merely tried in as brief way as I could to express the meaning, that if by reason of other work the judge was not able to hear some particular cause within a reasonable time, he might have authority to apply for some one to hear that cause for him.

With all deference to the Minister of Justice I do not see that section 38 of chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes has any bearing at all upon the question which we are now discussing. The question which is before the committee is as to the meaning of the term ' judicial duties.' Section 33 to "which the hon. gentleman alluded does not define judicial duties; it simply provides that every judge must attend exclusively to his judicial duties, or, to take the exact words :
No judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or of the Exchequer Court of Canada or of any superior or county court in Canada shall either directly, or indirectly as director or manager of any corporation, company or firm, or in any other manner whatever* for himself or others, engage in any occupation or business other than his judicial duties; hut every such judge shall devote himself exclusively to such judicial duties.
The assumption that this is a judicial duty would control the point I raised, if it were a correct assumption; but this inquiry by Mr. Justice Cassels is no more judicial than it would be if some person other than a judge had been selected to perform that duty, which is of an inquisitorial rather than of a judicial character. There are not two parties represented before him as I understand the situation, nor is it contemplated there shall he. It does not seem more a work of a judicial character than if the minister himself undertook the investigatida or appointed some person other than a judge. It can only be followed by report; it cannot be followed by any action on the part of the judge which would directly result in affecting the status of any person in the department. There are no persons before the judge as litigants. It is perfectly true that he is making an inquiry, but so was the judge who was appointed to investigate matters connected with the operation of the insur-Mr. AYLESWORTH.
ance law in this country. He does not seem to be acting in a judicial character more than were Judge McTavish and the two gentlemen who were associated with him in the work of that commission. For that reason it seemed to me that the expression ' judicial duties ' was not the best expression to select for the purpose intended. I do not know whether or not the gentlemen who -were the predecessors of Mr. Justice Cassels-Messrs. Courtney, Fyshe and Bazin-were to be regarded as performing judicial duties; but they were performing judicial duties to as great an extent as he is called upon to perform them under the commission issued to him. The other point of criticism, which is a very minor one, perhaps merely a verbal one, had reference to the use of the word ' other.' It seems to contrast judicial duty with a cause or matter with which judicial duty may be concerned, but which itself is not a judicial duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My reference to section 33 of the Judges' Act was because that section was referred to by Mr. Justice Cassels in his letter to the First Minister, which has already been read to the House. He felt some hesitation in undertaking this work because of the presence on the statute-book of the section in question, confining him to the discharge of his judicial duties. Upon further consideration of the meaning of this very phrase he came to the conclusion that the duties of this commission, if he undertook them, would be of a judicial character and would fall within the distinct exception in this section of the Judges' Act. That wTas my reason for referring to the phrase found in that section. With reference to the larger question, whether or not these duties can be properly described as judicial, I would with all respect suggest to my hon friend that he is confusing the meaning of the wrord * judicial ' with the meaning of the word ' court.' I do not for a moment argue that Mr. Justice Cassels when sitting in this investigation is sitting as a court. A court is a tribunal having the power to impose an obligation on some person. That essential feature of a court is absent from the functions which Mr. Justice Cassels is discharging in this inquiry; nevertheless his duties in that inquiry are, it seems to me. of a judicial character. A judge has many duties outside of a court, which duties are of a judicial character, although the judge is in no sense a court while he is discharging them. I think, therefore, that the circumstances that there may not be two parties before the judge in this inquiry does not in any degree prevent it being a judicial one, and the duties devolving upon the commissioner under his appointment being duties of a judicial nature. I likened his duties some time ago to the duties of a coroner. The work of a coroner is of a

judicial character, although his tribunal may not be a court; 1 express no opinion on that question. Work of that inquisitorial nature may be, and in this instance I think clearly is, "of a judicial nature. Then with regard to the word ' other ' in the amendment, it is used in contradistinction to the judicial work of trying a cause, which the presence of these other judicial duties makes it impossible for the nidge to do within a reasonable time. He has two pieces of judicial work upon his hands, and the clause I have drafted is intended to provide that where he is not able to do other judicial work of the Exchequer Court proper within a reasonable time he may ask in any particular ease for the appointment of a substitute.

I have already said that my criticism with regard to the word ' other ' was of a verbal character, and while I cannot say that I am convinced by the explanation of the Minister of Justice, I do not think it worth pressing to any extent. As far as the use of the word ' judicial ' is concerned, I may also say that I am not convinced. If any duties are imposed upon a judge, for the reason that he is a judge, you may perhaps properly describe those duties as of a judicial character, because it is as a judge that he performs them. But you must remember that it is not necessary to appoint a judge to do work of this kind. Any person in the country might be appointed for the purpose, and, therefore, it seems to me that you are bound in making the inquiry as to whether those duties are judicial or not, to consider the character of the work which the judge has to perform. He is to inquire and to report; he is not to hear and determine. If he were to hear and determine in the sense of hearing and determining between two litigants, or two parties in the relation of litigants, he would be performing work of a judicial character. Where he simply inquires and reports, he is not acting so much as a judge, but as an inquisitor. He is doing exactly the same kind of work, on a somewhat restricted scale, as that which Messrs. Courtney, Fyshe and Bazin were doing when they undertook the investigation of some of these departments. However, the responsiblity is with the government in respect to the language employed. Having expressed my views with regard to it, I am quite content to leave it there and not urge the matter further.

Since the appointment of the new chairman of the board I referred this Bill to him, and he makes a suggestion which, I think, was discussed in committee. The provision he proposes is in force in at least one of the United States boards. The object is to provide that a single member of the board of commissioners may be sent with power to hear evidence and investigate a matter and report to the board.
I thought you had that in the existing Act.

No, but it is recommended by the chief commissioner. There are little cases arising where one member could be sent out to take evidence, and the case may be so clear that his recommendation may be made the order of the board. I have read up some of the cases in the New York Board, and they seem to do a lot of business in this way. The effect is to greatly expedite the work. I propose the amendment as follows :
Section 13 of the said Act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:
13. Two commissioners shall form a quorum, and not less than two commissioners shall attend at the hearing of every case, provided
(a)	In any case where there is no opposing party and no notice to be given to any interested party, any one commissioner may act alone for the board.
(b)	The board, or the chief commissioner, may authorize any one of the commissioners to report to the board upon any question or matter arising in connection with the business of the board, and when so authorized, such commissioner shall have all the powers of two commissioners sitting together for the purpose of taking evidence or acquiring the necessary information for the purpose of such report, and upon such report being made to the board, the same may be adopted as the order of the board, or otherwise dealt with as to the board may seem proper.
2.	The chief commissioner, when present, shall preside, and the assistant chief commissioner, when present, in the absence of the chief commissioner, shall preside, and the opinion of either of them upon any question arising when he is presiding, which, in the opinion of the commissioners, is a question of law, shall prevail.
3.	No vacancy in the board shall impair the right of the remaining commissioners to act.

The board will consist of six members as constituted under this Act, of whom two may constitute a quorum. It is possible then for the board to sit in three divisions. There is provision made for a chief commissioner and his

assistant, and there was provision made for a deputy.
Under the old Act there was a deputy. There will be three heads in ease they want to sit in three divisions, a chief, an assistant and a deputy.
Is there provision as to a ruling upon questions of law by other than the commissioner and his assistants ?
That is in the old Act, section 12.

Before this Bill is reported I would like to make a representation to the Minister of Railways and Canals. Many people in the province of Quebec have represented to me that the commission ought to have a French secretary. The board does a very large amount of business in the province of Quebec; its jurisdiction extends over many matters, in many localities where the English language is not as well understood as it is for instance in the cities of Montreal and Quebec. I believe it was always contemplated that the board should have a French secretary. At the time the board was organized a young lawyer was named who now occupies, I understand, the position of accountant in the organization of the board. But for purposes of correspondence it is a very important matter in the province of Quebec. There is really only oue secretary. I have had a number of representations made to me by members of the bar, from country parts particularly in tlie province of Quebec, and by other people, to the effect that such an important tribunal as this ought to have a clerk who thoroughly understands the French language. I know that at the time this young lawyer was named it was supposed that he ^would act as French secretary of the board; 'as a matter of fact he occupies the position of accountant. I believe the absence of a French secretary has been felt as an inconvenience on several occasions. I make that representation to my hon. friend, and hope that the government will be able to remedy the grievance.

We have stenographers and translators who are able to answer letters in French that are written to the board in French. The secretary himself of course is appointed by the government, but the other officials are appointed by the commission itself. The matter suggested by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk! is worthy of consideration, and I wiil suggest it to the commission, and they will no doubt take it into consideration. Perhaps with a French translator we would not need another secretary who could speak the French language. But the commission ought certainly to be provided with some person who can handle the correspondence in French 271
I think that is quite reasonable, and I will confer with the chairman of the commission on that point.

I am glad to hear what my hon. friend says. There is a great deal of correspondence which is conducted in French, and I believe that the lawyer who acts as accountant or some other person, performs the necessary translation. But I think as a matter of right, if I may use that expression, a French secretary should be appointed to the board, as this is a tribunal which has a great deal to do throughout the whole province of Quebec. It seems to me that if the clerk is not qualified in both languages there ought to be a French clerk as well. I invite my hon. friend to consider that point because I know it has often been matter of comment in my province.

It is very difficult to understand, without having the original statute before me, whether or not the matter which I mentioned a moment ago is put in proper shape by this Bill. I hope that whoever is charged with the duty of seeing that the library is provided with a sufficient number of copies of the revised statutes of Canada, 1906, will give some attention to the matter. I have been trying for the last two hours to get the volume of the statutes which contains the section with regard to the appointing of commissions for public purposes, and also the volume which contains the Railway Act, but up to the present time my efforts have been absolutely unsuccessful. For that reason I cannot come to an understanding as to whether or not the legislation now submitted to the House covers the point which I mentioned a moment ago. If it is the intention that one commissioner in certain cases shall make an investigation and report to the board, and if it is also the intention that the board may sit officially in three divisions, each composed of two members, then it is important to provide that each one of these three divisions shall be properly constituted and that the person who presides shall have some power of pronouncing on questions of law. There is provision that the divisions which are presided over by the chief commissioner and the assistant commissioner respectively shall be so constituted ; whether or not there is any similar provision in respect of the third division I do not know. If that provision has not been made, it seems to me it ought to be made. However, having brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways and in view of my inability to obtain a copy of the statute in order to satisfy myself, I think that for the present I have sufficiently discharged my duty by bringing it to his attention.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
