Brandon drill hall, $20,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: I may say that we have allowed military buildings in Ontario to stand over. I think probably there will be no reason for allowing the Brandon drill hall item to stand over because the building is under construction. This is a revote which I am asking of $20,000 to make provision for the erection of the Brandon drill hall. The site is a lot situated on the corner of Eleventh and Victoria streets, being 215 by 120 feet. The building consists of a drill hall 120 by 75 feet and an armoury having a frontage of 90 feet and a depth of 120. The total cost of building, including drill hall, armoury, electric wiring, fittings, furniture, &c., is $70,881.92.
Who is the contractor ?
Messrs. Dumais and Lachance, Hull, Quebec.
What was the difference in the amount of the tenders ?
Four tenders were received. the lowest was $52,754 and the highest $50,500. The lowest tender was accepted.
How much has been spent already ?
The total expenditure to December 31, 1907, wras $12,445.92.
If the tender of $52,000 was accepted, that would mean that that was what the building was to cost. In this case the minister states that $70,000 is what it will cost.
Has there been any extra work other than the shooting gallery? Has the contractor been instructed to make any changes, or will he have any claim for extras ?
Not so far as we know.
Who is the architect ?
Mr. Thomas Sinclair is supervising architect and clerk of works. He receives 2 per cent commission. The plans were made in the department.
Can the minister furnish any particulars as to the number of troops to be served by that drill hall ?
I have a memorandum that Brandon is the headquarters of the 12th Manitoba Dragoons and * D ' squadron.
What was the original estimated cost ? I understand it is going to cost a great deal more than it was estimated it would.
I have no information as to that.

I think the citizens of Brandon do not expect that the votes taken last year and this year will finish the hall ; in fact they are counting on many more thousands be in? spent and depending on their representative having sufficient pull with the Public Works Department to increase the cost to a great deal more than the total amount estimated in the first place.

I think my hon. friend
is mistaken.
That is the general talk among some of the citizens of Brandon.
I suppose that is because such an exceedingly fine building is being erected ; the contractor is doing his work well.

This is another case of what I complained of the other evening, the expenditure of such large amounts in one town to the exclusion of other towns of almost as much importance both generally and from a military standpoint. Brandon is of no more importance in this respect than Minnedosa or Souris. In Minnedosa, for instance, they have not a decent place to store the arms which are deteriorating, and I am informed that some of the militiamen there are so enthusiastic and at the same time so discouraged at the results of their appeals to the Militia Department for some kind of small drill hall that they have subscribed privately to put up a small build-

ing simply for the protection of the arms belonging to the government. It is not very much encouragement to the company there, in which there are a great many farmers' sons, who have to come long distances to attend drill and who have attended the annual camp and have acquitted themselves so creditably as to have carried off for two years in succession the main prize, to see so much done for Brandon and nothing done for the rural corps. I do not object to Brandon having a good drill hall ; but I do object to such excessive expenditures for buildings in Brandon and Virdeu simply because they are represented by an ex-minister who seems to have a pull with the government, and at the expense of the rural militia.
It seems to me that we should have the Minister of Militia here to give information on this matter.

I have no objection to letting this item stand until he is here.
Dauphin public building, $15,000.

This consists of a revote of $2,500 and a new vote of $12,500. It is to complete payments in connection with the purchase of a site and the erection of a building for post office purposes, &c. The lot is 75 feet by 132 feet
Whom was the lot purchased from ?
Thomas W. Iredale.
What do you mean by '&c' ?
The building will have the land office as well.
What will be the total cost of this building when completed ?
The estimated cost, including everything is $36,000. That does not include the site.
What has the site cost ?
What is the population of Dauphin ?
In 1901 it was 1,135, but I think it has grown considerably since then.	-
Does the minister know whether any buildings were on this land before, or is it vacant ?

I am not able to say whether or not there were any buildings upon It. I may say that an inspector from the department who has a very good knowledge of the value of real property was sent to Inspect this land at Dauphin, and to compare its price with the price asked for other lots in the immediate vicinity, and he re-Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
ported that this was a far and reasonable price for the lot.

I wish to say that I am very well acquainted with all the towns about that size in the west, and I do not hesitate to say that $80 per foot frontage is a very excessive price for a lot in a town the size of Dauphin. I do not object to Dauphin having a post office. I believe these smaller towns in the west are as much entitled to public building's as other towns anywhere in the Dominion ; but I do say that a lot of 75 feet frontage could be bought in any town of the west of from 1,500 to 2,000 population for $3,000.
Does my hon. friend know of the sale of any lot in the business part of Dauphin having been made within the last six months at less price ?

I know the value of lots in other towns of similar size, and I know that Dauphin is not different in that respect from other towns. I do not hesitate for one moment to say that $6,000 for 75 feet frontage in any part of Dauphin is an absolutely extravagant price.

This is another instance of extravagance in erecting public buildings throughout the Dominion. Here is a village with only 1,000 inhabitants whose future is very uncertain, and yet the government are going to put up this expensive public building. In the village of Shelburne where I live, a village of 1,500, the headquarters of militia regiment for years, we have to rent a room on the third flat over a shop in which to keep the arms. The result is that on several occasions the rain has come through and injured the arms and accoutrements. Not a dollar has been spent on a public building in that village, yet in this village of 1,000 the government are going to spend $40,000.
This vote is not for an armoury but for a building for a post office and other public purposes.

The village of Shelburne has neither post office nor armoury. But it does not happen to be represented by an ex-minister or somebody with a pull. There is no big four in that section. But the big four can accomplish anything they want. All they have to do is to ask for something from the government and they get it. The time has come when we should have some pronounced policy on this question. We should have such a pronouncement before voting these lai'ge amounts of $50,000 or $60,000 for public buildings.
What are the postal statistics ?
The postal revenue for the nine months of last year was $4,310.65,
Wliat was the expenditure ?

The expenditure for the rent of the post office was $275 and the other expenses $1,608 including salary to postmaster, $1,125, and commission on money orders, $100. My hon. friend (Mr. Barr) must see that he has put forth somewhat narrow views. He says we should not erect a public building in Dauphin because we do not know what its future is going to be and have not yet erected a public building at Shelburne. My hon. friend might not be able to get all the members of this House to agree with him. While X should be very glad to consider the claims of Shelburne as well as those of any other town, yet I think we should not stop all expenditure on public ' buildings simply because we cannot erect one in every town of Canada. The resolution of the municipal council of Dauphin sets forth that the postal business in 1905 stood the sixth in Manitoba, that Dauphin has a rapidly growing population, and its postal business will rank fourth in the near future. It is the trade and district centre of northwestern Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan. It is the centre of a large and fertile country which is rapidly increasing in population. In erecting public buildings, we have to look to the future. We have to consider whether or not the town is a railway centre or whether or not it is the centre of a fertile country with a rapidly growing population.
Has the minister the census figures of the last census ?
No.
I could give the hon. minister a similar resolution from Shelburne or any other village.
I shall have to go up to Shelburne.
That resolution does not prove anything. We know the population is only a little over 1,000 and it is a small place.
Twenty years ago the whole province of Saskatchewan had only a few thousand. To-day its population numbers in the hundreds of thousands.

Dauphin is one of the most thriving towns in the west to-day. It has nearly 2,000 of a population. The Canadian Northern has made it a divisional point and is spending a very large amount in shops and other buildings-possibly $100,000 or $150,000. There can be no question as to Dauphin's future.
Another railway runs in there ?
I think there is a little railway projected that runs down some twelve miles from Dauphin or very close to Dauphin.
It is all Canadian Northern.
There is a little junction there.
Prince Albert Junction and Edmonton Junction.
Under what circumstances was the land bought? All we have had from the minister is that some one told him that the price was not too high.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) missed part of what I said. I explained that an inspector was sent to .examine the land and compare the price asked with the prices for which other lots similarly situated could be obtained, and he reported that the price is as low as that at which any lot suitable for public buildings could be obtained.
Who was the inspector ?
Mr. Greenfield of Winnipeg.

Where is the lot situated ?
Mr.' PUGSLEY. It is lot 16 and the easterly half of lot 17 in block 9, situated on Burrows avenue. It has a frontage of 75 feet.

Was the fact that a lot was required for a post office advertised ?
Mx-. PUGSLEY. No, that is not usual.
From whom was the lot purchased?
From Mr. T. W. Iredale.
Is it a corner lot?
It does not appear to be.
I would like to ask the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) if lots in Dauphin are more valuable than in his own town?
I do not know that they are. There are lots in the town I; live in held at $6,000 and $5,000.
What frontage?
Frontage of 30 feet,, with a depth of 99 feet.
This lot is two and a< half times that size.

I do not know anything about the claims of Dauphin for a post office, but I think that every member- of the.

House must be surprised to find $6,000 paid for a 75-foot lot in a town of 1,100.
In a rapidly growing town with a population, as we are told by the member (Mr. Crawford) of about 2,000.

I do not see how it can be growing very rapidly. It is an old town; I have heard of it for a long time. And to pay $6,000 for a lot of that size in a town of 1,100 people must strike every member of this House as ridiculous.
The population was 1,100 last census, but it is about 2,000 now.
What authority has the minister for saying that?
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford).
Does he speak from census returns ?
No, but I understand it is about two thousand now.
Then, you do not know.
Not positively.

After the statement of the member for Portage ia Prairie, it is quite evident that this has been a bargain day in this place Dauphin when they can sell land for $80 a foot. The member for Portage la Prairie tells us that in his own town, lots of a depth of only 90 feet, sell as a common occurrence
I did not say, as a common occurrence.
The hon. gentleman said that a lot 33 by 90 feet sold for $6,000.
No, I did not.
Well, if the hon. gentleman will state what he did say ?
You are making the* statement. And I say your statement is not correct.
Well, if I misunderstood the hon. gentleman, how much did it sell for?
Some lots sell for $6,000, some for $5,000, or $3,000 or $2,000. It depends on the location.

I accept the statement of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, for I know if it was not true he would not say it. The hon. gentleman has repeated the statement that a 33-foot lot sells for $6,000. That is nearly $200 a foot. Well,
I can tell him that if real estate is worth that there, it is worth more than in similar towns in Ontario.
Of course.

Well, from the hungry cry being sent up from the west now, it Mr. LALOR.
does not seem very far ahead of Ontario for the present. Is the report of the Postmaster General right in saying that about $200 a year is paid for rent, fuel and light for the post office premises in Dauphin?
The amount is $275.
The report of the Postmaster General gives it as $206.25.
Perhaps that would be for nine months.
Yes, probably.

The hon. minster (Mr. Pugsley) will remember the purchase of a lot in Sandwich. This is the renowned town of Sandwich, one of the oldest in Ontario, and situated on the Detroit river, where property is naturally held at a high figure. The hon. minster will remember that he purchased a lot in Sandwich much larger than this one in Dauphin and paid only $1,600 for it.
That shows that we purchase as cheaply as we can.
And the former purchaser made a profit of 50 per cent. I state this case as a matter of comparison.

I know that in some towns property can be purchased for a good deal less than other towns where the population is considerably less. A good deal depends upon the age of the town. A .town may be fifty years old but if it is not growing very much even though it has a fairly large population, real estate will not have so high a value as in smaller but more progressive towns. It may be that the town of Sandwich is not growing rapidly, and it may be that there are many sites available for post office purposes. I happen to know some places in the west where land, many years ago when population was not nearly so large as it is now, was held at a higher figure than the same land can be bought for to-day. In the course of time, values settle down, for people realize just what the land is really worth. Daup-liin has become a divisional point of the Canadian Northern Railway and is the distributing centre for all the fertile country to the west and northwest of it. It is rapidly increasing in population, I believe. From the knowledge I have of real estate. I am not prepared to say that this price for a lot and a half, well situated in the centre of business-for that is where we must select sites for post offices and custom houses-is an excessive price.
Has the contract been let?
No. In fact, we have not actually acquired the site, but we have agreed to buy on inspection by an inspector-

The minister has em- i phasized the fact that an inspector was sent 1 to examine the property before it was pur- 1 chased by the government, and cites it, ' evidently,' as though that must settle the matter. This House and this country have had some experience of the work of inspectors. There was a purchase in the city of Halifax where an inspector was sent down to determine the value of property, and yet, upon further investigation, it was found that we got very much the worse of the deal. I can recollect another case, in Moncton, where an inspector was sent down on behalf of this government to ascertain the value of land, and a similar circumstance seemed to exist there. But the government got the worst of the deal, and the middleman was introduced, as the evidence shows he has been frequently introduced by this government.
Does the hon. gentleman say that in the Public Works Department there is any evidence that lots have been purchased through middlemen?

I said there was evidence that the government did this, I did not single out any department. I want to refer the minister to another case to show what an exorbitant price is being paid for this post office site in a small town of 1,000 inhabitants.
The hon. gentleman misunderstood me. The information I have is that the population of the town, by the census of 1901, was 1,135, and that it is about 2,000 to-day.

If an increase of 100 in the population will help the minister, I am willing to concede that it has 1,100 or 1,200. But even that population does not seem to justify the expenditure of $6,000 for this small piece of land, when you compare it with a recent purchase by the same department in the city of Belleville. There they had occasion to purchase a piece of land for the erection of an armoury, a piece of land more than double the area that is being paid $6,000 for here. Not only is it double in area, but it is a corner lot, fronting on two of the most important streets in the city of Belleville, in the central portion of the town. Belleville is well known to be a very progressive Ontario city, situated in an old and well settled district, where land has a high value; yet the Department of Public Works was able to buy that piece of land for about the same price that is paid for this small piece of land in Dauphin. Now, I would like to know from the Minister of Public Works how frequently this piece of land for the post office has changed hands within a year or so before the government became the purchaser. In the Moncton land deal and in the Halifax land deal, we find by the investigation that
took place that there were a number of transfers just before the government bought the land. Perhaps that is the cue to this matter.
The hon. gentleman ought not to make a suggestion like that without some evidence.
I may tell the hon. gentleman that Dauphin had a population of 1,135 in 1901 and 1,070 in 1906, and I think I am fairly within the mark in saying that to-day it has a population of nearly 2,000.

As showing the increase in the value of land, I may mention that in my little town of Stonewall there were 585 inhabitants in 1901 and 1,08* in 1906. The Bank of Hamilton, a very conservative institution, two years ago bought a lot and paid $50 a foot for it. We have in that town perhaps one block of 550 feet square, and you cannot buy a foot of land in that block for less than $50 a foot.
Is that a corner lot?

Yes. They bought a corner lot for $50 a foot. That is a sample of the value of land. Nearly all the business is done in that one block. The bank is now putting up a building to cost $18,000. Hon. gentlemen coming from Ontario vilages do not realize how quickly land values go up in western towns. Take the town of Selkirk in the county of that name. We have a district there almost as large as a small province, 100 miles by 150, but there are very few public buildings at that point. Selkirk is 25 miles from any other town, and yet it will undoubtedly become a large town, because they have a water-power available at the St. Andrew's locks which will be utilized for manufacturing purposes and the town is sure to increase and prosper. It would not be good business to put up a small building in any of those western towns that are growing so rapidly, and the expenditure of _ $41,000 on a public building at Selkirk is justified by the situation of the town. Dauphin is in a similar position, 25 or 30 miles from any other place. It will likely become a very important point, and there should be a building put up there that will serve for the future.

We are told that in this town of Dauphin there is a building that has been occupied as a post office for some time back. That building must occupy a considerable space, and it cannot have much less than 75 feet frontage if it is used as a post office. It must cost some-i thing to heat and light that building, but ; the owner of it is willing to rent his pro-i perty to the government at a figure equal :	to about $275 a year in view of the increased
: interest on the value of the land and of

the building and of the cost of heating and lighting. I suppose there would not be more than $75 for heating and lighting, and if we call heating and lighting $75, this gentleman owning that building is will iug to rent it to the government for $200 a year, which at 10 per cent represents a value of $2,000 for that land with the building on it.
What kind of building is it?

I do not care, it must be good enough to use as a post office or it would not be used as such. There is your lot, plus your building, which the man is willing to rent for $200 a year, or perhaps less. That will represent 10 per cent on $2,000 for this lot, including the building. Now, in this case we find $6,000 paid for a vacant lot. I think the statement in itself is sufficient to show that the figure is unreasonable. But apart altogether from the question of price, it is a pity that the minister just coming into office would not lay down some principle according to which these buildings might be erected.
This building is to be used as a custom house as well.

Add that if you like, and you have interest on a capital of $2,000,
3 ou have heating and lighting additional, your janitor, and probably an additional staff in the office, meaning $3,000 or $4,000 a year that this country will have to pay as against $275 ; or if you allow rent for the custom house of $75, you have $350 or $400 at the outside, to say nothing of repairs and incidentals of that nature. I am quite prepared to admit that the late government went further than I thought they should have gone in erecting public buildings in places not sufficiently large to justify it, but I think that if the late government punished the people with whips, the present government are certainly doing it with scorpions, because they have out-Heroded Herod since they came into office and each year seems to be worse than the preceding one. I would say to my hon. friend that it would meet 'with the approval not only of the people of the country, but of his own friends as well if he would lay down the rule that public buildings should only be erected in the same way that private individuals would erect buildings. If a city or a town is doing a large amount of business, if it would be necessary to pay a large rental and if the government can borrow money cheaply, bv all means put up a public building. If a town is going to grow like Dauphin, when it has grown give it its public building, but it seems absurd to say that we will spend a large sum of money to erect a public building in a town because a few years hence it is expected to increase in size and importance.

I think that we should follow a good deal of the advice which my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. North-rup) has given because the time will come when all this will have to be stopped. With reference to public buildings in British Columbia and the Northwest, I found when I was in the west, that the government are in the habit of buying property and paying a very large price for it. I will not say whether they buy it from their own friends or not. That is not the point I am making. But, the price that the government pay seems to regulate the price of property in the town in which the government purchase property. I would not be surprised that if a good deal of the prevailing scarcity of money in the west was due to the fact that a great many people have put their money into real estate and it is locked up there in the meantime. I was in a town Where the government had bought a property for a public building for which they had paid a large amount of money. I could hardly believe that property in that place would bring as high a price as was paid.
Mr. rUGSLEY. Where was that ?

That was on the main street of Saskatoon. The government bought a piece of land and paid for it nearly a thousand dollars a running foot, the price being higher than would be paid in Montreal. You could not approach property on the main street in Saskatoon where the government are putting up a very costly post office. This is outside of the ordinary criticism that is made with reference to erecting post offices and public buildings here and there, but I wish to call attention to the speculative prices that the government are paying for property in these small towns. This has been going on to such a degree that a great many people have gone into speculation and there is a great scarcity of money in the west because it is locked up in that way. I heard not long ago that merchants in the west cannot pay what they owe to eastern merchants on account of their money being invested in speculative transactions, a large amount of which speculation is no doubt due to the fact that the government are paying these high prices for land. The government have lots of money and they can pay these prices.
I do not mean to accuse them of buying property from their friends although I believe that they do buy most of the property from their friends. Probably their friends know of the intentions of the government in advance, buy the property at an ordinary price, then put up the price and the government pay it.

We heard that same absurd speech with regard to the post office property that was bought at Winnipeg. The government held that property but a very

85SO
few months when it could have turned it over at $100,000 advance on the price paid. That condition lias prevailed in the west and we cannot understand it in the east. Take a city the size of Edmonton ; I priced ordinary lots there last summer for which they wanted $700 a foot. Hon. gentlemen talk about the large buildings put up by the government. What are the banks doing ? The banks are showing the greatest example of what they think of the future. There are no such buildings in this part of the country as the banks are erecting in the west, not only in Edmonton and Winnipeg but in the whole of the west. Even in the dull little town of Rossland the Bank of Montreal have a magnificent building. I was in Dauphin last summer and the people were claiming that there was a population of about 2,000 and 2,500. The most optimistic I met stated that there were at least 2.500 people. Dauphin is so situated that it is going to be a very important point. There is no doubt that it will be the distributing centre for the people all the way up to the Pas and Winuipegosls and I certainly think from what I ascertained as to rhe values of western land last fall that $0,000 for a lot in Dauphin is a very reasonable price. I am judging that from my own personal observation on the ground.

I think my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Zimmerman) forgets that he struck Edmonton just at the top of the boom and that the boom has fallen out. You cannot judge of the Northwest by boom prices, and I do not think it is fair to advance an argument of that kind especially when my hon. friend got the price just at the top of the boom. Everybody knows that you can buy land at Edmonton at a very much less figure than my hon. friend has quoted.
ilr. ZIMMERMAN. Not in the centre of the city.
Mr. "WARD. Well, this same land. My object in rising is to ask the Minister of Public Works if he will comply with what my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrop) asked him ; that is as to What transactions had taken place with this property in Dauphin during the past year?

My hon. friend (Mr. Ward) will see how impossible it would be to do that. I would have to send out and have a search made of the records of the registry office. We have no information whatever with regard to previous transactions.

My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has stated that the government have decided to purchase this property. The Minister of Justice must have that very information in his office. The abstract must-have been returned by the
solicitor who is looking after the title for the government. Therefore, if my hon. friend would send down to the Minister of Justice he could probably get the information that has been asked for by my hon. friend from East Hastings. The Minister of Public Works has stated that they must look to the future of places like Dauphin in erecting these public buildings, but I would suggest to him that it is not necessary that we should allow the sellers of property to look to the future and fix their prices about ten years in advance, which, I venture to say, has been done in this instance.

The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Zimmerman) has not answered the argument of the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron). All he has done has been to take a particular instance of undue inflation in the value of property. May I ask the minister whether there were any other sites considered and at what price ?

The only knowledge I have is that information came to the department that this site which was suitable could be obtained. A gentleman experienced in land values was sent there to make an examination and also to get values of other lots in the business part of the town which would be similarly situated. He reported that this was an exceedingly good lot and that the price was reasonable as compared with the values of other lots in the town.
Is there a copy of that gentleman's report? If we had that we would throw a good deal of light on the former value of this property.
I presume that report is in the department and I will have it here on Monday.
Were there negotiations with any one else ?
What strikes one from the east in going to the west is the value put on lots.
Whan he wants to buy them.

I happened to be in Edmonton on two occasions a few years ago. At the time of my first visit the Bank of Montreal had purchased a lot 50 by 300 feet for $15,000. A gentleman whom I knew took an option on a similar lot at the same price. I expressed surprise and said I would be afraid to take it. On my second visit I inquired about his transaction and was informed that the option had expired but that it was a bad thing for him as the lot had since been sold for one half more. The same thing applies in proportion to all of the western towns which are growing

and, of course, if we come to compare these prices with prices in a town like Belleville, they seem very high. I think it was the banks that set the pace in Edmonton.

1 also asked the other day on what principle the government established public buildings in the different constituencies. In looking at these votes for Manitoba buildings it would appear that they are erected only in constituencies represented by followers of this government. We find public buildings in Brandon, Dauphin, Emerson, Neepawa, Selkirk, St. Boniface and Winnipeg, all represented by supporters of the present government. That may be a coincidence, but my belief is that it is not. The hon. member from Selkirk (Mr. S. J. Jackson) referred to one of the members here as coming from Ontario and not being able to understand the value of land for public buildings in western towns. I claim to be fairly familiar with land values in all Manitoba towns and I have no hesitation, while I am not opposing the building of a post office in Dauphin, in saying that $6,000 for this lot is an excessive jirice. Dauphin is not a very big place, it is a railway divisional point, but not a railway centre ; only the Canadian Northern Railway goes into it.
The member for Hamilton was exceedingly unhappy in referring to the post office at Winnipeg. If the member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) had been here he would not have allowed him to speak as he did. He knew very well that the post office in Winnipeg had to be placed next the ' Free Press ' office no matter what it cost. The ' Free Press ' is owned very largely by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton). While we are not going into that there is a very nice story in connection with that affair. The post office building had to be placed so near the 1 Free Press ' office that a light-well had to be placed between the two buildings. This is an exceedingly extravagant price, $6,000 for that lot 75 by 132 feet, even if it is in the very centre of Dauphin.
It is in the centre, where the old post office was.
Grant that, but the land was still not worth $6,000, and I do not think it helps matters to say it is where the old post office was because that land would not be so very valuable.
Might I also urge on the minister to lay down some settled principle on which he intends to proceed in the erection of public buildings in the west?
I thought I had doue that two or three times already.

Not in my hearing and I have been listening attentively for it. There are many growing towns in that country which will have considerable population in the near future, and I think the Mr. PATERSON
minister will find himself in all kinds of difficulties unless he can lay down some definite principle which will involve the postal and customs revenue or other indication of the business likely to be done in the building.

I could hardly be expected upon such short notice to do what none of my predecessors since confederation, who have erected many public buildings in all parts of Canada, have done. I do not think it is possible to lay down a hard and fast rule, you cannot do that. You have to take into account very many things. We have to take into account not only the population of a place, but the business done and the revenue derived by the government. It may be a small town where the government derives a large inland or customs revenue. It is also fair to consider whether or not considerable sums of public money are being expended in a town. Take a town which is a seaport. With considerable money being expended for harbour work, dredging or wharfs, the claims of that town for the erection of a public building may not be so strong as the claims of a town which is inland and where there is no large expenditure of Dominion moneys. One has to have regard to a great many considerations, so that it is impossible to lay down a hard and fast rule. All I can say is that I am prepared to listen to reasonable representations on behalf of the different cities and towns for the erection of public buildings. I am quite prepared to give careful consideration to any representations which are made by hon. gentlemen opposite as well as to those made by our friends on this side of the House. In the present estimates it will be seen that there are quite a number of public buildings being erected in constituencies represented by our opponents.
Not in Manitoba.

There may be some reason for that. A large majority of the constituencies in Manitoba are represented by gentlemen sitting on this side of the House, and it may be that the claims of the constituencies represented by our friends opposite have not been very strongly pressed upon the attention of the Minister of Public Works. However, the reasonable requirements of the people in all sections of the country will receive careful consideration.
I understand then, that patronage is to enter very largely into this question ?
I have not said so.
Then, the other principle which the minister has laid down is the revenue derived by the government. Am I to take that as the principal reason he adduced ?	.
I said that a large number of considerations had to be taken into account.
Then I think we may conclude generally that the matter is to be left to the discretion of the minister.
To the sense of justice of the minister.
Is this building on the main street of the town?
It is on Burrows avenue.
There are two business streets; one is Gartmore Road and the other Burrows Avenue.
What is the customs revenue of the place ?
The post office revenue is $4,310.
Customs revenue last year was $10,000.
The present post office building is rented ?
Yes, at $275 rental.
What other demands, if any, have been made for this building, by whom and when, and how long has this project been before the department ?
As long ago as 1906 a memorial was presented by the Board of Trade. It has also been pressed by the town council and the municipal council of Dauphin.
May I ask the hon. member for Dauphin if the present post office building covers the whole 75 feet frontage ?
No.
How much vacant land is there on either side of it ?
The present post office building has about 30 feet frontage, and there is a vacant space on each side.

So that there is 45 feet vacant of the 75 feet. It looks strange, if this is such a desirable property and is worth this large amount, that 45 feet of it should have stood idle for years. One would have thought land of such great value would be built up completely.
Is the present building a two-story building ?
Yes.
Is it occupied for any other purpose than a post office ?
The postmaster lives in it.
Has the government bought the building as well ?
No. It is a frame building, and is not safe for a post office.
The owner of the building has sold the lot to the government ?

Yes. It has been the expectation of the postmaster for several years to sell this property for post office purposes.
Emerson public building, $3,500.
This is a revote. The site has been purchased. It has a frontage of 60 feet on Main street by 140 feet on Dominion street. The building is required for post office and customs purposes.
How much was paid for the lot ?
What is the population of Emerson ?
That is not a very flourishing town, is it ?
It is an ambitious town.
What is the total estimated cost ?

The last three sessions of this parliament I have been making a claim for the little town of Carman. I have no objection to money being spent so long as the people are getting good value. I am only too anxious to see that Manitoba gets its share of the large public expenditure. Carman has a population of over 2,000. It is one of the oldest, and I think it is the prettiest town in southern Manitoba. It has three lines of railway running into it- the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Jim Hill railroad. Therefore I am quite within the mark when I call it a railway centre. It is a very convenient and necessary place for a port of entry. It has sent here petition after petition asking for some consideration out of the public chest but without success. Last year, as you will find by referring to Vol. 3 of ' Hansard,' I got the promise that this town would get some consideration or at least that its claim would be looked into. That promise has not yet been fulfilled. The town of Carman certainly deserves more consideration, especially when we see what other towns in Manitoba are getting. Last year its postal revenue was $3,415.38 whereas the postal revenue of Emerson is only $1,120, yet it is getting a public building that will cost some $20,000. Neepawa has a postal revenue of $4,783.30. Selkirk has a population of 2,700 and a postal revenue of $2,385.80. Dauphin has a postal revenue of $4,310.55. In my opinion the town of

Carman is better entitled to a building for a post office and custom bouse than any town in Manitoba.
In what constituency is it ?
In the constituency of Macdonald which I have the honour to represent.
Is there any public building in the county ?

Only a provincial building, the lands title office. I might make a further claim on behalf of Manitoba as a province. I have a list of the appropriations for the little province of Nova Scotia but it would take too long to read it. Comparing these appropriations with those for Manitoba and the revenue in each province, I do not think that the province of Manitoba is getting a fair deal. All we ask is fair treatment. All we ask is to be dealt with as the other provinces. I hope that the Minister of Public Works will consider the claims of Carman and give me at least the further promise that these claims will be looked into and an appropriation made.

I am very happy to say. in ail sincerity, that I shall look carefully into the claims of Carman. My hon. friend cannot expect me to promise that an appropriation will be made. That is a matter for consideration.
Should the minister find that the conditions are as reported, will he make an appropriation for the town ?

speechtext: Would not that be bribery ?
Not at all. If it would be bribery in any direction, it would be for the benefit of the government.
A part of this has been spent. What was that for ?
The site has been bought.
Was it paid for ?
It appears in the statement up to the 31st of March, $1,500. I presume it has been paid for. An order in council was passed on the 27th of August last for the purchase of the site at $1,000.
Several years ago Emerson was a town of over 3.000 but to-day it is down to 000. I saw a public building put up in that town which cost $125,000 and is offered at $25,000.
That is a doleful picture.

I only mention it to remind the minister that it was not because of any great business ability that he was able to purchase a lot for $1,000 in a town Mr. STAPLES.
of that importance. It is an unfortunate fact, as every one knows who has been in Emerson more than once, that it has greatly decreased in recent years both in population and in the value of land. It is on the boundary line, but, for some reason, which may be known better to the people there than to outsiders, the town has not been growing. I do not know that the minister would be doing wrong in providing a building there, because, as it is on the boundary, and an important customs port, a custom office as well as a post office are needed.
It may be of interest to the hon. member to know that for nine months of the last fiscal period the customs income was $15,677.

It is a place at which a great many Americans come in, bringing settlers' effects, and so will be an important port of entry notwithstanding the fact that there is not a very large village there at the present time. And I suppose that this building will house the post office and customs house and also the inland revenue.
The post office and customs house, but as to the inland revenue I am not sure.
If it were so, it would be all the stronger justification for the expenditure. What is the amount to be spent?

When I was making my remarks, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) suggested that, if the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) made the promise I asked, it would be considered bribery.
Some of our friends opposite might so regard it.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) speaks of bribery in such a case, what would he consider the proper name to apply to his own case when there has been spent in his constituency, from the year 1897 down to 1900, the sum of $2,145,030.13? On the ground on which he takes exception to my request, I should say this was wholesale bribery actually committed.
Neepawa public building, $10,000.

This is a revote, and is to make provision for a public building. The site has been purchased.
Mr. W? J. ROCHE. What is the size of the lot?
I have not the figures before me. But the size of the building is 65 feet by 48 feet.
The lot is 99 feet square.
What was the price?
$3,000. It is made up of lots 14, 15 and 16, on the corner of Mountain avenue and Cameron street.
Have there been protests against the selection of the site for this building?
I have not heard of any and my deputy tells me he has not heard of any.
Perhaps the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) can tell us?
No documentary evidence of it has been filed with me.
That so? I would like to read a little article that appeared in the Liberal paper of his own town, his own political organ.
Sure about that ?
About what? That it is the Liberal organ?
You said my political organ.
Well, I am not going to say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crawford) entirely owns it.
Don't say anything that is not according to the facts.
Does the hon. gentleman deny that it is supporting him?
I am not making this speech.
And that he is supporting it as well? When was the site purchased?
It was authorized by order in council in 1906, and steps immediately taken to purchase it after that.
This was the particular lot authorized to be purchased?
Yes, the order in council always specifies the lot.

Here is the protest of the Liberal ' Press,' of Neepawa:
The post office site.
There is no getting away from the fact that there is very general and deep-rooted dissatisfaction with the site chosen for a federal government building to be erected in Neepawa for postal and customs purposes. It will be generally admitted that .any public building should be so located as to be convenient for the greatest number of people and especially for those who use it most. A centre of population is desirable, but a centre of business is much more essential. In neither respect,
however, does the site chosen in Neepawa fill the bill. It is so far north as to inconvenience almost everybody in the two south-end wards and not far enough to be any more convenient to the north-end people than if it were two or three blocks farther south, where it would have been in the business centre and near the territorial centre as well as the centre of imputation.
The site chosen never will be central. Conditions are such that there can be no clustering of business around the post office, while two-thirds of the population and four-fifths of the business is now south of the site.
That is a pretty large proportion.'
The probabilities are that, five years hence, four-fifths of the population and nine-tenths of the business will be south of it. It is, and always will be, as unsatisfactory to the farmers as to the business man, for no matter which end of town a farmer may wish to do business at, he must go a considerable distance to the post office.
Perhaps that will refresh the memory of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie as to whether there have been protests. The town is divided into two portions, the north and the south. The major portion is the south. The north end is where the station is located, from which the street runs up to the business part of the town, perhaps, three-quarters of a mile. The business houses are almost entirely on the west side of this street, and it is on this street that the site has been selected. I think I am correct in saying that, except a butcher shop, grocery, Chinese laundry and implement warehouse, and a couple of blocks down from this post office site, a hotel, there are no business houses on that side of the street. I am personally aware that there has been great dissatisfaction with this choice of a site. I have seen many articles, not only in the Conservative newspapers but in Liberal newspapers as well, condemning the choice of these lots. I notice that the minister says that the order in council was passed in February, 1906. Right opposite this site is what is called the Liberal club room. There is a lot and a half in that property, and it cost $600, or at the rate of $400 a lot. The property bought for the post office cost at the rate of $1,000 a lot.
Was that a corner lot?
I am not sure. At any rate it was nearer the south side which was the business side of the town.
When was that purchased?

The article I am reading was in 1906. I will tell you what this lot cost when it was bought. By looking up the land titles office records it will be found that on January 5, 1906, this lot for the post office was purchased from W.

J. Mathers for $2,000, and it was transferred by him to W. J. Harrison on March 30, 1906. In less than two months afterwards the property was transferred from Harrison to the King for $3,000 ; in less than two months it had increased from $2,000 to $3,000. It may be significant that the hon. member who represents the constituency and who lives in the north end of this town has property north of the site of this post office. The business end of the town is almost entirely south, and businessmen, irrespective of politics, protested against this site. This article in the press says the site is inconvenient, not only for businessmen, but for farmers as well. This Liberal paper states it never will be in the centre of the town, and great dissatisfaction has exised. I think some other influence than the benefit of the town and of the business interests has been at work in the selection of this site.

I would like to ask the hon. member for Portage la Prairie if any public meetings were called in regard to the selection of this site for a post office, and did the people say where they would like it to be situated?

There was a public meeting called at which I was present myself, and one of our Tory friends said that if they had the control of the situation they would place it opposite the land titles office, away at the other end of the town and away from the business centre. I admit there was a division of opinion over the location of the post office, but the post office was placed as near the centre of the towm as possible. Now, some of the largest business interests in the town are half a mile north of the site selected. The south side of the town, where the hon. gentleman says the business interests are largely located, is not right, as they are not more than a third of that distance from this site, not more than a quarter of a mile, if it is that. Now, one of the sites that some of our friends wanted to get was only 172 feet from this present site, but that was going to cost $6,000 instead of $3,000. I may say that I had a good deal to do in advising the selection of this site, and I thought it was not wise to pay $6,000 for a site when you could get one for $3,000, and when a large percentage of the people were in the opposite direction. I think I have one of the largest business concerns in the town and that is half a mile north of this location. We have three business places at the north end, half a mile north of this site, while the furthest place on the south is not more than a quarter of a mile away. But the main business firms have not more than five or six hundred feet to travel to reach this post office, while we on the north have to travel almost three quarters of a mile. To satisfy all interests and to save expense, I advised that the post office be Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
placed as near as possible in the centre of the settled portion of the town, and that is where it is. The hon. gentleman, in talking of the business places, did not mention the business places on that side of the street at all. There is the Union Bank that cost $20,000 on that side of the street, with in 500 feet of where this post office is to be located. We have one of the largest hardware stores in any country town in Manitoba on that side of the street, two harness shops and one of the largest and best hotels in Canada on that side of the street, within 300 feet of the post office site, and one of the best livery stables in the country very close to it. There is no question as to the location of the site being central. I thought it was wise to save $3,000 in the purchase of that site, as it was only 172 feet from the point where a great many thought it should be situated. I think that our hon. friends opposite will be liberal enough now to give us some credit for trying to save public money.

I hardly think it was economy that influenced the hon. member in recommending this site, especially as the board of trade in his own town protested strongly against the selection of the present site. * Who compose the board of trade? The business men of the town. Are they not the better judges? I do not think the hon. member was influenced solely by a desire to save $2,000 or $3,000 in the purchase of a site, when the business men of the town who desired the location to be where it would suit business interests, protested strongly against the present site.
Did they want the $6,000 site purchased?

I do not know what the price was but they recommended a different site. The hon. gentleman is entirely astray when he says this location is in the business centre. I think his constituents will be surprised when they read his remarks in the ' Hansard,' unless he revises them considerably before the 1 Hansard ' comes out ; they will be surprised to see the defence he has put up for the recommendation of this site.

I would like to make a further statement. The only protest I have received in an official wav in regard to this site was a largely signed petition from a large percentage of the people of the town, urging that if there was any protest filed in regard to this site no change should be made and that the site should remain where it is. I have that petition in my desk and it is largely signed
From the people on the south side?

The south side and the north side. I would like to say in re-

gard to the board of trade in the town of Neepawa that one of the strongest Conservatives in that town said : We might as well be honest about it, if the Conservatives had their way we would have it down opposite the lands titles office, which is entirely away from the business centre of the town.
Is that what is called Mitchell Corner ?
No.
Did the hon. gentleman favour that personally ?

Yes, personally I favoured that but the majority of the people thought it should go on the main street. The Mitchell corner is one row of lots off the main street. Personally I would have favoured that because it would have been just as central and as cheap.

The hon. gentleman speaks of the northern part of the town being three quarters of a mile from the post office. As a matter of fact, has not the business in the northern part of the town been decreasing and is it not becoming centred down south of the post office ?
All the elevators, the grain business, outside of some shipping in cars, and the milling business are at the north location.
I notice that there were $12,000 voted last year. Part of that was spent. For what purpose ?
Up to the 31st December last year there was an expenditure of $3,437.56. That included $3,000 for the site, the remainder being expended for survey, legal and travelling expenses, advertising, &c.
How is it that you have only marked $2,000 here as being expended because the revote is $10,000 ?
There were a couple of thousand dollars voted for the site earlier.
The hon. gentleman is not well informed.
I would like to say that there were $2,000 voted before this.
Not last year ?
I am not talking about last year.
The year before.
But there were $2,000 spent.
There were $2,000 voted the year before and $12,000 last year; that would make $14,000 altogether.
Well then $2,000 must have been spent. For what purpose ?
That goes into the purchase of the land.
The land was not purchased in this year. It could not be because that would be a revote and it would lapse at the expiration of the financial year.

The order in council authorizing the purchase of the land was passed on the 3rd of February, 1905. I think it probable that the land was purchased in the then current year; but at all events in 1905-6.
Then that money was spent in that year. There were $12,000 voted last year in addition. There has been $2,000 of that spent since. How was that spent ?
Three thousand odd dollars in all that should have been spent.
But the estimates say that the first $2,000 was spent.
Does the hon. gentleman want that information ?

Yes. I notice that a great many times, whether the minister understands it or not, he does not take the trouble to give the House the information. I think there is a principle involved that we should deal with at some time or other. We vote money from year to year which is either needed or not needed. If it is not needed it should not be voted because it is always on the estimates and is a standing bribe whenever an election is called up. We do not seem to be able to ascertain *how much was spent. There has been a portion of the vote spent but when we ask how much was spent and what proportion was spent for the site we. are unable to get that Information. This is the same as some other items. With respect to the last item that we dealt with we were told that a site was purchased but we could not find out what the expenditure was. We ought to be able to get all this information.

tleman the information as to the cost but I want the hon. gentleman to understand that when he asks me and I do not know what should be the proper information I do not give it. I do not profess to tell what I do not know.
and therefore the other $2,000 must have been spent and he has not given an account of the way in which it was spent. Therefore the other $2,000 must have been spent and the minister has not given us an account of where it was spent.

Who was the middleman ? It seems that the property increased in value $1,000 in a few months.
I do not think it follows that there was any middleman. I have not heard of any.

How are the places iu Manitoba in which buildings are to be erected, selected ? When I was in the west I saw some fine towns that are not mentioned here, like Hamiota, Carman, Mani-tou and others, some larger than these.
You would condemn us very much if we attempted to put public buildings in all the tows at once.
But some of these towns are larger than those mentioned here.
In which one would you say I should recommend the erecting of a public building ?
Take Carman, for instance, a splendid town.
I have said I am going to consider that.
The trouble is the minister has been considering all of these. Will he give us a promise that he will include any one of these buildings we have suggested in the supplementary estimates ?
I am not in a position to say what will be contained in the supplementary estimates.

It is only necessary to compare the cost of this lot in Neepawa, $3,000, with the cost of the lot in Dauphin, $6,000, to see that either the price of the Dauphin site is extravagant or that an inferior and unsuitable site has been chosen at Neepawa. I have the highest opinion of Neepawa, it is a smart, thriving town ; in fact I was sorry to part with that town when they took it away from old Marquette because it always gave me a good majority. When it was in Marquette no public building was granted to it. I have also a high opinion of Dauphin. They are much the

same in population and I am sure that no one will say that Neepawa is surpassed by Dauphin. I also think that town property is as high in Neepawa as in Dauphin.
What do you think a really good site in Neepawa should cost ?
I would not place value on it as I do not live there. But, the member has stated that tor a site which I believe was where the townspeople desired it, $6,000 or $7,000 was asked.
How can you give such a close value for Neepawa and not for Dauphin ?
I am drawing a comparison between the two towns. My own private opinion is that the Dauphin price was exorbitant.

Would my hon. friend say that $0,000 which some gentleman wanted for the other site in Neepawa, which my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) declined to recommend, would be reasonable ?

1 do not know where the other lot is. The Board of Trade selected a certain site. That board is composed of business men and the site recommended by them was not selected, but another site was selected for which I claim the price paid was unfair because the member for Portage la Prairie says the ordinary value is from $3,000 to $6,000 for these lots.
The population of Neepawa in 1905 was 300 more than that of Dauphin, the figures being Dauphin 1,530, and Neepawa, 1,895.
The population of Dauphin now is represented to be 2,500 people.

We must take the census. Neepawa is more of a railway centre than Dauphin, as it has both the Canadian Northern and Canadian Pacific Railway. It all goes to show the exorbitant price we have to pay for the building of a post office on Buxtows Avenue.
The site for which $6,000 was asked was only 66 by 90 feet.

I see that $167 was paid for surveying the lot and making a plan. The minister gave us that information last yeai\ Does not that seem to be a very extravagant figure for surveying and making a plan of a village lot ?
It would strike me as high unless there was some exceptional reason for it.
The surveyor may have had to come from Brandon, as there was no surveyor at Neepawa.
How far is that ?
About a hundred miles.
It seems to me totally absurd when compared with transactions of that kind in this part of the country.
It is more than the usual cost, which runs from $25 to $50. It was paid in 1905. I will take occasion to have it looked into, and I will bring information as to the particular reasons for it.
A surveyor in our country will go ten or fifteen miles and survey a hundred acres, running the lines and making a plan, for from $5 to $7.

In addition to surveying the lot, the surveyor had to take the levels of the ground in order that the plans might be prepared at Ottawa, and to test the ground to see what the foundation would be like.

I may say that the surveyor was no friend of ours. He is one of the prominent surveyors of Canada. I can assure our friends that there was no graft in connection with it.
Mi-. W. J. ROCHE. What is the surveyor's name ?
Moses McFadden.
What is the estimated cost of the building exclusive of the site ?

$41,000. The total estimated cost, including the site, is $44,437.
Mi-. W. J. ROCHE. I see by ' Hansard ' of last session that Mr. Bennett asked :
' What does the minister intend to spend on this Neepawa building ? ' And Mr. Fisher, who was acting minister at the time, stated : 'I should think about $25,000, but the plans are not yet prepared.'
The contract price was $28,000, and the additional expenditure is for the cost of the site, the heating, electric wiring, fittings, lock boxes, sidewalks, fencing, &c.

It seems to me that an expenditure of $44,000 for a public building in a small village like that is extravagant. In the province of Ontario you will find. dozens of small villages of that size a ad larger that have had no expenditure for that purpose and are not asking for it. It seems to me that these large expenditures in small villages, unless there is a strong probability of their growing to be large places, are not justifiable.
I should explain that this building is to be for a post office, examining warehouse and militia armouries as well.

What militia have you got there ? In these votes for armouries we should have the Minister of Militia present to give us information as to the size of the force and why these expenditures are needed. In the towns and villages of Ontario we have no such expenditures. We only have them in a few of the large cities. But if it he right to put up these public buildings in these small towns in the new provinces, it is right that we should do so in the old provinces. And if it be not good policy in the old provinces, it is not in the new. There should be no discrimination. And whenever we are called to vote any expenditure for militia purposes we should have the Minister of Militia present.
There are two rifle companies there with their equipment and a cadet corps as well. They require some place in which to store their arms.
What is the cadet corps ?
They are boys from fourteen to sixteen years of age.
How many men ?

Eighty men and thirty boys.
Selkirk public building Manitoba, $30,000.
This is a revote of $10,000 and a new vote of $20,000. It is a two-story brick building with stone basement, 44 feet broad and 48 feet deep. The site cost $2,000.
The sites are coming down. Here is a place a good deal larger than Dauphin, yet the Dauphin site cost $6,000.
Is the contract let?
Yes, it is let to Brown & Garson at $24,000.
Does that include light and heat?
No. The heating'and boiler are estimated at $2,500, electric wiring. $1,000; fittings, $5,000; sidewalks and fencing, $1,000, besides contingencies. Total, including the site, $40,111.60.
Last year we were led to believe by the acting minister (Mr. Fisher) that the expenditure would be $20,000.
The cost of the building.
No, the total expenditure. Yet we are now up to $40,000.
We should have fuller explanation. Last year the acting minister (Mr. Fisher), in reply to the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), said :

Tenders have just been received. The site cost $2,000. It is 58 x 150 feet at the southeast corner of Manitoba and Main streets. The building will cost about $20,000.
His reply would lead the House to believe that that was the total amount of expenditure. When we get an explanation we should have the whole thing in detail.
I am giving it to the hon. gentleman. I lnyve given the amount of the contract, the cost of heat and boilers, electric wiring, &c.
When we come to an item such as this and the minister gives an estimate of the cost, we take it for granted that that will be the whole cost.
I draw a distinction between a contract for the erection of a building and the total cost, including fittings, &c.

We have been deceived in every case. Up to the present every year the answer has been practically the same. Here is an instance where, instead of the estimates given by the minister, the property is to cost $50,000 to $100,000 more. Is it not a fact that when the total work is completed it will cost a great deal more than the estimate?
My hon. friend is aware that when we ask for an amount in the estimates, we do not ask for the whole cost in one year, but ask what is intended to be spent during the current year.
When it is stated that a building will cost so much, does that mean only the portion of the work to be done during that year ?

I take it that that would mean the estimate given by the chief architect to the minister of the cost of the building. But, if nothing else is stated, that would not be supposed to include the cost of the site, heating, wiring and so on.

Does the minister think it a good policy to begin a building such as this and only finish it in three years or so ? Especially, in a little town like Selkirk ? Ordinarily, a building begun in such a place is completed in three months.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. We are asking for enough money to finish the building.

The building was started last November-up to that time, not a stroke of work had been done. The foundation was put in and perhaps two or three feet above that. The work is now going on, and it is expected to be finished in July.
The contract was let in October.

Yes, and I would point out to the hon. member for Grenville

(Mr. J. D. Reid) that two years ago the estimate given by Mr. Hyman was $25,000. The contract was let for $24,000. The owner of the lot asked $3,000 for It. It was a corner lot. At the other end of the same block, the Traders Bank has put up a pressed brick building to cost $30,000. The price asked for the lot was considered too high. Mr. Greenfield, who is In charge of the public works office In Manitoba was sent to Selkirk and inquired as to the value of property there. The owner afterwards offered to take $2,500 but ultimately accepted $2,000, which price was considered satisfactory and the lot was bought. So, there is nothing wrong with the site. There are to be rooms in this building for the Indian office, the inspector of fisheries for Manitoba and Keewatin, the customs office, the forest ranger for the county of Selkirk, and the examiners of masters and mates. Selkirk is the point where these things centre. There will probably be $200,000 or $250,000 worth of shipping there. The population in 1906 was 2,700. The postal revenue for nine months was $2,385, which would be about $3,200 for the year, in Stonewall also, we have a postal revenue nearly as large as that of Selkirk.
It is evident from what the hon. gentleman (Mr. S. J. Jackson) has stated that the Minister of Public Works of two years ago deceived us as to the cost of this building.
Why, the contract was let for $1,000 less than he estimated.
But we understand that this was to be the total cost, including the purchase of site and equipment of the building.
The hon. gentleman, perhaps did not inquire particularly as to these other things.

It is not so very long since I read a speech of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. S. J. Jackson) in which he took credit for inducing the government to construct this building. And he did not stop at that, but went on to claim credit for every mile of railway constructed in his constituency. I began to wonder if he thought himself Sir Thomas Shaughnessy. He took credit for the snagboat that runs up and down the river. You would think he had more influence with this government -evidently he has considerable-than any other member.	[DOT]

I said that four years ago in one municipality there was not a single mile of railway, and that last November, nearly 100 miles of the Grand Trunk Pacific had been graded and would soon be ironed, and also that there were 40 272J
miles of a new line of railway forced upon the Canadian Pacific Railway because the Grand Trunk was the shorter line. There was also the Canadian Northern, making a total of 150 miles of road that was not there when I was elected four years before. I certainly took credit for supporting the government that brought about these improvements.	i

I suppose the inference the hon. gentleman's hearers would draw was that, if he had not been elected, the Grand Trunk Pacific, when it came to the line of his constituency, would skip it, and not construct a line there at all.
The people appreciate the expenditure that the government have made in that section of the country in the last four years.

I think the hon. member for Selkirk had better move round all over the country, as he seems to take railways with him wherever he goes. In the matter of heating for these public buildings, will public tenders be asked ?
Yes.
The minister assures us that the tenders will be asked for the heating in every case ?
I should say in every case-yes.
Will these be public tenders ?
Tenders will be asked from different people in the business.
That is, it will not be public competition, but restricted to party friends ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) can see that the advertising would be out of all proportion to the cost. I can assure the hon. gentleman and the committee that we will take care to get competitive prices.

I want to say a word with reference to the controversy that has arisen here. As I understand the purpose of asking these questions, and the reason why we expect proper answers to be given, as near as they can be given by the Minister of Public Works, is this : When you propose an item for an expenditure in a particular place the first question we ask is : What is the country to be committed to, what is it going to cost ? We mean by that, What is the cost of the whole undertakings, what will it stand the country ? The minister gives an estimate of what he is going to ask -parliament to vote, that is intended

to inform the House what the country is being committed to in toto, not the amount of the contract, not the cost of the land, not the price of the site only. We must take that into consideration, but that is not all. For instance, the minister might ask for an expenditure of $100,000. Now if he told us we were committing the country to the expenditure of $200,000, does he think that parliament would give it ? Not at all. Therefore we naturally ask every time: What is going to be the cost of this in toto ? When we look at the discussions last year, we find this year that the expenditure" have crept up in almost every case beyond what we were told last year they would be, they do not accord with the facts that are given us this year as to the actual expenditure. In every case the expenditure has largely exceeded what we were told. Are we not justified then in saying that the House was misled, absolutely misled ? Because we gave the vote last year on the understanding that the country was only committing itself to the expenditure of so much money, while we find this year that the expenditure has increased by thousands of dollars over what we were told it would be. Of course we understand that the minister only gives us an estimate and there will be some difference, but we ought to have a pretty close estimate, otherwise we would not be justified in commencing an expenditure of $25,000 if it afterwards turned out to reach $50,000 or $75,000. That is why we are particular to get this information at the commencement of the undertaking.

My hon. friend will see how that occurred. Last year the question was asked as to what the building would cost, and the minister said: Tenders are being received. Now when tenders are received for a building the architect always estimates what the building will cost, and when tenders come in they can be compared with the estimates. No doubt that is what the minister meant at that time.

No, I cannot admit that. In every instance we ask when the first estimate is placed before the House: What is this going to cost ? That means what is the whole undertaking going to cost. We do not mean what the land is going to cost, what the cost will be according to the plans, or the contracts, but we want to know what will be the entire cost.

I certainly understood the hon member for Grenville to say that when the minister was asked as to the cost of this building he replied that tenders had been received, and the cost was estimated to be so and so. Now that_would apply to the cost of the building for which the tenders were received.

House in committee on Bill (No. 151) respecting the Grand Trunk Branch Lines Company.-Mr. Crawford.

Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to be good enough to allow the Bill to stand.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
