House in committee on Bill (No. 20) respecting the Belleville-Prince Edwrard Bridge Company.-Mi-. Porter.

I think that the hon. member who is in charge of this Bill (Mr. Porter) is not here. Still, if you consent to put a Bill through in the absence of the promoter in one case you ought to do it in all cases. He should be here to attend to the Bill.
Has the Bill been printed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Apparently it has.

There was some question with regard to this Bill as to the rates to be charged. We discussed it one evening at some length. The hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) was interested in it and we had quite a discussion as to the rates payable to and fro. That night

we got to a certain point when it was suggested that we leave it over until the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) was here.
Yes, and he is not here to-night.
I have no position to take on it, but I want it to be put in proper shape; that is all.

I have no position to take either. I would be willing that the bridge should be free. In the Private Bills Committee we agreed on a tariff. I have not the Bill as reprinted before me to know if it is correctly reprinted or not. The suggestion that was made when the Bill was up before was that the tariff should be submitted to the Lieutenant Governor in Council instead of the Governor in Council, and the hon. member for West Hastings expressed himself to me as being perfectly satisfied with that change. It was said that it was a provincial measure and should be dealt with bv the provincial legislature, and it was suggested that the tariff should be made subject to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario. The hon. member for West Hastings said that he was perfectly willing that should be done. So am I.
I am not going to make any objection to it.

I took the exception to this legislation. It seems to me that we are certainly invading the jurisdiction of the local legislature. This was done a few years ago and this is merely an amendment. I thought then and I still think that this parliament should not come down to che discussion of the tariff or tolls over a highway bridge that is wholly and unquestionably within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. I made the suggestion that instead of section 8 there should be substituted a section placing upon the company the onus of applying to the provincial government to have the tariff approved of. I do not think that this section should ever appear on the statute-book of the parliament of Canada. The only way to remedy the matter is to have a general clause to enable the company to have such a tariff as may be approved" by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council of the province of Ontario. I think that in justice to this parliament that amendment should be made and that we should pay some attention to the requirements of the British North America Act.

The amendment suggested by my hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) that the words ' Lieutenant-Governor ' be inserted in the Bill, I suppose, would overcome the objection that has been mentioned by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). As I
understand this amendment, as proposed by the hon. member for Prince Edward, it is that the tolls should be subject to the order of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, which practically means that it gives absolute control to the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario instead of the Governor General in Council, as is now in the Bill ; so that if the word 'Lieutenant ' Is inserted in the Bill it meets the objection that the hon. member for Westmoreland has stated, does it not ?

No, for the reason that this parliament, by this legislation, undertakes to fix the tolls. It is true that there is a clause which says that the Governor General has to approve of the tolls which are charged. If you were to say the ' Lieutenant Governor in Council,' that might in a measure remedy or obviate the difficulty, but it seems to me that we should not even attempt to fix the tolls, but that we should have a general clause stating :
Providing, however, that the rates and tolls collected and charged shall be subject from time to time to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province of Ontario.
If these rates were established as they are in the Bill, but subject to the Lieutenant Governor in Council, would that not meet the case?
This puts it into the hands of the company as to whether they shall apply or not, and they may never apply.
But cannot the people apply to the Lieutenant Governor in Council ?
No, I submit not ; that is the point which I have in view. .

By adding the word [DOT] Lieutenant ' before Governor in Council we would bring this within the jurisdiction of the local government, which would meet the wishes of the hon. member and carry out what I am trying to state the Bill should be.

I do not wish to oppose the IJill, but I am objecting to this on principle. It seems to me the parliament of Canada should not undertake to fix rates and tolls on a provincial highway, and it should never be set out in the statutes of Canada that there shall be charged so much for a baby carriage, so much for a horse and carriage, so much for an adult, &c. I would expunge every word of this tariff and substitute a general clause empowering this bridge company to collect such tolls as from time to time may be approved of by the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province of Ontario. My hon. friend's suggestion to insert the word ' Lieutenant ' would not remedy it, because

you were here fixing the tolls, and If they are not satisfactory to the people and are satisfactory to the company there is no redress for the people unless, indeed, this company choose to apply from time to time to the provincial government.

But you may do as you have done in several cases, make the tolls subject to be revised from time to time by the Lieutenant Governor in Council. That has been done with several Bills. Wherever we have incorporated companies to build bridges across streams for highway as well as railway purposes we have set out the tolls.
That came within our jurisdiction.
So does this.
I submit not.
It does because we incorporate this company. Why? Because it is passing over a stream of water that is navigable and there is a draw in the bridge to allow boats to pass.

That is not within our jurisdiction although we may usurp those powers. A bridge across a navigable stream does not give jurisdiction to this parliament ; it is within the jurisdiction of the provincial parliament. There are some four or five large bridges over the St. John river and every one that has been built by companies has been built by companies incorporated by the provincial legislature of New Brunswick. The companies obtained the privilege from the Public Works Department of Canada to construct their bridges over a navigable stream.
I think that in the cases of the bridges at Prince Albert and Edmonton we set out the tolls. We did the same with the Victoria bridge and again when the Victoria bridge was enlarged.
That was a railway bridge at Edmonton.

There is provision for a passenger bridge as well. I have always understood, and I think I am correct, that this federal parliament is the only authority that controls the crossing of navigable waters. I think we provided for the tolls over the St. Maurice river when we gave 15 per cent of the cost of all bridges costing over $25,000. We have exercised this right, whether correctly or incorrectly, for many years.

This is not a bridge over a river, but a bridge over an arm of Lake Ontario, a mile wide. The bridge itself is three-quarters of a mile or more in length. There is a swing and vessels of the largest size pass through there. The Bill does not assume to fix arbitrarily a tariff, it simply

fixes a tariff which the companv is not to exceed, and I am instructed that this Bill was on two occasions brought before the provincial authorities who declined to have anything to do with it on the express ground that this parliament alone could deal with it as navigation was involved, and with all due deference to the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) I think he will find that where navigation is involved, as in this case, over a body of water of this size, that this parliament is the only body with jurisdiction.

I contend that this legislation is an -interference with civil rights which is subject to the jurisdiction of the provincial parliament. I also contend that a company of this character asking these privileges or the original privileges should be incorporated by the provincial parliament, and if the bridge goes over a navigable river or even over an arm of the sea, the company has the right to build the bridge thereupon, subject to the approval of tlie Department of Public Works for Canada. There is a provision in the Public Works Act of this Dominion whereby in similar cases and with a similar condition companies can make their applications, and it is for the Public Works Department to determine whether or not the right shall be granted. The mere fact that it has been done in the past does not give us jurisdiction. We have the right where it is a public work for the general benefit of Canada ; I am not going to discuss that point, but if this is proper legislation for the parliament of Canada, it necessarily follows that we have the right to fix the tolls, and the duty is upon us to do so and it should not be left to the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province of Ontario. But my contention is that we have not that right, and that this is a subject matter for the control of the provincial authorities.

I have given the reasons why the conclusion was reached that we had the right, and that this was the only parliament that had the right. Might I remind my hon. friend, who is a lawyer, of the long litigation over the Streams Bill of Ontario ? What was the decision of the Privy Council in that case ? It was that navigable streams were under federal control, and streams that were not navigable were under provincial control.
That does not in any way affect my argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: want to give the special reason. It will be admitted that lands under these waters, or under any navigable stream, belong to the province, and this parliament usurps authority to control or deal with these lands, when it authorizes individuals in the name of a company to place piers or to do anything upon these lands. This parliament has no right to authorize any one to do that, and tjie provincial legislature of New Brunswick has acted properly in claiming jurisdiction for itself by incorporating such companies, giving them the right to deal with the land under the water and authorizing them to seek from the Public Works Department of the Dominion permission to do that in so far as it might in anv way interfere with navigation. The point taken by the Minister of Railways in connection with section 2 is absolutely unanswerable and for the same reason. This Bill is an interference with the property and jurisdiction of the province of Ontario. Although this parliament has seemingly committed the error in the past, I do not think it should extend or perpetuate that error by interfering m any way with the tolls that mav be charged because that would be an interference with civil rights.

In part the hon. gentleman is right and in part wrong. Pie is wrong in saying that as the land belongs absolutely to the province, we have not the right to give the authority asked. Go to Rainy river, that may be dividing this province from a foreign county, but we have given a charter to a company to cross there The land there belongs to the province, but the federal parliament is the only one that can giv e authority to build across there, and we have given the right to build the abutments of the bridge on the land on the Ontario side. We do the same when it is a case of passing from one province to another. It is only the federal parliament that has the authority to give that right.
That is under the express terms of the British North America Act.

If the hon. gentleman's contention is that because the land in the bed of a stream belongs to a province, that deprives us of the right to give authority to build a bridge there, I have given instances where we have given that authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is another feature of interest in this. My hon. frien from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) speaks of this as being distinctly a provincial work.
It strikes me. on the surface that it is. but sometimes we endeavour, whether wisely or not, to withdraw a work from the exclusive jurisdiction of the province by declaring it to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. It does not appear that in this instance that was ever done. It does Mr. EMMERSON.
not appear that in the original charter of this company the work was declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, and the question might arise whether it really has become a work which comes under our Dominion authority at all. I think we would do well, under the circumstances, to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that the Bill be allowed to stand, in the absence' of the hon. gentleman who has it in charge.

House in committee on Bill (No. 153) to incorporate the Saskatchewan Power Company.-Mr. McCraney.

When this Bill was before the committee on a former occasion, the question was raised whether it was not a subject more particularly for provincial legislation. I pointed out that under section 21 of the Saskatchewan Act, the Crown lands of that province are in the Dominion as representing the Crown. Consequently the river bed, the waters of rivers, the shores are vested in the Dominion, and complete jurisdiction over them is in the Dominion parliament and not in the provincial legislature. Since that time I have been handed a letter, written by the Deputy Attorney General of the province of Saskatchewan to Messrs. Smith & Johnston, of this city, who are representing the promoters:
Regina, April 28, 1908. Sirs,-I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 22nd instant in reference to the Saskatchewan Power Company Bill and have also heard from Messrs. Chrysler, Bethune & Larmonth in connection with the matter. Upon consideration of the matter and of the Bill as amended, this province is, I understand, offering no further opposition to the Bill.
Your obedient servant, PRANK FORD,
Deputy Attorney General.

I have serious objection to this Bill because it looks to me as though it were simply got up by a lot of promoters for speculation. There is no proviso that they must commence work immediately.
It simply states that if the powers granted shall expire by non-user during four consecutive years, or if the company does not come into actual operation within three years from the passing of the Act, the charter will lapse. Should we pass this Bill, the town of Saskatoon will be tied up for at least three years from any other possible chance of having any other water-power.

This Bill gives no exclusive right of that sort, and there is no reason at all why any other company could not come here and get similar powers. The


vested rights only come in when the plans are approved by the Governor in Council.

How could you get any other power on the river if a dam is put across it? That will prevent any further power being obtained above, and a dam cannot be placed below because that would spoil the other. I was in Saskatoon last* fall and 1 saw there- a place wherfe I believed power should be developed. Saskatoon is growing very quickly, and to be tied up for three or four years, as it will be if this Bill passes, would be very serious, not only for the town itself, but for other municipalities adjoining, interested in getting water-power. The people out there want this water-power developed, they want all the advantage they can get from it, and we ought to see that the promoters of the Bill undertake to proceed with the work at once. But if we pass the Bill as it is, we shall give these people at least three and probably four years-because all they would have to do would be a few hundred dollars worth of work to entitle them to claim they had begun operations-of absolute control. If there were anything in this Bill which would compel the company to go on with the work at once and spend so many hundred thousand dollars per annum, I would not hesitate to agree to its going through. But the capital is $1,000,000, and for the next four years not even $100 have to be expended. In my opinion this is a piece of legislation that ought not to go through this House, because it would give a body of men an opportunity of peddling the charter around the world and making a lot of money out of it, whereas it only cost them the charges of putting it through this House, while at the same time they are tieing up the water-power for years. Saskatoon will undoubtedly grow and in the next few years it will want this water-power. I protest against this Bill going through in its present shape, and unless a clause is added by which the expenditure shall be proceeded with at once, I would be justified in opposing the Bill.

I do not know whether my hon. friend was in the House the other evening when I read a letter received by me from the city clerk of Saskatoon. The original Bill as introduced in the Senate was forwarded by me to the mayor for consideration of the council, because I knew that this matter had been discussed by them, and there had been some agitation in favour of the municipally developing power. Here is a letter which I have received respecting the Bill as it is now before the House :
I am in receipt of your letter, also your telegram of April 15, and in reply would say that I have been instructed by the city council to write you thanking you for the interest you have taken on the city's behalf in regard to the passing of the Saskatchewan Power
Company's Bill. The council are of the opinion that it would not necessitate the sending of a delegate to Ottawa on Wednesday, the 29th instant, as clause 3 seems to be in keeping with the petition that we forwarded to you some time ago.
When we come to clause 3 the hon. gentleman will see that there has been an attempt to protect the interests of the city by providing that they shall have proper notice of the plans and an opportunity to be heard.

I have no doubt that these gentlemen have gone to the city council and told them that they intended to commence the work at once. I have no doubt that the people want this work to go on immediately. But the hon. gentleman knows that the damming of the river is not a very expensive matter, I suppose $100,000 will construct all the dam that is required for this water-power. If these men are sincere they should not hesitate to go to work and build that dam at once. The river is narrow where they intend doing it, and the banks are so high that the construction of a dam would require but a small expenditure, and they should not hesitate to go to work at once. The hon. gentleman knows very well that immediately this Bill is passed one of these gentlemen will take that charter in his pocket and start for England or some other place and sell it and get a rake-off, and that is all they intend to do with this charter. We should put a clause in this Bill that they shall commence work at once, this summer, and expend $100,000 developing it, otherwise this charter is null and void.

I notice a suspicious circumstance in the fact that among these names is that of the celebrated James R. Stratton who is a past master in this kind of device. They are trying to get hold of this thing as a speculation, and then peddle it around the country and make money out of it. I think the city council of Saskatoon are not paying proper attention to their own interest, otherwise they would not desire that any company should get possession of the only available water-power that is within reasonable distance of the city.
I wish to correct my hon. friend. The gentleman named here is not the Hon. J. R. Stratton, he is another man altogether.
I understood he was out there for some time last summer speculating ; and knowing his operations in Ontario. I naturally concluded that he was engaged in the same business out there.
Perhaps the Minister of Public Works knows if this gentleman is a well known capitalist from New Brunswick.
This James Stratton I think is a lawyer, and was formerly a resident of New Brunswick.
This Mr. Stratton I understand is the gentleman who used to conduct the elections for the Minister of Public Works in New Brunswick.
I think Mr. James Stratton has always been a good Conservative.

In the last local election in New Brunswick this Mr. Stratton came all the way from Saskatoon down to Ottawa, only a week or two before the elections, I understand, at the instance of the Minister of Public Works ; and I understood that he was down in New Brunswick carrying on the campaign.
You must not believe all you hear.
The minister cannot deny it.
Mr. Stratton was in England at the time of the elections in New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the wording of subsection 2 of section 3, which appears to contemplate that the Governor in Council shall, at a particular time and at a particular place, put aside all other things and take up the hearing of this particular matter. It seems to me the procedure contemplated by clause 3 is somewhat unusual. It is not usual but very unusual, for the Governor in Council to grant hearings to any body. There are some exceptional circumstances under which hearings are granted, but all hearings take place before a minister or a committee of ministers. It seems to me that the proper procedure in this case would be that the application for hearing should be to the Minister of Public Works, then he should report to the council, and the Governor in Council could approve. I would like to make that suggestion to my hon. friend, because I think that is the proper procedure in any matter of this kind. It would seem that for parties to fix the date and say that they would appear here, and that the Governor in Council must hear this particular case, is a very unusual proceeding.
I would be willing to adopt any reasonable suggestion of that sort.

I would ask the hon. member (Mr. McCraney) who has charge of this Bill if he would accept an amendment compelling these people to go on with the work during the present year and to expend a certain amount ? or does he intend to insist that the clause should be left as it is so that, practically, the charter may be car-
Mr. BENNETT
ried about for sale and probably the work tied up for the next four years?

The clause which my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) is discussing is the last clause in the Bill. I have not considered, nor have I discussed with the promoters, the question which he has raised. Even if we go on with the consideration of the Bill, I do not suppose we shall reach that clause. When we do reach that clause, I shall probably be able to give information on that subject.
Has the Bill in its present form been submitted to the civic authorities of Saskatoon ?
Yes. I will send the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) a letter which I received from the city council approving of the Bill in its present form.
Did the promoters assure the council of Saskatoon that they would proceed with the work during the present year ?

I cannot inform my hon. friend as to what assurances were given by the promoters to the city of Saskatoon. But the city authorities had before them the Bill with the clause as it is now before the committee.

I think it would be well for the hon. member (Mr. McCraney), in justice to the city of Saskatoon which he has the honour to represent, that he should write to the city authorities at once and bring their attention to this clause, so that we may know that they have been advised of the seriousness of the matter. I, for one, would like to be thoroughly assured that the inhabitants of Saskatoon realize what this may involve. I do not wish to opp.ose the passage of the Bill with the present incorporators, but, on behalf of the people of Saskatoon and of the towns that will be started in that locality, I think there ought to be some assurance that the work will be commenced within a reasonable time. Otherwise, this Bill means the tying up of that whole country in respect of one of its most important public services. I do not know the men who are concerned in this company, except Mr. Stratton. I do not say anything against him personally. I would be just as glad to see Mr. Stratton go through with it as any other man provided we are assured the work will go ahead. But, in view of the seriousness of the matter I hope the hon. member (Mr. McCraney) will to-morrow send a cony of ' Hansard ' to the city authorities of Saskatoon that they may see the little discussion we have had. They can then say whether they are quite satisfied to let the Bill go through.

And what becomes of the argument of the Minister of Public

Works (Mr. Pugsley) and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) with regard to the proper authority to give these privileges ? This seems to be a local affair ; it does not go outside the province. It may cross a navigable stream
No.
Then, if it does not, what argument can be used in this case that will not apply with greater force to the Bill if just dealt with ?

I have been greatly bothered about this Bill. When it was before the committee on a previous occasion ,1 raised this point of the jurisdiction of parliament to deal with the matter. My hon. friend (Mr. MeCraney) who was promoting the Bill called my attention to the fact that by the terms of the Irrigation Act, all the waters of every river in the Northwest, and the bed and shores of every stream are vested in the Crown in right of the Dominion. He raised the question whether the provincial legislature could give authority to erect a dam upon property belonging to the Dominion of Canada. I suggested that he should confer with the Minister of Justice, who was the proper authority to advise on the subject. The hon. gentleman (Mr. MeCraney) has assured me that it is the opinion of the Minister of Justice that the BUI could properly be passed by this parliament. That being so, even though I had some doubt at first, 1 do not see that I should press my views, more particularly as the government of the province of Saskatoon has written, through its Deputy Attorney General, stating that the advisers of the province see no objection to the passing of the Bill.

With reference to that, I remember that there was a dispute about the fisheries in the province of Quebec on the Matane river, if I remember right, it was decided that the foreshores belong to the people.
But the Irrigation Act expressly reserves these rights.
But, once the land is sold, the Act cannot reserve it.
Oh, parliament can do anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there is always danger of error in amending a Bill like this at the table in a hurried way. I have an amendment here which I will not move, as the discussion on the Bill is not likely to be finished to-night, but I will hand it in and I would suggest to my hon. friend (Mr Mc-Craney) that he should look it over and consult the law clerk of the House about it. I propose that, instead of saying that the time and place for hearing shall be fixed by the Governor in Council, the following shall be embodied in the Bill, following the words
' time and place ' in subsection 2 of section 3:-
At which application will he made to the Minister of Public Works for his approval of such plans; and the Minister of Publio Works, after hearing such application, at such time or such other time as may be agreed upon by him, shall report to the Governor in Council, whether in his opinion such plans should be approved, and the Governor in Council may approve of such plans, &c.

St. Boniface public building, $20,000.
['I move that progress be reported.\nProgress reported.']

The site for this building cost $4,500, and it is estimated that the total cost of the building, including site, heating, electric wiring, fixtures, furniture, &c., will be $39,920.82, and this amount which we are now asking is expected to complete the work, including fitting and furniture.
Is this lot in the centre of the town ?
I am not acquainted with the locality. It is on the corner of Pro-vencher avenue and Aulneault street.
What is the size of the lot ?
66 feet on Provencher avenue and 120 feet on Aulneault street.
What is the cost of the fittings ?
Heating and boilers, $2,500 ; electric wiring and fixtures, $1,000; fittings and furniture, $5,000; sidewalks and fencing, $1,500.
The building is erected now ?
The building is pretty well along. There was expended to December 31 last, $19,920. That includes the site.
When will it be completed ?

It is expected to be completed on September 4 next.
Winnipeg-new examining warehouse, $30,-
000.

This is a revote and it is asked to make provision for the erection of a new examining warehouse in the city of Winnipeg. This is to be a very large building four storeys in height, brick and steel, with istone facings, concrete and stone foundations. It is to be fire-proof throughout. In erecting these large buildings for the purposes of the customs examining warehouses, particularly, it has been thought that they should be as near fire-proof as possible.
What is the full cost expected to be ?

The total probable cost, inclusive of the site and heating, electric wiring, fixtures, &c., is estimated at $417,744.59. The amount of the contract is $276,000. The site cost $88,125. The remainder covers the cost of heating, boilers, electric wiring, fixtures, fittings, furniture and sidewalks.
Who has the contract ?
McDiarmid & Co., Limited, Winnipeg.
Who drew the plans ?
They were drawn in the department.
It is strange you have men here capable of drawing plans for a building like this in Winnipeg, while for a shed in Quebec there are no men capable of drawing the plans.
The hon. gentlemen forgets what kind of a shed that is.

I notice that this vote has been up once or twice before. I was in the examining warehouse at Winnipeg last summer, and this new building is certainly not coming any too soon because it is much needed. I think it is a disgrace to the government and the country, and it does not allow the people who have the work to do an opportunity for properly doing it.
I am sure my hon. friend will commend us most highly for endeavouring to wipe out that disgrace or stigma as quickly as possible.

I will, if proper foresight and economy are used in the expenditure of the money. I do not know about the cost of the site. Land, of course, is very high there. I presume that you purpose building alongside of the present building ?

We have endeavoured to have the building erected at the lowest possibly cost consistently with securing a first-class building for the purpose. We asked for tenders in the usual way. There were three tenders received ranging from $276,000 to $319,000, and we accepted the lowest tender.
Will there be any extras ?

Not that I am aware of.
I think the steel alone will cost about $100,000.
Are there any schedule prices ?
No, a lump sum contract.
Where is the site ?
Corner of Rorie street and McDermott avenue.
From whom was the site purchased ?
It was purchased from Wm. Mackenzie, D. D. Mann and Roderick J. Mackenzie.
Was there a commission paid to any one for purchasing it ?
Not that I am aware of.
It was never purchased without a commission.
That is a hard thing to say.
Well, it is only in line with what we have found when we have got the information out.
I have been here for a good many months and I have never heard the suggestion made that there has been any secret commission paid to any person who has bought land as a site for a public building.

In nearly every case we have had this session, the minister has given us the amount of the commission ;
I cannot remember the instances.
Paid to people for buying property for the department ?
Yes, real estate agents. Do you buy land on the Intercolonial Railway for nothing ?
My hon. friend does not suggest
That you are as bad as they are with reference to the purchase of pr< perty on the Intercolonial Railway. You have a reputation that is a hundred per cent worse.
The minister has a nice way of putting it when he says there is no commission paid. Take the Transcontinental Railway. I will not refer to that.

I would ask my hon. friend who has taken his seat (Mr. Sprouie) to point out a single instance in which the Department of Public Works has been shown to have paid a commission upon the purchase of land.
Were not commissions paid for the purchase of this property on Mackenzie avenue ?

A man was appointed specially to act for the government. I do not understand that the employment of a person to buy land, and the open payment of a commission, as was done then, is what was referred to.
That is what my hon. friend refers to.
That is not what he says.
Yes.

We have the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) explaining it, but that is only paying commission in another form. Another way is that a friend of the government gets a hint, he purchases the property and makes a great big profit on it. The minister would say that there was no commission paid in that case.
Tell me of a single case in my department in which such a thing has been proved.

We will probably before the end of the session, if we can reach the items in the Public Accounts Committee.
Mr. PUGSLEYr. Yrou have the fullest opportunity of examining the Public Works accounts.
Yes, we have examined some and the minister knows it has been rascally.
I do not know anything of the kind.
The minister knows it.

I have made inquiry and I have never found anything that would justify the statement of the hon. gentleman. There may be some cases which would be open to some criticism, but there is nothing at all that I have seen that would justify the severe statement the hon. gentleman makes. It is all very well to take hearsay evidence, insinuations and suggestions, but in order to get the facts you must have proof and have some one who can speak from knowledge. As far as I can observe there has been no proof on which you can place reliance in regard to anything wrong in respect to the purchase of land for public buildings.
Last year information was given to the House that we paid $40,000 commission for buying lots of land down there for public buildings.
Surely my hon. friend must see he is wrong. Does he say that for the purchase of properties on Sussex street commissions of $40,000 were paid ?
I do say so.
To whom ?

I think one White. He paid $3,000 for elections in London and he said he was friendly to the government and therefore it was justifiable for him to give it. I am sure I am within the mark when I say he got $40,000.

My information from my deputy is that Mr. White received $1,500.
That is as near the mark as my hon. friend usually is.
I will remind my hon. friend ; my memory is not so bad as that and I went over the transaction with great care.
You say it was paid to White ?
I said my impression was the name was White.
You said positively

I did not say positively,
I said my impression was. I do not want the minister to pin me down to what I did not say. When I make a statement I stand by it.
You say now it was $40,1)00 ?
No, I said, speaking from memory, the amount I believed was $4Q.OOO and I think I can hunt it up and show him I am correct. I said my impression was the name was White but I was not sure.

I was not here last year but I venture to challenge my hon. friend to produce evidence of that. I do not believe anything of the kind ever took place, and I happen to know that the gentleman who has been appointed to purchase the properties is purchasing them upon a small commission. It is absurd to say that $40,000 was paid.
Not solely as commission.
The hon. gentleman said as commission and I challenge my hon. friend to look up the evidence and submit it to the House.
I am not at all concerned about the hon. gentleman's belief if he was an atheist or anything else, but I am concerned about my own knowledge and I shall hunt this up.
I venture to say you cannot find anything of the kind.

My hon. friend need not be too positive. It is not the first' time he has been positive, nor is it the first time he has been shown to be absolutely incorrect. I will take the trouble to look it up, I am not going to be beaten down in that way.
I am not trying to beat you down.

What commission
was paid ?
It was a small commission, I think 2 per cent.

I remember the discussion on this last year. There was not only

Mr. White but, if I remember right, another gentleman in Ottawa and the amount was more than .$1,500. The minister has taken the ground to-night that his department has not been in the habit of paying commissions for the purchase of land. We on this side are not in a position to disprove that statement as far as he is concerned, because we have not before us the Auditor General's Report for the expenditures since he assumed office, but we can prove that up to this last year amounts have been paid to certain individuals for purchasing properties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend assume that the payment of a commission would be improper ? I am not discussing whether commissions Have been paid but I say that in many cases if one known to be an agent of the government goes to purchase land he will immediately find the price raised. That is human nature. It is the part of wisdom that persons shall be employed to get land who are not known to be agents of the government. And if a fair business commission is paid on a transaction of that kind it is a good transaction for the treasury as for one dollar spent in commission you probably save $10 in the price of the land. Of course I am assuming a fair and reasonable commission.
As far as that is concerned I do not take issue with the minister ; but when Dr. Sproule asked what the commission was the Minister of Public Works took it as an insult and as absurd.

I did not intend to say anything offensive. My remarks were induced by the suggestion or insinuation which we have had to-day that there was some secret commission, a middleman who had bought the property and had got a commission in some way out of it. That is very different from the appointment of men like Mr. Riopelle who was appointed openly to purchase the properties on Sussex street. What made me speak as I did was the unjustified statement that we had paid as high as $40,000.
What is the total amount paid ?
I think that the commission was 2 per cent and as the property costs between $500,000 and $600,000 the commission would be $30,000 to $12,000.

That was not what invited the reply from the minister. My first question was what commission was paid and the minister answered that it was absurd to ask the question and that there was an insinuation of something wrong.
Did not the hon. gentleman say : It is always the case, always a commission? I took that as suggesting that secret commissions were paid to middlemen.	*
I did not until the hon. gentleman said it was absurd to ask such a question.

I do not think any hon. member of this House will agree with the minister that the payment of this commission is justifiable. There are in the department many men just as capable as any man in the city of Ottawa to make terms for the purchase of these lands. It was well known in the city of Ottawa that these gentlemen were the agents of the government. Every man on Sussex street knew that the government were purchasing these lands. Then why did the government throw away $12,000 on one of their friends when they had many men in the department quite as capable of doing the work.

The hon. gentleman perhaps forgets the evidence that was given by Mr. Riopelle before the Public Accounts Committee, why this commission should be paid. It greatly exceeded $12,000, because in the first instance Mr. White and two or three other gentlemen took a preliminary canter around, announcing to the people that they were going to purchase for the government. I think they were paid pretty nearly $8,000. Mr. Riopelle frankly admitted before the Public Accounts Committee that when he went over the ground he told everybody what he was there for. He established a regular bureau at his office on Rideau street, and the department furnished him with a clerk and a messenger. I think the expense ran altogether to from $20,000 to $25,000. Mr. Riopelle assigned an excellent reason why his intervention was sought. It was that after a conference with Mr. Hyman, they came to the conclusion that there was no person in the department fit to conduct such negotiations. That was an awful reflection on the Department of Public Works. I would ask the minister if the services of Mr. Riopelle and the clerk and messenger are still continued?

My information is that Mr. White and the other gentlemen to whom my hon. friend refers were not employed for the purpose of purchasing the properties, but were appointed as valuators. The department was desirous of getting, these properties as cheaply as possible, and in cases where they could not be obtained at prices which the department thought reasonable, proceedings would be taken by way of expropriation, these two gentlemen were appointed for the purpose of valuing the properties. I think Mr. Riopelle was the only one employed for the purpose of making purchases. Mr. Riopelle and his clerk are still employed by the department, but the services of the messenger have been dispensed with. We intend to retain their

services untilflthe expropriation proceedings are completed.*
How much is it expected that there will be further coming to Mr. Riopelle?
I am not able at the moment to tell my bon. friend.
What were the valuators paid?
I do not know.
The minister has not told us yet from whom the land for this building in Winnipeg was purchased?
It was purchased from Messrs. William Mackenzie, D. D. Mann and K. Mackenzie.

Through whom?
Mr, PUGSLEY. I have no memorandum beyond the names of the vendors and the price.
Will the minister get the information and let us know through whom the purchase was made, and what was paid as commission and for the examination of titles?	,
I shall be very glad to do so.
Was the land acquired by expropriation?
The order in council authorizes the purchase from Messrs. Mackenzie and his associates and therefore I assume that it was not acquired by expropriation.
Will the $417,000 complete the building?
Yes, and pay for the site, fittings, furniture and everything else.
When was it finished?
"We are asking now for $2,000. There will be a further vote of $6,000 required for furnishings.

To come back to the question of commissions, I have found the reference in ' Hansard.' The acting Minister of Public Works at that time (Mr. Fisher) was asked what was the cost of the properties purchased by the government and he replied $400,000. He also stated that Mr. Riopelle of Ottawa had acted for the government in getting options on them. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) asked what about the commission and the acting minister replied:	'He is paid 5 per cent,
I think.' Now, 5 per cent on $400,000 would amount to $20,000.
My hon. colleague, Mr. Fisher, was either misreported or was in error.
I take this from ' Hansard.' I was not so very far out in my recollection. That $400,000 was only for part of the land.
Much more than the half-pretty nearly the whole.

The government had a vote last year for additional land. Would the minister inform us what is the total quantity of land?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. There was an exchange apparently with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think this is a description of the land:
It is composed of the southern fourteen feet of lots 61, 87, 96 and 118, and the northern 52 feet of lots 60 and 88, according to a plan of survey of lot 85, east of Main street, of the parish of St. John, registered in the Winnipeg land titles office, Winnipeg division, as plan 63; and also that portion of lots 95 and 117 of said lot and plan which may he described as follows:	Commencing at the northwest corner of lot 95, thence south along the west boundary of said lot 52 feet; thence east parallel to the south boundary of said lot a distance of 98 feet; thence along a curve to the north of 521 -6 feet, more or less radius to the northeast corner of lot 117; thence westerly along the north boundary of lots 117 and 95 to the place of beginning.

Is this building to be used exclusively for immigration purposes? What length of time are the immigrants allowed to stay in it? Is any portion of the supplies to be furnished by the government other than beds?

It is to be used exclusively for immigration purposes. As regards the manner and the length of time, that is in the control of the Department of the Interior.
Winnipeg-new immigration building, including additional land, $2,000.

This is to make payments in connection with the erection of the immigration building at Winnipeg. The building is 200 feet by 61 feet 4 inches. It is four storeys high from the basement. It is built of brick, the roof is covered with copper, the floors are fire-proof, the staircase is of iron, the partitions are covered with iron lath and cement plaster. It is made pretty nearly fire-proof. I may say that the expenditure up to the 31st of December last was $252,585.33.
Does that include the heating apparatus, the furniture and everything connected with the building, or is it only for the building?
That $252,885 covers everything, fittings and all.

That is a very good reason why the Minister of the Interior should be here. It is not treating this House properly to have any minister absent when supplies are being voted concerning which only he can give the information. The Minister of Public Works cannot give the information I ask because the Minister of the Interior is not here. But these are things we ought to know before we allow the estimates to pass. Wffien an item comes under two departments, both ministers should be present.

All we are asking for is $2,000 to complete the payment. The information my hon. friend desires can be had when the estimates of the Minister of the Interior come before the committee. What information is it he requires?

Is the building to be used solely for immigration purposes? Does the government furnish any supplies to the immigrants? How long are the immigrants allowed to stay there? Is there any charge in connection with the supplies to immigrants who have the means to pay? The estimates of the Minister of the Interior are usually in block sums-four or five items in all, and we get very little information. If the member interested does not happen to be present, the information is not given. If this item goes through without our getting the information I ask, the chances are we will never get it.
I can give the practice at St. John and also at Quebec. The right to furnish meals to the immigrants is let by contract, and the meals are supplied at a very small sum above actual cost.
Are none paid for by the government?

No, unless perhaps in the case of a very poor immigrant.
Winnipeg-new post office, land and building, $100,000.	I

This is a revote. It is for the erection of a new post office situated on Fourteenth avenue between Garry and Fort streets. It has a frontage of 1.34 feet and a depth of 166 feet. The rear line measures eighty feet in extent. The front portion of the building is to be six storeys high, it has a basement. The total cost, including site, heating, lighting, fittings and furnishing letter boxes will be $774,004.97. There was expended to the 31st December $656,159.97.
When will it be completed?
It is practically completed now.
Two years ago the minister said it would be completed that year.
When it|te building is completed, it will not be large enough to accommodate the work required to be carried on.

Winnipeg is growing so marvellously, it is difficult to anticipate the requirements of the near future. This is a very large building. The lower stories will afford 17,000 superficial feet of space and the upper stories 15,000 feet. The post office alone has 10,000 superficial feet.
They will have to get additional space.
They thought years ago that the old post office was large enough.
We are here to think of the future, especially when we are spending millions.

We have heard of the practice in other departments as to the opening of tenders. Would the minister (Mr. Pugsley) explain the practice in his department as it has been and as it is since he became minister!'

In the advertisement calling for tenders parties are notified to direct their tenders to the secretary of the department. When tenders reach the secretary in ordinary course, they are laid away in the safe. When the time comes for opening them, they are opened in the presence of the deputy minister and the minister.
Not the stenographer?

No, the deputy minister and the minister.
Winnipeg-postal station ' B,' north of Canadian Pacific Railway track, $35,000.
I would move that this vote be reduced by $10,000. There is in the vote as it appears a revote of $10,000, which amount was spent during the last fiscal year.

What is the total cost to be?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. The total probable cost including site, heating, electric wiring, fittings and furniture is $76,629.33. The total expenditure to 31st December last is $51,629.33, leaving to complete $25,000.

Amendment agreed to.
Public Works-chargeable to inceme-Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories-'Battleford public building, $7,000.

This is a revote. It is to make provision for a site and to begin the erection of a public building at Battle-ford for post office, &e. We are negotiating for the site and have sent a representative from the department to Battleford to look over the ground and make a recommendation.
What is the building to be used for?
For a post office, and I understand that the Dominion lands office, telegraph office and immigration office will also be in the building.

In which Battleford is the building to be erected?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. The old town of Battle-ford.
And negotiations are going on for a site in old Battleford?
Yes.
What is the site expected to cost?
We hope to get a suitable site for $2,500 or $3,000.

Then why this vote for $7,000.
Mr. PUGSLEY". It is hoped to proceed with tile building and do something on it this year.
What is the total estimated cost, including heating, electric lighting, furniture, &c.?
The chief architect tells me that he estimates it at about $35,000.
Are the plans being prepared?
They have not yet been prepared.
I understand the $35,000 estimated is exclusive of the site?
Yes.
How long has this item been in the estimates?
It was in last year, but whether it was in the year before or not I am not informed.
What is the population of old Battleford, as it is called?
By the census of 1906 it is 933.
And what is the population of the new town of Battleford?
I have not the figures before me.
Is not old Battleford going back?

The people are very hopeful of its future and it seems to be getting along very well. It has two churches, two hotels, flour mill, sawmill, newspaper and telegraph office. I am not prepared to say that it is going behind; in fact, I do not think that is the case.
The building is to cost $35,000 and the site $3,000-$38,000 in all. Does that include every contingency of expenditure?

I do not know the owner of the property, never saw him, never met him and I never wrote to him or he to me. I thought that the price was too high and eventually the department got the land for $1,000 less.
The parties knew that it was required for government purposes.
They could not help knowing. A government inspector was sent from the department.

The Minister of Finance has stated that it is a well known
fact that if parties know that property is desired by the government they raise the prices. No doubt that is true and I think the system of purchasing land should be changed. In the town where I reside with nearly four times the population of Humboldt I guarantee that on the main street you could get a lot with a 60 feet frontage for $1,500. To say that in a town of 500 population it is necessary to pay $3,000 is ridiculous.

I would like to ask that this item be allowed to stand till the minister takes a little pains to find out the facts. I never expected to run up against anything like this. It is beyond any decency and I am going to ask that the item stand.

I do not see any advantage in allowing it to stand. I told th * hon. gentleman that before I became minister this was carefully inquired into. The department sent one of the most reliable experts in land value in the west, a man of the highest character, Mr. Mahler, a gentleman who was employed by both governments, and who valued some of the buildings which were taken over by the Saskatchewan government, to value this land. An agreement has been entered into to pay $3,000. The lot is 75 by 132, it is a corner lot, centrally situated, and I see no reason why the item should stand. I will get any information in the department with reference to the matter and I will submit it and it will be open to the hon. gentleman to discuss it at another time.
Did this commissioner make inquiries on the spot or look for any other lots and get prices on them ?
That is what I understand he did : I understand he compared prices with other lots.
What were the prices of other lots ?
I cannot say to-night; it is three years ago.

I have a word to say in reference to this kind of public improvement. It is pretty hard to build a harbour except where there is navigation. But in erecting a post office or public building it seems to be the kind of public improvement that you can pass around any place. I do not think that the members on the government side should try to make the people believe that the money that is expended on these public buildings all comes from the Liberal party. It comes out of the funds of the Dominion of Canada. I know of a constituency in which there is no public building although it is one of the oldest constituencies in the Dominion of Canada one. of the most fertile and one which has a very lively town in

the centre of it. Unfortunately for that town and county-or rather fortunately- the sitting member is a gentleman on this side of the House. At a meeting held there not long ago this question came up and one of the speakers I believe, the ex-president of the Liberal association, said : The present member for this riding has asked for a post office but cannot get one. What you want to do is to send a Liberal to Ottawa and you will get your post office. Graft or intimidation of this kind is used to the utmost extent in the erection of public buildings. It is a bid to get a few parliamentary votes, but I have to tell you that the people of that constituency have had that gauntlet thrown down to them for the last twenty years that if they elected a Liberal they would get a post office. I say they are entitled to that building and they resent that base attempt to bribe them in their franchise by telling them to vote for this government or they will never get a post office. I have heard that statement from a Liberal. The people of Ontario and of that constituency denounce that kind of thing. We will not stand for it, we will do without our post office rather than sacrifice our franchise.
If they were entitled to it for twenty years why did not your friends give it the last eight years they were in power ?
What I said was absolutely true.
Why did not your friends build it?

They were spending $40,000,000 and you are spending $130,000,-
000.
You will find that post offices were not being erected in such small towns as they are now erected in.

In many western towns, even where the population is not very large, the post office revenue is much larger in proportion to the population than in the east. This building will be a post office, land office and customs house.
Does that make any difference in the value of the site ?

The hon. gentleman is aware that in many small towns in the west of from 500 to 1,000 people if you go outside the main portion of the town you can buy lots for $100 or $200, but in the centre of the town the lots sell for a very high price. I understand there was discussion with reference to the town of Dauphin and I was told by a gentleman who has lived there a great deal and knows it very well that a lot had been bought for $11,000 by a private individual for his own purposes, not for the government.
How big was the lot?

44 feet wide. The government site was purchased for $6,000 for a 75-foot lot, and the $11,000 lot was within 300 feet of it. I venture to say that in Humboldt there may be a dozen lots right in the centre of the town that you could not buy for less than $1,000 apiece, the price being paid here. I do not think it is an out of the way price. It may be a little high but in many towns of from 500 to 1,000 people, $3,000 for three lots, one of them a corner lot, would not be considered high.
Would that be a fair criterion for the prices of lots in Blairmore?
Perhaps the hon. member knows more than I do about that.
I was not as deep under the surface in that transaction as the hon. member.

If the hon. member insinuates that I was interested in the Blairmore townsite he is altogether mistaken, and it is a cowardly thing for him to do, but it is what you might expect from the hon. gentleman.

The hon. member knows towns in his own constituency and in mine better entitled to buildings than this, and can he give reasons for the erection of a public building in this town and not in the others ?
I have given reasons. I have said that lots were sold at $1,000 apiece before there was a building there. Before there was a town, lots sold at $1,000.
Why are they sold so high ?
Because the people wanted them, it is a case of demand and supply.
Does the hon. member mean to say that anywhere in the western country in a town of 500, land is worth $250 a foot. That is what your lot cost in Dauphin.

The hon. member heard the same statement as I did in the corridors made by a gentleman from Dauphin that a lot within 350 feet of the lot sold to the government had been bought by a private company there for $11,000 and the lot was only 44 feet wide.

I heard it but I did not believe it, but Sir, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) has said that right in the centre of the town which is a good town, one of the best in the Northwest, lots can be bought for $1,500.
Is there any reason why the hon. gentleman should believe one statement rather than the other?
I accept the statement of the hon. member for Marquette.
Knowing nothing whatever about the subject.

It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to say that. I say there is not a member from the west on the other side of the House who will say that these three lots, one of them a corner lot, in the small town of Humboldt, are worth 83,000.
The best way to test the accuracy of my statement is for the hon. minister to put in the supplementary estimates $1,500 for the lot, and I will produce it.
Without attempting to cast any reflections upon the town the hon. gentleman represents, I might say that it Is on a side line, it is an old town, and it Is not a divisional point.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. It is a divisional point.
It is not on the main line of a railway.
It will be on the main line of a railway to Edmonton.

Humboldt is a divisional point on the main line of the railway. The price of land there is governed by demand and supply, like any other commodity, and I can assure the committee that town lots of 25 feet frontage were changing hands at $1,000 each before there was a building in the town. We cannot account for these things, but such is the case.
Mr. SPROtJLE. Why do you pay such a price when you can get the accommodation for the post office to-day for a rent of $75 a year?
They are paying as much more for the land office and possibly as much more for the custom house for buildings entirely unsuitable for the purposes for which they are used.
Weil, admit that you pay three times as much, it would amount to only $225 a year. There are many places yielding a revenue of over $2,000 a year which have no post office at all.

I admit that there are places that should have post office buildings which have not. This is not only for a post office, but for a land office, and it is particularly important that we should have a place for the safe keeping of the records of the land office.
Mr. SPROtJLE. You could build a fireproof registry office for $3,000. In Ontario and other provinces you will find villages yielding a revenue of twice or three
or four times as much as Humboldt, and yet they are not getting a post office or applying for one. It does not seem to me to be defensible to spend such large amounts for public buildings in small new places and to neglect places which are two or three times as large.

In the land office
there are six people employed, in the custom house two, and in the post office two, making ten public servants who have to be accommodated.

One point that should not be overlooked is that after you buy a site at a very high price in a new town in a new district and put up an expensive building, you may find in a short time that the town may sink to nothing, and you may have to move the land office and other buildings somewhere else. I remember very well, on the line where my hon. friend from East Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) used to live, the land office was moved successively from Cannington to Alameda, Oxbow and Estevan. There were four moves, and there would have been a corresponding waste of so many public buildings if this policy had been carried out in those early days. I think it is a mistake to jump into a new town when it is just on the boom and put up a public building. The people may flock out as quickly as they flocked in, and you may find in the end that the buildings may be all waste.

The hon. gentleman has given one very good reason why a land office should be built. He has instanced the land office at Cotran district. It was first established at Carlyle, where I lived somewhere about 1882 or 1883. It was moved from Carlyle from lack of accommodation and because there was better accommodation up at Cannington. A few years later it was moved from Cannington on account of lack of accommodation. It was moved to Oxbow temporarily. From there it was moved to Alameda. From Alameda it was moved, because of lack of accommodation, to Estevan on account of the latter being so much nearer to the great bulk of land available for homestead entry and because it was the junction of two railways and much more convenient for the immigrants to make entries. But the main reason why the land office has been moved around so often has been lack of accommodation. If there had been proper accommodation at Carlyle in the first place, the chances are it would never have been moved,

The very fact that it has been moved shows that the new places were very much more convenient for the purposes of a land office. The hon. gentleman himself admitted that it was moved to Estevan because it was nearer the; centre of operation.
And because there was no accommodation at the other places.
And because the people to be served In this new district would have to go so much further to do their land business.

If the minister has a conscience, and I think he has, this discussion should result in a great deal of good to this country. In my judgment the prices paid for these lots are absurd. I am quite willing to sanction the erection of public buildings throughout the whole Dominion, so far as they can be built by the Public Works Department, so long as the money is properly spent, but I will not approve of the purchase of lots at such high prices as those shown to have been paid. It seems absurd to pay $6,000 for a lot where there is not a tow'n but only the site of a town. That is simply paying an inflated price. There is no reason why the government should pay such exorbitant prices. Rather than pay such prices, the minister should refuse to supply the building. I can take you into many flourishing towns in Ontario where you can get the building lots very much cheaper. I want to refer to the town of Sandwich, where a gentleman purchased 208 feet on the main street for $2,000. Sandwich is one of the oldest towns in Ontario.
Was it bought at ordinary sale ?
Yes.
Would you not say that was very cheap ?

It is about the price you can get lots for in any town of that size throughout the Dominion except in places in the west where the prices are inflated and exorbitant. The man who purchased that lot for $2,000 sold the half of it to the government for $1,700.
The lot sold the government was 104 feet for $1,700. That was not out of the way.
That would look fairly reasonable compared with $3,000 for a lot in the western country.
Three lots.

Judge them by the feet. You get 108 feet for $1,700. There is not a town in this Dominion which would not give the lot in order to have a public building. I think myself that the government should buy their lots but only pay reasonable prices. The minister ought to lay down some policy with regard to the erection of public buildings.
We are not charged with the responsibiliy.

The Posmaster General lays down a policy so far as free delivery of the mails is concerned. There must be so much revenue and so much population. I would not have the nerve to ask for a $30,000 public building for a place with 500 of a population. There should be some policy laid down. Make the population 1,500 or 1,000 or 2,000 and take the revenue into consideration. Then you will have something substantial to go on.
Would you give a public building to every town having that population ?

-Always taking into consideration the revenue and the customs. I put in a claim the other day for a public building. I advocated a public building for the town of Tilbury and the minister kindly said he would take my application into his consideration.
Maple Creek public building, $20,000.	1
Have you bought the site ?
The property is situated on the comer of Gaspard street. It is 150 feet by 130. The building will be a two story brick building with stone foundation. Dimensions 59 feet by 54.
What is the price of the lot?
It is a government site
What is the population of the place?
According to the last census, 687.
What w-ill be the total cost, everything included?
Including everything, $32,000.
What railway is this town on?
On the Canadian Pacific Railway.

I saw Maple Creek ten years ago and admired the town site at that time. I had the pleasure of seeing it again last season. It looks to me as if it ought to be an important town, but it seemed to me that it was about the same size when I saw it last season as it was on the occasion of my first visit. This would indicate that some of the western towns do not go ahead as some of their enthusiastic admirers seem to think.
I was in hopes the other Mr. PUGSLEY. The postal revenue is side would lay down the basis.	$2,424. Apparently Maple Creek does more
business than many towns of larger population.
It is the centre of an important ranching district.

Yes.
Medicine Hat public building, $22,000.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. Of this $15,000 is a revote. This is to complete the building.

What will be the total cost?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. Including everything, $17,108.06.
Mr, BENNETT. When will it be finished?
It should have been finished on December 4 last. It is now about ready for the roof ; there has been delay.
Was the contract let by tender?

I believe the site that is being bought at Prince Albert for a penitentiary is admirably well suited for that purpose. We have purchased from different parties lots of 183 acres, 165 acres, 125 acres and 174 acres. The total cost is $30,000.
Where is it located?
It is within the boundaries of Prince Albert. I am told that it is a very desirable property.
Better cut it up and sell it for post office sites. If you get prices such as you paid in Humboldt you will make money.

Is the contract let?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. No. The plans have not been prepared yet.

And no steps will be taken under this vote to construct the building ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. I should suppose not. We might prepare plans and something might be done, but I am not really prepared to say.
What will be done in the meantime with the land that has been bought?

It will be left. I understand that the Minister of Justice is of the opinion that this will be needed for the purposes of a penitentiary within a short time. I am told that the site is exceedingly well adapted for the purpose.
What is the population of Prince Albert?
I have not that information before me, but I should think it would be about 5,000.

It seems to me that this 640 acres of land at $30,000 within the town site of Prince Albert is not out of the way. It figures out at about $47 an acre. There is a lesson here for some of the hon. gentlemen who have been claiming $1,000 a lot in smali towns.

Is it necessary to have 640 acres for a penitentiary? Is there any other place in Canada where the penitentiary has half that?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. We are urged to make a further purchase.
Mr. s. .T. JACKSON. In my constituency we have the Stony Ylountain penitentiary with 640 acres.
It is all rock.
There are 40 acres of rock where the building is. And, if I mistake not, besides what I have stated, they have 240 acres of hay land.
No contract will be entered into under this vote ?
Not for a building.

I do not see what you need so much land for unless you are going to speculate in it.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. At the penitentiary in Dorchester, N.B., they have, I think, 700 acres.

With a couple of hundred convicts, you can work a lot of land.
Regina post office, custom house, &c., $88,000.

This is to complete the public building. It is on the corner of 11th avenue and Scarth street.
air. SPROULE. What is the total estimated cost ?
air. PUGSLEY. Including every thing, $212,565.87. It is to be used for post office and customs house. Regina is a rapidly growing town.

Could the minister give us any information about the site and the price ?
air. PUGSLEY'. The purchase was made from the Knox Presbyterian Church of Regina, at a cost of $10,000.
Saskatoon public building, $15,000.
air. PUGSLEY. This is under contract. The total cost including site, heating, electric wiring, is $90,614. We paid $9,000 for the site, which is situated on the corner of Second avenue and Twenty-first street. The building is to have a frontage of 64 feet by

72. It is to be used for a land office, customs, inland revenue, post office and weights and measures.
The hon. gentleman's predecessor claimed that this building would cost in the neighbourhood of $42,000 or $43,000.

That was an under estimate. Mr. Stewart is the clerk of works; he gets $4 per day. The contract was let on the 27th of June, 1907, and calls for completion on the 1st of April, 1909. The amount of the contract is $64,500.
Where do the other $26,000 come in ?

That is made up by the boilers for heating, the site, survey, legal expenses, printing, advertisements, heating, electric wiring, fixtures, fittings, furniture, sidewalks, fences, superintendence and contingencies.
Yorkton public building, $15,000.

The site cost $4,000, and is 100 feet by 120. The population of Yorkton by the last census was 1,363. The contract has not yet been let. The chief architect has not made the plans yet, but I presume it will be a building like at Dauphin, running from $30,000 to $35,000, exclusive of the land, probably.

Yorkton is a thriving towm. I think this price is about $40 a foot, which is exactly the price paid for the lot in Humboldt. But Yorkton has-a population three times that of Humboldt, and lots in Yorkton should be much more valuable than Humboldt.
