QUEiSTION OF PRIVILEGE-MR. BERGERON.
On the orders of the day being called :

I rise to a question of privilege. In the Regina ' Leader,' which has been placed in my hands, I find an article concerning myself to which I desire to draw the attention of the House. I shall not read the whole article, as it contains matters which are a subject of discussion which I do not want to take up w'ith that paper, but I shall read the portion of the article which I wish to contradict, and which deals with a matter of fact. The part to which I object is as follows :-
All Canada knew, moreover, that in the Prince Albert by-eleetion, Mr. Hanltain and Mr. Bradshaw were doing their utmost to stir up anew all the anti-Catholio prejudices on the autonomy school clause, and were making every possible use and abuse of the text of Mr Turgeon's nationality and religion. Knowing all this, Mr. Bergeron deliberately went to Prince Albert on the eve of that byelection, stood deliberately on the same platform with Mr. Haultain and Mr. Bradshaw in a campaign meeting and did deliberately all he could to procure Mr. Turgeon's defeat and Mr. Bradshaw's election on a platform conceived in anti-Catholic prejudice and nothing else. So entirely did Mr. Bergeron identify himself with the anti-Catholio candidate in Prince Albert and wish for Mr. Turgeon's defeat, that on the following evening at Rosthern he publicly referred to Mr. Bradshaw as ' our condidate ' and gloated over his possible election. Mr. Bergeron's championship of the minority is indelibly besmirched with shameless insincerity.

I desire to say that there is not one word of truth in the whole of the part of the article which I have read. I was not on the platform with any of the gentlemen mentioned. I never said one word, directly or indirectly about the local elections and I never called Mr. Bradshaw or anybody else ' my candidate,' I may say that both of us, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and myself, kept scrupulously out of the legal fight. We spoke of nothing but federal issues.

I would like to ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) whether it is correct, as stated in the press that a Mr. Joseph Bernstein, who, I think, was an interpreter at Halifax, has been dismissed as the result of an investigation held recently. I would also ask whether or not the same'commissioner investigated any other matter-whether there has been any investigation into the circumstances which were commented on in the press with regard to certain facts disclosed in the police court in London some two or three months ago.
Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior?. The complaints against Mr. Bernstein have been fully investigated and the result has been the production of a great deal of conflicting evidence. If the House desires, I shall lay a report of the investigation on the table. The conclusion arrived at by the investigating officer was that although the charges against Mr. Bernstein were not fully substantiated, it was a question whether the amount of suspicion which had been engendered against him had not done away with his usefulness. I do not know what my hon. friend would do if he had such a report presented to him, but I must say it left me in a somewhat undecided frame of mind. With regard to the Dickey matter, we have had several inquiries concerning it which I am not in a position to place before the House, but so far as I have beee able to ascertain yet, there has been nothing disclosed beyond what has already been published. That is to say, we have not been able to substantiate the more extreme charges which were made against Dr. Dickey. He has offered an explanation of his conduct, and I have not been able to overthrow that explanation although I have examined it as carefully as possible.
I understood the hon. minister said that the same commissioner was investigating both matters.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. Perhaps I did say that the same commissioner would investigate both, but what I wish to say now is that I had a separate investigation made apart from that altogether.
That has not been concluded ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has, but it is of a character which I would not feel warranted in placing before the House. It was an entirely confidential investigation. The investigation which was made by the officer who inquired into the case of Bernstein was on the surface. He took what information he could which was open to the public.

Has the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals been directed to the fact that he Algoma Steel Company has stopped operations for the present and that the stoppage is said to be due to some extent to the lack of orders. I would also ask whether the minister has under 'consideration the possibility of placing further orders with the company in order that work might be resumed whether these orders might come from the Intercolonial or the Transcontinental Railway Commission.

GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals. Of course the consideration of any large work such as that would have to depend on our getting the cash to carry it on. The difficulty in the Soo works has been brought to the attention of the Railway Department. As far as the Intercolonial Railway is concerned, I have not been considering the purchase of any rails from the Soo industry, but the question is under consideration with the Transcontinental Railway Commission to see whether anything can be done to relieve the situation.
I am sorry to hear . that the country is in so bad a condition financially as the minister seems to suggest.
I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Lemieux) what steps have been taken in connection with the strike at Owen Sound ?

I have not yet received any report from the officers as regards this riot-
I do not know that I should call it a strike -which has taken place at Owen Sound. My information is that there was no strike in the proper sense of the word. I am informed that there was no engagement by the company and therefore no employer and no employee, and the law could not be applied. That is my own private information. I have no official information. I have asked the Deputy Minister of Labour to prepare a report. If my hon. friend will call my attention to this riot a little later, I may be able to impart more information to the House.

subtopic: DAMAGE BY WATER TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
DAMAGE BY WATER TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Has the attention of the 'Minister of Railways been directed to a statement in the public press that a portion of the National Transcontinental is partially flooded, and I notice the suggestion that there seems to have been some mistake in the estimate of what high water levels might be expected. I would ask wheiner or not there is anything in the report that a portion of the railway in the vicinity of La Tuque will have to be reconstructed and that a portion of the track will require to be rebuilt at a distance from the place where it has already been partially constructed.

subtopic: DAMAGE BY WATER TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: That matter has not been brought to my attention but I shall make some inquiries.

subtopic: DAMAGE BY WATER TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
Let me just read the despatch in the Montreal * Gazette ' of 16tli inst. :
La Tuque, Que., May 15-(Special).-The unusual height of the St. Maurice river this spring has apparently shown up a had engineering mistake in the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway in this district, which may necessitate a complete redrafting of the plans. At the present moment several miles of the roadbed of the new railroad are several feet under water; in fact, one of the contractors came into La Tuque this afternoon and reported that he had paddled in a canoe for two miles over the tracks of the railway, there being two feet and more of water over the tracks during the entire distance.
The floods will undoubtedly cause havoc on the work, the swiftly rushing water undermining the roadbed. It is also stated by the engineers that the piers on the new bridges have been greatly damaged, and many of them will have to be rebuilt during the summer, and the bridges probably elevated.
There is every indication that in planning the road the engineers miscalculated the high water levels, and have laid the road in such a way that it will be flooded whenever the St. Maurice rises unusually high. The river this spring has risen higher than it has done for many years past, and the whole country in this district is flooded. This is, perhaps, fortunate, as it has shown the mistake by the engineers before the road was completed. Whether the plans are changed or not the present floods will cause great expense to the contractors, as the roadbed will be practically ruined by washouts.

subtopic: DAMAGE BY WATER TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I shall make inquiries.

to the recent amendment of the Immigration Act. The minister has promised it on one or two occasions but it has not yet come down.

I ask the Minister of Railways when we may expect that the report of the Royal Commission on the Quebec Bridge will be printed. As there is a committee named to inquire into certain matters connected with the bridge it is important we should have that report printed in full as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
I understand that the copy is all in. It seems to be a question whether there is to be an index and table of contents. The printer makes this explanation :
The report consists of technical matter and a number of technical signs were required which had to be ordered and we expect to receive these every day. They were ordered some weeks ago. The above remark applies to volume 1; there will be a second colume consisting of evidence, &c.
I would suggest that we might have the report without the index as soon as possible and the index might be added afterwards.

Is the Minister of Labour aware that there is a strike going on at the Montreal post office ? Is he aware that Mr. Peter Lyall, the contractor, refuses to pay the men under the fair wage clause of this contract? Is it the intention of the government to take any action to compel him to pay the wages he has contracted to pay?

There is, of course, no strike in the Montreal post office, if the hon. gentleman refers to the employees. There is, I understand, a difficulty between Peter Lyali & Sons, the contractors, and the bricklayers and stonecutters who are engaged in constructing the addition to the post office. The contract between Peter Lyall & Sons and the government contains the fair wage clause. The contract was let on October 12, 1907, and the fair wage-schedule was prepared by the Department of Labour in accordance with the fair wage resolution of 1900. speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on tbe motion of Mr. Ayleswortb for tbe second reading of Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act and the proposed amendment of Mr. W. J. Roche thereto

Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to detain the House at any great length discussing this matter as it has already been referred to and considered pretty thoroughly by members on both sides of the House. However, there are a few features of the case that I would like to draw the attention of the House to and to emphasize. The question of the preparation of the voters' list for a federal election in the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia, which is involved in the first section of the Bill introduced into this House by mv lion, friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayiesworth), is one of the principal features that has been discussed so far. Between 1885 and 1898 the Dominion government kept control of the lists to be used in elections for federal purposes. In 1898 the government of that day saw fit to delegate to the different provinces of Canada, under certain restrictions, the power to make up and revise the lists that should be used in Dominion elections. I have no doubt that the government of that day felt that they had good reasons for bringing about that change. I did not have the advantage of being a member of the House at that time, nor of having been in the position to look thoroughlv into the matter or to participate in the debates that took place, but I notice, from the extracts which have been read in the House, that there was a distinct line of cleavage as between the Liberal party, then the government of the day, and the Conservative party, or the party in opposition, as to whether or not it was advisable to make that change in tiie franchise law. It is equally apparent to me from those extracts that have been read here that while the government of the day delegated this power to the provinces they did not divest themselves of the right or power at any time, for certain reasons and under certain conditions, to take back unto themselves that power to have control over their own lists. Speaking generally, in so far as T see the matter now. I believe to a verv great extent in the principle of the federal government controlling the preparation of their own lists for federal elections, but whether that was or was not a wise move in 1898 is a matetr that I am not going to discuss. I am not going to quarrel with the position taken by the government or the position taken by the opposition. It was an experiment and the question is : Has it worked out satisfactory in all cases? If there are cases in which it has not worked out satisfactorily, the government have re-
Mr. GRAHAM
served to themselves the right to take control of these lists in cases where the privilege has been abused. I will deal first with the question as it seems to me to affect the province of Manitoba, and secondly with the question as it affects the province of British Columbia. In so far as the question affects the province of Manitoba, I have sat in this House and listened to members who have spoken on both sides ; I have, as it were, taken the part, if I may say so, of an outsider in order that I might come to a fair and reasonable conclusion as to whether or not our hon. friends opposite from the province of Manitoba have any grievance with regard to the provisions of this Bill as it would affect them. I am sure my hon. friends opposite will not expect me to give more credence to the statement made by themselves than to the statements made by hon. members from Manitoba on this side of the House. I think I will be taken as having acted fairly towards them if I say that in coming to the conclusion at which I have arrived I have given to them the same degree of credence that I have given to my hon. friends on this side of the House. It lias been borne in upon my mind, in listening to this discussion, from that standpoint that whatever reason may have been present in the mind of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice when he introduced this Bill or in the minds of members of the govern-inen who agreed with him in introducing it. as to the necessity of applying its provisions to the province of Manitoba, there are the greatest reasons for retaining this provision in the Bill. It strikes me that there are only three arguable grounds upon which our friends opposite can base their objections to this Bill as it was originally brought into the House. The first ground is the taking away of the right of the province of Manitoba ; the second ground is the fear that has been stated to exist in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite from the province of Manitoba that the preparation of the lists will partlv be done under government officials, under the Bill as it was originally introduced, and that they will not receive fair treatment at the hands of officials appointed by the government, and the third reason, if these two are disposed of, is the fact that they are singling out or separating Manitoba from the other provinces of Canada and applying this legislation to it. To my mind these three reasons are all the real reasons that can be urged against this legislation. Let us proceed to take these reasons one by one and to discuss them briefly. Take the first reason, namely, the taking away of a right. I think my hon. friends will not dispute the point when I say that there is no inherent right in the province of Manitoba or any other province of Canada to prepare, for federal elections, federal lists. That is not a right given to them the same as many other rights were
given to the provinces by the British North America Act. What they have is not an inherent right. It is simply a power delegated to them by the Franchise Act passed by the Dominion parliament in 1898. Now you can delegate a power for a time and you can take back that power. Having delegated that power, not only can you take it back from the province of Manitoba but you can take it back from every other province in the Dominion. In 1898 this parliament delegated to the different provinces a power which was inherent in itself and so the taking back of that power is not robbing a province of its inherent right nor is it seizing the franchise of the province of Manitoba.
Mr. SPROUT,E. Is It not discrediting the honesty and fairness and the sincerity of Manitoba in making up the voters' lists when you take back the power from that province and not from the other provinces?
I will deal with that phase of the question in a moment.
Are you delegating powers to the provinces in any proper sense of the term when you merely accept their work in the preparation of the voters' list?	*
When you accept their work?
Is it delegating powers to a province when you merely accept the work of the province for your own purpose?
My statement is that certain powers are delegated to the provinces with regard to the preparation and revision of these lists.
The hon. gentleman said a moment ago that this parliament delegated the powers to the provinces.

This parliament did delegate power. It said :	We will take
the lists of the province of Manitoba as they are prepared and revised by provincial authority.
You adopt their work merely.

You adopt their work, but you must have delegated certain powers or otherwise the Dominion itself would have to prepare the lists. I stand by my first statement in the matter. If I am correct in my premises that disposes of the first objection, because, as I pointed out, there is no inherent power vested in the province of Manitoba to hold control over federal voters' lists any longer than the federal parliament permits it to hold that control. Now, as to the fear expressed by hon. gentlemen opposite from Manitoba that the officials appointed by the Dominion government will not be fair in the making up of the lists, surely that fear is dissipated by the suggestion of the Prime Minister with regard to the preparation of these lists.
What does my hon. friend understand that suggestion to be?
I will state what I understand it to be. I have read a good many of the newspapers on that point and no two of them seem to have grasped the same idea.
What does my hon. friend think to be the reason for that-stupidity in the newspapers?
Sometimes, perhaps.
Or a lack of definiteness of the part of the Prime Minister?

Sometimes the newspapers have been stupid and purposely so, and while I do not mean to say that I am less stupid than the newspaper editors, there is no doubt in my mind as to what the Prime Minister meant. The proposition of the right hon. the Prime Minister is that the county court judges of Manitoba be appointed to revise the present existing lists or the lists as they may exist after the latest revision by the provincial authorities; that, taking those lists as a basis the registration clerks and other officials shall be appointed not by this government, but by the county court judges. That would take the whole modus operandi of the preparation and revision of these lists for the federal elections absolutely out of politics,
Does the hon. gentleman mean that the judges having revised the lists under the provincial law are to immediately begin to revise them again under a Dominion law?

The judges may have revised them under the provincial law. but before that revision many names are put apon these lists by the registrars who are appointed by the provincial government, and the proposition is that these registrars, or those who shall place before the revising judges the lists, shall not be appointed by the government of Manitoba or by the Dominion government either, but shall be appointed by the judges and responsible to the judges for their work.
Under what provision of the Manitoba Franchise Act do the registrars put names on the lists?

I notice in to-day's 'Citizen' that the Hon. Mr. Rogers, Minister of Public Works for Manitoba-a gentleman whom I know very well-states that no name can be put upon the lists or taken off the lists except by the judges of the province under the present law.
That's right.

The Hon. Mr. Rogers does not state that quite fairly because he

knows that the registration clerks receive applications at stated times and stated places and many of these applications are written in on a list handed to the registrar, and if these lists are submitted regularly the judges cannot strike these names off unless they are objected to and the objections sustained.
Is there not a provision in the Provincial Act to enable representatives of both parties to be present when these sworn applications are received?
I have no doubt.
And is there not a provision that immediately the representative of either party may hand in an appeal to the registration clerk?
That may all be, and for the present I am not quarrelling with the Manitoba Act.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

I do not object to being asked a question now and then during my address nor does it bother me much, but I do object to standing up here to be cross-examined by hon. gentlemen opposite with question after question. I do not interrupt very often when hon. gentlemen opposite are speaking, and I only wish the same courtesy to be extended to me. My hon. friend from Prince Edward county (Mr. Alcorn) will have his opportunity to speak. However, I have no objection to answering his question.
The hon. gentleman says the Premier announced that he intended to have lists made wholly under judicial authority.
Hear, hear.

And that a certain modus operandi was suggested by the Premier for that purpose. Where in the right hon. gentleman's speech does tha hon. gentleman find that modus operandi laid down? I might call his attention to this fact, that at the close of the right hon. gentleman's speech I asked this question:
Has the right hon. gentleman mapped out or has he in his mind any modus operandi by which his new lists will be made altogether under judicial authority?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think so. 1 think we will be prepared to do so at the proper time, when we are in committee.
Where else in the speech of the right hon. gentleman does the hon. gentleman find any modus operandi laid down ?

If my understanding of the right hon. the Prime Minister's suggestion is correct, and if I am stating what is correct, would my hon. friend (Mr. AI-Mr. GALLIHER.
corn) be prepared to accept an Act on lines such as I have suggested?
The lines are so very faint I do not think any one could accept or reject it.

My hon. friend says the lines are very faint. At the risk of repetition I would say that my understanding of the proposition of the Prime Minister is that every official, including the revising judges, who shall take part in the preparation of these lists in Manitoba for federal purposes, shall be an official absolutely beyond the control of politics. Can you suggest any fairer method of preparing lists ? Can any politician, either on the Conservative or on the Liberal side, say that this is not the fairest way in which a list can be prepared, to take it absolutely out of politics and place it in the hands of county court judges ? My hon. friends cannot complain of the county court judges in Manitoba for in running over the names I find that five of the seven are appointments of their own, and I think I know them all, all honourable gentlemen in every sense of the word. I make that comment to show that no fault can be found with the majority of the judges on the ground that they will be Liberals.
Mr. ALCORN'. Where in the speech will the hon. gentleman find that ?

The hon. gentleman will get his chance to speak and I shall be pleased to listen to him. As I say, my understanding of the proposition of the Prime Minister is that the lists of Manitoba, taking as a basis the lists as they will exist after the last provincial revision before a Dominion election, shall be revised by county court judges, that they shall be taken absolutely out of politics, so that every man, Grit or Tory, will have a fair opportunity of being on the list and a fair opportunity will be given to each party to have the names of any who should not be on the list struck off. I do not believe it is possible to suggest a fairer method.
Why apply that only to Manitoba?

I am going to that.
I think it is clear that any fear hon. gentlemen may have felt that the lists to be prepared under this Bill as it originally stood would be unfair, is met and completely obliterated by the proposition of the Prime Minister. Thus reason No. 2 disappears.
Reason No. 3, the singling out of Manitoba. I shall refer in this connection to some quotations of the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). I will be fair enough to admit at the start that if no good reasons are shown for singling out the province of Manitoba, that province

should not be singled out. I make that as a flat proposition to start with. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has asked:	Why do you select Manitoba and
not Ontario or Nova Scotia or any other province? If you have a school of nine children, to use a homely expression, and one of those children for some cause or other deserves punishment, if you like to call it so

Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh, oh, hear, hear.

My bon. friends laugh, but I said I was using a homely illustration ; probably punishment is not the word, let us say deserves correction. My hon. friend would not say it was fair to the other eight provinces of the Dominion that you should correct them all for the fault that was committed by one.
How about the little boy, British Columbia.

I shall come to the little boy ' British Columbia ' later on. I do not intend to forget British Columbia. If no reasons can or will be given in the discussion why Manitoba should receive different treatment from the rest of the provinces, which is probably a better way to put it, I agree with my hon. friend that this Bill should not go through ; but if it can be and has been shown and the very arguments of my hon. friends opposite as well as those of my friends on this side, have forced me to this conclusion-that in Manitoba, without reflecting on the government of that province, a state of affairs exists and has existed for some time by which justice is not done to all concerned,
I would go almost as far as the Prime Minister himself did when he stated that it was the bounden duty of this government to interfere.
The hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. It. L. Borden), at page 8688 of 'Hansard', referring to the words of the Prime Minister in the debate of 1898; on the Franchise Act, quoted as follows :
But if the day comes when a fraud is committed against this parliament, when legislation of a hostile character is brought forward in the legislature, then it will be always open to this parliament to resume its own powers and to enact a franchise law of its own.
The leader of the opposition himself during that debate said he quite understood the principle that the Dominion government was not depriving itself of its rights for all time to come but could take back to itself again its right if necessity arose. The Prime Minister said :
But if the day comes when a fraud is committed against this parliament

was a fraud against the Liberal party or not. It need not necessarily be a fraud committed against the Liberal party, in fact I think the fraud is much broader and would be, if it is a fraud at all, a fraud against all the electors of the province, whether Liberal or Tory.
Again the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) at page 8690 of ' Hansard ', in speaking of the perfection of the Manitoba Act says :
And this law, enacted by the legislature of Manitoba, under a Conservative administer-ation, has been subject to so little criticism that I say here I do not believe there is in the Dominion of Canada a single province which can show legislation more satisfactory, more fair and effective than that which we have been discussing.
But my hon. friend must know that while we may have an excellent Act on the statute-book, if, in the carrying out of that Act, abuses occur, if the Act is not administered fairly, the results are just as vicious as if the Act itself were vicious.
It is then the administration and not the terms of the Act itself to which the hon. gentleman objects.

That is what I am objecting to at present. My hon friend also at page 8694 quotes the following words used by the right hon. the First Minister:
But, sir, I ask my hon. friends if they will not admit that, although the legislation W'hich to-day exists in Manitoba and the manner in which it is administered may be satisfactory to the Tories, it is not satisfactory to the Grits, and that is the reason why we have introduced this legislation.
And my hon. friend the leader of the opposition very astutely rather played on those words and asked: What if we came into power and we should find a provincial Liberal government in office in Nova Scotia and should want to change the Act as regards Nova Scotia, because, although it may be satisfactory to the Grits, it is not satisfactory to the Toribs? My hon. friend sought to leave the impression that the First Minister was merely making this change in the law in Manitoba because the lists did not please the Grits and do please the Tories. But he knows well that outside that little quotation I have read, there have been grounds brought before the right hon. gentleman, and afterwards proved in discussion here, which show unfairness in the administration of this law. Nay, it has been shown that the grossest kinds of frauds have been committed in some parts of Manitoba in the preparation of those lists. These frauds I do not lay at the door of the govermhent of Manitoba, but they must be laid at the door of the officials appointed by that government and of who acted as the agents of those
I think the leader of the opposition said that it was not clear whether this fraud the men

officials, and I suppose that the government of Manitoba is the responsible party in the end.
With regard to the reasons why Manitoba is singled out from the other provinces, I intend making some quotations from the speeches of hon. members on this amendment. I have already pointed out that in 1898, the right hon. tile First Minister stated that while the government of Canada would be justified, on the ground of fraud or of hostile legislation, in taking back control of the federal lists, there were other grounds on which it would be justified in doing so. Let me refer to the speech of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford). Discussing the very point mentioned by the Hon. Mr. Rogers in his interview with the ' Citizen,' the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) brought out some interesting facts to show what the officials appointed by the provincial government had to do with the preparation of the lists in Manitoba. On page 8314 of ' Hansard ' the hon. gentleman said:
Who limits the time for registration? The executive council of Manitoba. Who decides that there should be but one registration clerk and one booth in each constituency? The executive council of Manitoba. Who "fixes the places of registration booths and the hours during which they are to be open? The executive council of Manitoba, the political machine. Who appoints the registration clerks who have very considerable discretionary powers? The executive council of Manitoba. Who fixes the courts of revision, allowing but for a single day, for a part of a day or a number of days? Who fixes the time for the sittings of the court of revision and the duration of those sittings? Who limits the hours during which the court of revision can sit? The government of the province of Manitoba has full control over the courts of revision and everything else, in so far as registration and the revision of the voters' lists in the province of Manitoba are concerned.
The judges, of course, sit where they are authorized to sit. and, during the time they are authorized, decide as to who should or should not be on the lists.
Will the hon. gentleman be surprised to learn that the judges name the places, the dates and the hours?
Since when?
In practice ever since this Act has been on the statute.
Did the hon. gentleman read the proclamation the other day?
And they are confirmed by order in Council, but it is they who fix the dates.	I
What does the hon. gentleman say to the last proclamation?
Will the hon. gentleman deny that the judges name the places, the times and the dates for the holding of the courts of revision?
And have them confirmed by order in council.

If my hon. friend will take the last proclamation issued in the Manitoba ' Gazette ' of April 25, he will see that what is complained of is still being done in Manitoba even yet, in the face of the Bill being brought down to supply a remedy.

I can assure my hon. friend-and my statement can be verified by the judges themselves if necessary -that the judges fix the dates, the places and the hours during which they shall sit. The government of Manitoba interferes in nowise with those. Upon the report of the judges being brought to council, an order in council is passed and the proclamation issued.
Mr. GALlJHER. My hon. friend admits that the judges make their recommendations to council, and the council may or may not put them in form of an order in council.
What does the council do?
It will probably be hard to answer what, in all cases, it does. But that is only one point of the many I have here. I have here half a dozen different ones that are not challenged.
They were all challenged and answered long ago.

My hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) has challenged them all holus bolus. He pleads the general issue, in other words, but that after all is not a very good answer to a direct statement. Now, let me quote from the hon. member for Portage la Prairie at page 8360 of ' Hansard ' with regard to the distances people have to go to get on the list. Holding up the proclamation, the hon. member said:
Well, here is the proclamation, and you can read it for yourself. For a man to * get on the list in Gladstone he will have to travel two hundred miles coming and going. To be registered in Russell, he will have to travel 156 miles; in Emerson, 216 miles; in Selkirk, 200 miles; in La Verandrye, 210 miles.
Now, let me point out to my hon. friends opposite that there are different degrees of fraud. Where, in the administration of a franchise Act, it is rendered practically impossible for persons duly qualified to be placed on the voters' list to reach the place appointed for them in order to have their

names placed on that list within the time allowed, you are committing, in a degree, fraud against those citizens. Now, there is a state of affairs, which, if it existed in British Columbia, would bring down the condemnation of every man, Liberal or Conservative.
It is not correct.

My hon. friends opposite had their opportunity of cross-examining the hon. member for Portage la Prairie who made this statement and who knows the facts. These hon. gentlemen know that I cannot know these facts personally. But I am quite sure they will do me the justice to say that I have just as much reason to accept the statement of my hon. friends on this side as I have to credit the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite.
What is the name of the man who has to do this?

I think my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) cannot be serious in that question. -Certainly, I cannot give him the information. But the hon. gentleman would have quite a walk if he went afoot to ask this man his name. Now, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) permit me a question? What is the length of Manitoba from north to south aud its breadth from east to west?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot answer that. But I travelled Manitoba in the old days and I know a little about its physical features. I know that, very often, you have to go around a long way by reason of natural physical impediments. Two places may not be far apart as the crow flies but you cannot always travel that way, as muskegs and swamps intervene that you cannot cross. Now, it has been said that registration clerks have no powers in connection with the preparation of these lists. Let me give an instance, given by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) at page 8365 of ' Hansard
In connection with those voters in the particular case I was going to refer to at Lans-downe last year, here is where an abuse crept in to the extent of 40 voters, owing to the fact that the registration clerk failed to do his duty. Applications were made to strike 40 names off the lists, but when the case came before the judge, owing to the fact that the registration clerk had failed to notify the electors whose names were protested the judge would not deal with it at all, and those men were allowed to remain on the lists.
That shows you that this matter is not all in the hands of the revising judge, for others-aud these appointed by the executive council of Manitoba-have duties to perform. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid
Laurier) proposes that these men shall not be political appointees, but shall be appointed by the judge who is chosen to prepare and revise these lists.
What year is that?

I am informed that that was In 1907. Now, let me quote from the speech of the hon. member from Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) with regal'd to the actiou of the registration clerks. X quote from page 8617 of ' Hansard ',
The hon. leader of the opposition and other gentlemen opposite have challenged us to show where any person was left off the list of electors by any official of the Manitoba government, or where any complaints had been made against the lists that had been prepared, My -hon. friend from Selkirk gave last night a good many instances of this kind, hut I might refer in addition to the incident at Balsam bay where 28 voters applied to the registration clerk to put their names on the list, but they could not get the registration clerk to receive their applications and they were disfranchised. The registration clerk, in making the return wrote to his friend, who was the candidate for the constituency, and said': ' Nobody had applied hut the few Grits, and you bet I did not put them on/
Have you that letter ?

I took the trouble to ask the bou. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) if that letter was iu existence and how the letter had come out. He told me that the case came up in court and this is how it was brought to the attention of the public. Will my hon. friends opposite say that that was not a fraud committed on these electors? If these citizens were justly entitled to be placed upon this list in order that they may exercise their, franchise, was not this refusal of this registration clerk, because they were Grits forsooth, a direct, a gross fraud practised against these citizens?
The hon. member (Mr. Galliher) knows that the reply has been given to that statement. I do not wish to repeat the facts. But there was not a man of these disfranchised-they were all put on the list.

They were, for the time being. Hon. gentlemen opposite can reply to what I am saying in good time. The hon. member (Mr. Burrows) who makes the statement I have quoted is responsible and I give the statement on his authority. But I will quote some statements later that my hon. friends cannot take this objection to. Now, let me quote from the hon. member for Dauphin-page 8261 of ' Hansard '-with regard to the disfranchisement of the Lac du Bonnet electors. I would like to quote another statement made by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) in that regard.

Another case which has been cited before, a very glaring case-a case which shows wo had grievances under this Act-was the deliberate disfranchisement of 38 electors at Lac du Bonnet. In this case the revising officer, Mr. Heap, in order to enable the people who were living at Lac du Bonnet to be placed on the list, and at the request of representatives from that district, adjourned his court and agreed to go to the lake and take the applications of the residents there.
Now Mr. Heap saw himself that it was not possible to deal out fair play to these men if he did not appoint another place which could be reached by them, where they could have their names put on the list. He did so, and what was the result ?
The train goes to Lac du Bonnet once a week, remains about two hours and returns. The clerk sent word that he would be there on a special train, the residents met him, and he took all their applications. They were bona fide electors. . Nobody raised a claim that they were not entitled to vote. But as soon as the government found out that he had adjourned his court, they notified him that his action was illegal; and notwithstanding the fact that the registration board certified to the list, when the election took place, the sheets containing these names were torn off, and these men were disfranchised.
I have a copy of his certificate here.
Better read the two certificates.

I will read the one X come to first. When their own officer was trying to do what was fair and to give these men an opportunity of being placed on the list, what did the government do ? The government, or those delegated for the purpose, did not draw any thin red line through these lists, as the hou. member for Selkirk has said, but they tore them off liolus bolus ; and I am informed by an hon. member who took the trouble to look it up, that notwithstanding they had torn these thirty-eight names off the list, when the list came down here certified by the clerk to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, fourteen of those names that had been torn off were interlined on that return, and that was returned as the proper list to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. It is quite reasonable for Liberals to assume that these fourteen names were not friends of the Liberal party. Now in regard to the resolution of the Trades and Labour Council of Winnipeg, the hon. member for Dauphin quoted that also. This resolution was published in their organ, and I draw7 attention to it in order to show that it is not only the Liberals w'ho are complaining of the manner in w'hich the local Act is being carried out, but those belonging to the great labour party as well. On page 8625 we find this in the speech of the hon. member for Dauphin.
The resolution which the Trades and Labour Council passed unanimously and which the Mr. GALLIHER.
boards printed in large type on its front page was as follows;
Whereas the facilities for registration of voters have proved altogether inadequate for the purpose, therefore be it resolved:
That this trades council demand of the government that registration be re-opened and be kept open for at least five days.
And my hon. friend went on to say that the Roblin government did not reopen the registration proceedings. Again, on page 8631, the hon. member for Dauphin alludes to w'hat took place w'hen the returning officer, in the last Dominion election, urged that an additional poll should be opened in one of the ridings of Selkirk, at Lac du Bonnet, so that the people might have an opportunity of exercising their franchise. My hon. friend said :
If the provincial polling division had been followed in the Dominion elections of 1901, the people of Lac du Bonnet, in Selkirk, would have been obliged to go to Cromwell to vote. This would have involved a railway journey from Lac du Bonnet to Molson, and another railway journey to Beausejour, and a drive from Beausejour to Cromwell, in all a drive of forty miles. It is very difficult, in fact impossible, for the electors to go from one place to the other, as there is only one train a week. If the train happened to go on election day it would be all right, but trains do not, as a rule, run on election day any more than on any other day if it does not suit their convenience. The Dominion returning officer put a poll at Cromwell and another at Lac du Bonnet, and they had to divide the list to agree with the polls. That was one of the cases in which action was taken against the returning officer for using the thin red line, as stated by the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
So that wherever it was sought to give the electors an opportunity to record their votes w7e find that even the returning officer was arrested for attempting to do so. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word with regard to the affidavits that were placed on * Hansard ' by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole), in his speech on this Bill. My hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) seemed rather to reflect upon the hon. member for Winnipeg because he had read those affidavits in the House. Now, Mr. Speaker, if that rule were to obtain in this House, I think we would find among our hon. friends opposite very many offenders in that regard. If it is wrong to read an affidavit in the House which discloses improper acts on the part of any person, our hon. friends opposite, who have heretofore read such affidavits in this House, would be to blame fully as much as my hon. friend from Winnipeg. The whole question is as to the truth or falsity of these affidavits. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), in his speech a few days ago, paid me the compliment of saying that if I would rise in the House and, in my fair and manly way, as he put it, would give my

opinion of this matter, I might speak in a manner differing somewhat from my hon. friends. Now I do not want to destroy the opinion the hon. member for North Toronto had of me ; still I must say that if I had in my possession affidavits which I knew to be true, or had every reason to believe were true, and which disclosed wrongdoing in the preparation of the lists in the province of British Columbia, 1 would rise in my place in this House and read those affidavits, if occasion called for it. I think that the hon. member for Winnipeg only exercised his privilege in reading those affidavits, nay more, it was his duty, not only to his party but to the country at large, to read them as he did. Therefore X think that the reflection cast upon my hon. friend from Winnipeg by the hon. member for Macdonald for reading those affidavits, was not at all warranted. And how did the hon. member for Macdonald treat those affidavits? Did he venture for a moment to say that the contents of those affidavits were not true ? No, he met them by flourishing a cheque and saying, there is the cheque that paid for them.
Hear, hear.

Yes, and I intend to say, hear, hear. The question is not whether those men who made these affidavits were paid for the time that they lost in leaving their work and going to make them; the question is as to the truth or untruth of those affidavits. What is the use of saying whether these were paid for or not if the cheque which my hon. friend there held was paid for by his friend's friends too ? But, be that as it may, so long as the statements in this affidavit are true it matters not to me whether the men were paid for their time or not. If they are true the gist of the whole thing and the application of the cheque has nothing to do with it whatever. If they are untrue, of course, it is a different thing. But, there must be either one or two conditions with regard to these affidavits. If these affidavits are not true then what should be the result V These affidavits were made in the city of Winnipeg right under the nose of the Attorney General's department of the province of Manitoba by residents then and now, as I understand, of Winnipeg. I heard that one of them has taken a trip away, but the majority are there yet, and if there is anything untrue in these affidavits the Criminal Code of Canada provides a means of dealing with men who make false statements under oath. It is the bounden duty of the Attorney General's department of Manitoba to prosecute all these men if they have made false statements in these affidavits. I am not going to say that the Attorney General's department was derelict in its duty in not doing that. I am rather inclined to take the charitable view of the case and to say that the reason that these men were not
prosecuted is that the contents of these affidavits are absolutely true. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), when the four or eight affidavits were quoted and the circumstances staled, remarked that that was the herd that the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) and the right hon. Prime Minister were travelling with. How he came to that conclusion I do not know. Not only were his friend's friends-if I am wrong I wish to be corrected-travelling with these four or eight men. but they were travelling with a herd of 450 men, a herd bigger than the herd of buffalo which my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) has imported into this country. It is not unreasonaple to suppose that hon. members on this side of the House, knowing the contents of these affidavits, would not wish to have men of that description on the list and would wish to have men who were placed on the lists under these circumstances removed in order that they might have a fair election. I will read some extracts from these affidavits. My hon. friend from Winnipeg read these affidavits, but made very little comment upon them. I propose to take a short time in making some comments on these affidavits. We will take first the affidavit of Theodore Rudneski ;
Province of Manitoba, to wit:
I,	Theodore Rudneski, agent, make oath and say as follows:-		
I am personally, intimately acquainted with W II Hastings, the organizer in the province of Manitoba for the Conservative party, and I have been acquainted witb the said Hastings for upwards of two years.
About the middle of the month of January 1907. I pointed out to the said Hastings that a large number of foreigners, particularly of the class usually known as Galicians, were residing in various parts of the city of Winnipeg who were at that time entitled to take out naturalization papers in Canada, but who had not at that time done so and who were otherwise qualified to become electors in the elections then in contemplation in the province of Manitoba.
This is how it started :
Shortly after the middle of January, 1907, the said W H. Hastings, in my presence, made arrangements with a committee of six composed of Joseph Makarski, Thomas bnezek, Prank Szablewski, George Czornij, Michael Humilowicz, Thomas Jestremski, to proceed at once to make up a list of Conservative Galicians eligible for naturalization.
I noticed that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) asked my hon. friend from Winnipeg if this were not in connection with naturalization and not in connection with the preparation of the lists. My hon. friend does not imagine for a moment that we are so guileless as to believe that the Conservative party in Manitoba are going to pay for the naturalization of 450 Galicians unless with the object of having them placed on the list as good

Conservative voters. The first step in placing a foreigner on the list who is not a British subject is to get him naturalized and it is with the naturalization of these people that these affidavits have to do. I will not read all the affidavits but I will read some parts of them that strike me very forcibly:
Prior to the third day of February, 1907, the committee aforesaid and other friends of the Conservative party made up a list of some 450, more or less, Galicians, Polanders, Germans, and other foreigners said to be at that time eligible for naturalization.
Prior to the said third day of February, 1907, the signatures of a few of the men on the list of 450 as aforesaid, were obtained

The signatures of a few of these men were obtained.
-by different parties to blank oaths of residence

	.
Blank oaths of residence:
-and oaths of allegiance on the forms in common use in connection with the naturalization of aliens, but the greater number on the list aforesaid had, prior to the third day of February, 1907, signed no papers whatever, or taken no oaths or affidavit whatever with a view of complying with the requirements of the Naturalization Act.
The great majority had signed no papers. A number of them had signed what? Were they aware of the papers they were signing? Was it filled in? Not at all, but it was a blank form of naturalization paper.
On Sunday the third day of February, A.D. 1907, I, this deponent, and Thomas Sne-zek, Frank Szablewski, Thomas Jestremski, Billey Chicocki, Vladmir Rudko and Julian Nowacki went, at the request of the said W. H. Hastings, in the Maw block on Market square, in the city of Winnipeg, and set to work about two o'clock in the afternoon to prepare the naturalization papers for the parties on the list of 450, thereabouts, above referred to.
And they continued that work until two o'clock on Sunday, just these men there present, nobody else, none of the applicants.
I was personally present at the time and place aforesaid, and I saw the said Thomas Jestremski sign as commissioner, the various naturalization papers aforesaid and certify that the contents of the said papers were sworn to or affirmed by the respective parties mentioned therein, without any of such parties swearing or affirming or being present on the occasion in question.
Actually the commissioner, the man employed, the man paid by the Conservative Party to get these men naturalized so that they might be put on the lists as good Conservative voters in North Winnipeg actually purported to swear men who were not present at all, and he actually affixed their signatures as having sworn when they had in reality made no deposition at all.
Will my hon. friend allow a question?
Surely.
Has my hon. friend read the affidavits of Mr. Hasting's and the other gentleman concerned in which they absolutely deny this? Why not give as much credence to these affidavits as to the others?

I have not read the affidavit of Mr. Hasting's. I am not taking second-hand proof. I am taking the sworn statement of the very men that Mr. Hastings employed to do this work. This is direct evidence. Talk about the thin red line, but when it conies down to sweariug in 450 invisible men you are drawing a very much finer and more evanescent line. This affidavit goes on to say :
12. The only commissioner present at the time and place referred to in paragraph 7 hereof, was Thomas Jestremski, and it was necessary in order to complete the naturalization papers for the 450 applicants, more or less, above referred to, for the said Thomas Jestremski to sign his name some twelve or fifteen hundred times, more or less, and the said Thomas Jestremski complained from time to time towards the latter part of the session in question of fatigue and complained that he was too tired of writing to complete all the papers. To overcome this the said Jestremski told others of the parties referred to in paragraph 7 hereof to sign the names of the said Jestremski to a number of the papers which were being made out as aforesaid, and the same were signed accordingly.
Thomas got tired of his job before it was all complete. The provincial government can give authority to any one to take affidavits in connection with the placing of names on the list, such a person can then go about among the people, as they do on both sides of politics, and in three or four days hand in a list of names of men who have taken affidavits without those men having to come personally before the registration clerk. However*, this Bill, like others, must be taken up for consideration clause by clause, and it should be the endeavour of every hon. member to make the Bill as good a measure as possible. Merely expressing niy own opinion hurriedly, I would say that it seems to me that the wording of the clause leaves it open to the serious objection that my hon. friend (Mr. B. L. Borden) sees in it. What, as I fancy, is intended is that, if the returning officer places a mark upon the ballot of a voter through Inadvertence. his doing so is not to have the effect of disfranchising the voter, but the ballot should be counted. Left in its present form, this section might possibly give rise to the abuse suggested by the leader of the opposition. But if the section be so framed as to allow only for cases of omission or inadvertence, then it will not be open to the same objection. For, after all, we have to consider the right of every elector to exercise his franchise; and, when he casts his vote, that vote should not be cancelled because of an error of the deputy returning officer. We all know what took place in the Wentworth election two or three years ago. I had in mind, in this connection, a case decided in the Supreme Court of the state of Washington. It is the case of Moyer and Van de Vanter, and is reported in 12 Washington, page 377. I have not gone into the case itself but have merely taken the syllabus. It says :
The provisions of the general statutes, section 391, directing that in the canvass of the votes any ballot which is not endorsed by the initials of some one of the election officers shall not be counted

That is, as in our case, if the returning officer, being required by the statute to initial the ballot, through error or inadvertence, fails to initial it, the principle announced by the Supreme Court of Washington would validate that vote. For it says that not to count such a ballot would be :
-in conflict with the constitutional provision entitling all male persons having certain qualifications to the right to vote at all elections, since the effect of such statutory provision would be to debar voters of their constitutional right to vote, without fault on their part.
In other words, declaring that it was unconstitutional to say that a vote should be void and bad and could not be counted through an error or omission on the part of the returning officer. That is the extent to which they have gone in the state of Washington, and I understand that the same ground has been taken in the courts Mr. GALLIHEK,
in Michigan. So it does appear to me that if, through inadvertence, a returning officer happens to place an initial on a ballot where it should not be, a man who has an inherent right to be on the list should not on that account be deprived of his franchise. It is an easy matter to distinguish between an error or inadvertence and a deliberate act ; I do not think the court would have any difficulty in deciding that. So I say that if, through inadvertence or omission of the returning officer to do a thing which the law called upon him to do, and through no fault of the elector, who had marked that ballot in accordance with the law, it seems to me that it is due in fairness to that elector that his ballot should be counted. I think probably this section 17 could be so redrafted as to do away to a certain extent with the reasonable and proper objection that was raised by the leader of the opposition, namely, that it would be absolutely wrong to leave it in the hands of a dishonest returning officer so to mark a ballot that John Smith could be identified.
Where does the hon. gentleman find anything about inadvertence in this section?

I am saying that I think the section can be redrafted so as to include only such cases as I am suggesting. As I say, the court can easily distinguish between what is an error and what is deliberate. For instance, no returning officer has a right to write the name of John Smith on a ballot, or to mark the initials of a voter. The only difference between this Bill and the present Act is that, under the present Act, the returning officer, if he is dishonest, can put these marks on the ballot, and the result is that the ballot would not be counted, and the voter is deprived of his vote by the wrongful act, not of himself, but of the returning officer. This Bill would in effect say:	Notwithstanding that the returning
officer wrongfully puts a mark on the ballot the voter shall not be deprived of his franchise. But if this provision is going to open the door too wide, surely we can come to some conclusion with regard to drafting, so that at all events the error or omission of a returning officer will not deprive a qualified elector of his vote.
