I admire the men on this side of the House who are coining out boldly and manfully in defence of Manitoba, of British Columbia, and of the unorganized districts of Ontario and Quebec which are attacked by this Bill. When yon see these men fighting for their existence iu this House and for the rights of the people, you cannot but admire the position they are taking. The right hon. gentleman says that in years gone by the Conservatives attempted to cram down the throats of the then opposition a nefarious measure. 'Why then should he bring in such a measure as this and attempt to cram it down the throats of the opposition ?
At page 8557 the Trime Minister says :
We held to the opinion that the preparation of the lists should be left in the hands of the provincial authorities.
That is referring to the conditions previous to 1885.
-still, we had, in the language of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, to keep watch over the provinces and if we found that conditions arose which would not he fair to this House, then it would be our duty to resume our powers and to have the list prepared by ourselves.
What are the sections in the Provincial Act of the province of Manitoba to which the right hon. the Prime Minister alludes when he says:
If we found that conditions arose which would not be fair to this House then it would become our duty to resume our powers and to have the list prepared by ourselves.
The right hon. gentleman was unable in the whole of his speech to refer to any section in the Act of the province of Manitoba that was unfair or unreasonable. He was unable to show this House or the people of the Dominion that the Provincial Act of Manitoba was unfair or unreasonable in any way, and was not for the general benefit of the people of that province.
The right hon. gentleman referred to tho overlapping of constituencies in the western provinces, but he could find similar overlapping in every eastern province. In almost any province in Canada he will find overlapping more serious and very much greater in proportion than he will find in the western provinces. For instance iu my own riding there is overlapping and there are irregularities in regard to voters' lists and the same thing prevails in many Ontario constituencies. The hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. B. L. Borden) was able to state that for the one irregularity that could be pointed out in Manitoba he could show two in the province of Nova Scotia. I feel sure that on investigation the Prime Minister and his cabinet would find that the Manitoba Provincial Act is reasonable, that it does justice to the people of that province irrespective of party and that the proper course for this government would he to. adopt that Act. Pages of the Prime Minister's speech on Thursday last were devoted to the defence of Bench, but after the statements made by the bon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), I am sure that those who were attempting to defend Beach will feel that his position in the eyes of this country is not a good one The Prime Minister said :
If the polling divisions are not divided by the boundaries of the Dominion constituencies, I do not see any necessity for intervention; it is only where they are divided, so far as I can see, 'that the necessity for intervention arises.

But when you come to look into the results of the forcing of such a Bill as this upon the province of Manitoba before the last Dominion election, it is found that many irregularities resulted.
Let me read from the Prime Minister's words at page 8311:
On this side of the House there is an intimate conviction that the lists in the province of Manitoba are very unfair to the political party to which I belong. The members from Manitoba who sit on this side have given what seem to me conclusive evidence on that point. I have looked into the Manitoba Act. In many respects, it is a commendable Act.
In the whole of his speech he was unable to point out one section of that Act which was not for the general advancement of the franchise in that province and when he refers to the members who are supporting him in this matter, I cannot but feel that by this time he is surely cognizant of the fact that they have not been furnishing him with the proper kind of information in regard to the western provinces Then at page 8315 he says:
I ask my hon. friends if they will not admit that although the legislation which today exists in Manitoba and the manner in which it is administered may be satisfactory to the Tories, it is not satisfactory to the Grits-and that is the reason we have introduced this legislation.
' Mr. Speaker, there is practically the crux of the whole question. The First Minister admits frankly and fairly that as far as he is concerned he must have partisan administration in the province of Manitoba and the unorganized districts or he cannot carry the next election; and I believe it is our duty to see that this province and these unorganized districts are protected and that he shall not secure that advantage.
At page 8317 the Prime Minister says:
That is the proposition I have to make. The judge who is empowered to adjust the lists will be entrusted with the work of correcting all errors which may have been committed in the preparation of the lists in Manitoba.
If that is the only proposition he has to make to the members of the opposition, the Provincial Act provides for that in the province of Manitoba and there is no need of discussing this question any further. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) asked him the question :
Will the right hon. gentleman point out some of the abuses committed by the registration clerks?
Although that question was asked twice the right hon. gentleman was unable to point to one abuse by the registration clerks.
Having read carefully the speeches of the Prime Minister and.his prominent supporters in defence of this measure, I can only
Mr. ARMSTRONG,
say that I do not find any argument that will substantiate their statements in regard to the forcing of such a clause upon the people of Manitoba. The opposition are called obstructionists. I think that on Friday last we were able to give to the House and the country proof that we are not obstructionists. But. Sir, we are patriots, we are ready and willing to stand by this province, and by the unorganized districts and to see that justice is done to them.
The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) laughs at my statements. Does he think it is right that this measure should be crammed down our throats. I cannot believe that he is supporting this Bill with his splendid energy and voice, nor can I believe that he will stand by and see this little province saddled with an obnoxious measure such as is now proposed. Coming from the province of Ontario, he will not wish to see the province of Manitoba saddled with the marked ballot which for years kept the Ross government in power Is that the object of the hon. the Minister of Customs ? Does he want to force upon the people a numbered ballot ? Does he think it is in the interest of the country that a man should be able to go into a poll and write his name practically on a ballot ? Clause 17 is one of the most unfair clauses we could possibly place in an Election Act. Let me read it :	_
Provided, however, that no ballot papers shall be rejected on account of any writing, ' number or mark placed thereon by any deputy returning officer.
That practically means that the door is flung wide open to acts of corruption. It means that what was practised upon the province of Ontario up to the advent of the present Ontario government is to be perpetrated upon the whole Dominion. I cannot believe that the Minister of Customs has given his sanction to this Bill. I cannot help believing that when he comes to speak, as no doubt he will shortly, in defence of this measure, he will not attempt to defend that clause. On his own side man after man has pronounced that clause a most unfair and invidious piece of legislation which should never have been proposed by the Minister of .Tustice. If they have not done this on the floor of the House they have done it in the intimacy of friendly conversation. The Minister'of Justice knows that it is unfair. The First Minister is well aware that It is most unjust and unreasonable. Yet we are called obstructionists because we are trying to have it eliminated, and the right hon. gentleman is threatening us with dissolution. Well, all I can say is that we welcome dissolution. it is high time that the people were given an opportunity to drive this government out of power. It would be the best thing that could happen this country if we should have a dissolution and have these
barnacles cleaned oft the ship of state. Let this government go into the dry dock of pub-lie opinion and get the barnacles scraped' off, they will soon met their fate in the next election however. According to the Montreal ' Star ' of to-day, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) declared in Montreal that provincial politics must go hand in hand with federal politics for both are destined to work for the good of the country. I can hear the Minister of Agriculture down in that province telling the people of the wonderful advantages this Bill is going to give them. He went on to say:
While provincial issues must be more particularly discussed on such occasions, he wished to warn the electors of the county of Brome that they must be ready for another campaign in a very short time. The opposition at Ottawa are trying to usurp the powers of government.
Just fancy the Minister of Agriculture, with his sixty majority, going to the province of Quebec and telling the people there that the opposition at Ottawa are trying to usurp the powers of the government. Did he tell them it was high time the opposition were on the treasury benches? Did he tell them about the corrupt acts of this government, about the corruption carried on in every department of the government, not excluding his own? No, but he went down and said :
The opposition are trying to usurp the powers of government. The latter have been entrusted with that duty, however, and if we cannot carry it out with the present parliament, we will appeal to the country in three or four weeks and have another parliament to do the work of the country.	.
I want to tell the hon. gentleman that he cannot go to the country any too soon, and when he does he will find that this moribund government, with . one foot in the grave, will be compelled to give up the offices they now so unworthily hold. The hon. minister was trying to buoy up his own courage.
He was feeding the chickens.

Perhaps. Or talking about his cold storage scheme and other measures which he has not yet been able to make any practical use of. The government appear to be very unhappy over the Manitoba list. But we do not find any complaint from the Liberal members in the legislature of that province. We do not find any complaint from the men who are living in that province and who represent the people on the opposition side in the provincial legislature. They have not been making any outcry against the present voters' lists there. They have been unable to see that any unfair advantage is taken of them. Hon. gentlemen opposite, however, have recourse to all kinds of
means to force this measure on that province.
When we consider the unhappy position in which this government is, we cannot help but conclude that the country is ripe for dissolution. The government to-day are practically in the hands of the money lenders. Look at the position in which the Grand Trunk Pacific stands to-day financially. Look at the position in which our bonds are in the old country market. Consider the tens of millions of dollars which we shall have to borrow in the old country in the near future. To-day we are obliged to pay	four, five,
six and as high as seven per bent for our money. Is it not time, therefore, that the present government should be ousted and a business government be given control? This government are in the hands of the middlemen and the grafters. When we compare the way our finances are managed at Ottawa with the way the provincial finances of Ontario are administered, we cannot congratulate the present administration. I need hardly point to the Quebec bridge and the corruption in the different departments. With regard to this measure, the opposition have been contending all along that clauses 1 and 17 should be eliminated. In this matter each province to-day is a little kingdom unto itself, but the central authority is trying to change that condition. What they ought to do is deal out justice to Manitoba. They are trying, however, to ignore provincial rights and, further, to take the ballot from the people in the unorganized districts.
Reference has been made to the position taken by the Prime Minister in 1901 with regard to the measure which was then contemplated. I can only say that the Bill must have been drafted in the Justice Department and that some one in the government must have been responsible for it, for we find that it is was ' printed by the King's Printer ' some one must have directed this. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says that he is ignorant of it. Then, who is the dominating force in regard to this measure ? Was it the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). And is that hon. gentleman dominating the government in regard to this matter and forcing it upon the provinces of the west ? I cannot but believe that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) is largely responsible for the present Bill. We have the hon. member for Carle-ton. N.B., (Mr. Carvell throwing slurs upon the laymen of this House and parading his greatness as a lawyer and a legal luminary before the country. As I understand it, law is based on common sense. But when you read clause 1 and clause 17 of this Bill, you cannot but see that, instead of being based on common sense and fair play, they are based upon the very opposite. That hon. gentleman asked why it was that more days were allowed for registration in Manitoba

in 1903 than in 1905. But, though he asked the question, he would not give the opposition an opportunity to explain. The obvious reason is that, in 1903. every man had to be registered, but in 1905 only those who had not been registered before needed to have their names put upon the list, and so it would have been folly to have allowed an equal number of days for registration.
Our duty in regard to this measure is plain. The Liberal-Conservative party are fighting for a square deal and we should be weaklings not to fight for our position. The Liberals of Manitoba are not asking that the present measure should be forced upon that province. The Prime Minister appealed to the sense t>f honour and fair play of hon. members on this side. Why, we have been fighting for nothing else than honour and fair play. Hon. gentlemen opposite accuse us of obstructing the business of the country in this House ; but when these hon. gentlemen look back upon their own record, they can hardly find fault with us for the position we take. The Prime Minister tells us that Leach is a respectable man. Well, so is rreston a ' respectable ' man ; so is Vance a ' respect-aide ' man : and tin1 O'Gorman's, and the Lewises and the Pritchetts and all who have been doing the dirty work of this government-so are they all ' respectable ' men.
If this Bill becomes law, the candidate in Manitoba or the unorganized districts will not have an opportunity to see the voters' lists practically until polling day. What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker ? Is that playing the game fairly ? Is that giving the square deal to the opposition ? Is that a reasonable measure to cram down the throats of the opposition ?-to use the words of the Prime Minister. The Conservatives ask that the government allow the judges to take the present lists, and, where overlapping occurs, let them make the changes. That is all that is necessary in order to attain the end which the government says is the end desired in this case. We find the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) admitting that there were no irregularities in the Manitoba law ; and the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Duncan Boss) practically said that, so far as he was concerned, he knew of no irregularities in the Manitoba law. Man after man on that side is unable to find fault with the Manitoba law as it exists, but still all are ready to take advantage of the little province of Manitoba and of the unorganized districts.
I cannot but think that this is all part of a great election scheme prepared in advance by this government. Months ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bro-deur) came from Europe amidst a great blowing of trumpets and firing of guns, with government ships to meet them as

they approached our shores and many willing helpers to tell the news that a treaty had been made between the Dominion and the French republic. After these gentlemen landed, at public meetings in different parts of the country they gave the people to understand that the treaty was a wonderful thing that would give the people of this Dominion immense advantages in the French market. But when that treaty was laid on the table of this House, the members of the opposition were able to show that it would not benefit our agricultural classes and that only a few manufacturers would reap advantage from it. But this was only part of the election scheme. We had also the all red r<5ute. In the imperial conference, the Prime Minister took a position in which I am surprised to see hon. gentlemen opposite supporting him. He listened approvingly to a scheme of transportation by fast steamships on the Atlantic, then overland across our own country, thence by steamship to New Zealand and Australia. Next we heard it heralded throughout this country that the premier was going to have a fast line of steamships to Australia and New Zealand. But, when we came to this House expecting to find that some definite .steps had been taken in regard to this measure, we found instead-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) will see that he is wandering a little away from the subject.

Possibly I am, Mr. Speaker. I was going to show that this measure was but a part of a government election scheme. This is the crowning act of the drama and the worst, for it takes an unfair advantage of the people and, instead of being for the general welfare, it will allow corruption to be sown broadcast throughout the country. Well, that is another blunder of the Minister of Justice, because we have seen many blunders on the part of that hon. gentleman since he became a member of the cabinet. I cannot think of a worse blunder than this. It simply means that ballots can be marked, that bn Hots can be stolen, as this government have been in the habit of doing, and burnt, as the Ross government have been in the habit .of doing ; it means that all kinds of corrupt acts are liable to be tried on if this measure becomes law. Are the requests of the opposition unreasonable ? N'o, Sir. we are not unreasonable in asking the government to withdraw sections 1 and 17. because we believe that those sections will encourage corruption in elections. If hon. gentlemen who are so strenuously defending this Bill on the other side of the House will look back and read the words- of the Hon. David Mills, or the Hon. Edward Blake, or of their own Mr. Sifton, or Mr. Fitzpatrick, and see what those gentlemen said in fa-

vour of adopting the provincial franchises, they would not persist in their advocacy of a measure like this. The Minister of Justice says that the Manitoba Act is tyranny and oppression as compared with this Bill; but he was unable to point to one section in the Manitoba Act which was either tyrannical or oppressive. I say that these two clauses in this Bill will open the door to all kinds of corrupt practice, and 1 think that this government should be better employed than in bringing down legislation of this character and asking us to pass it. There is no room in this Dominion for men who will bring down measures such as this, and try to force them down the throats of the opposition, when they know very well that they will have the effect of depriving of their franchise electors in the outlying districts of this Dominion. Now who are the people living in these outlying districts ? They are the friends, the kinsmen and the relatives of members of this House. Instead of hon. gentlemen taking the position they are taking, they should bring down a measure that will do away with electoral corruption. The government should have brought down legislation dealing with corruption in elections. There is no provision in this Bill for holding by-elections at a certain time, no provision made as to the character of the returning officers, no provision with regard to corporations contributing to election funds. Civil servants are still allowed to take part in the elections, there is no statutory declaration for financial agents to take. The door is thrown wide open to criminals and the Lewises, the Pritchetts' and the Prestons will have full swing if this Bill becomes law. Are these people in the outlying districts not worthy of the protection of this government ? The Minister of the Interior says that he is willing to allow men who are only receiving $30 a month in the civil service to go on the platform and take an active part in electoral campaigns. Did I understand aright, the Minister of the Interior to say that because officials in his department were only receiving some $600 or $800 a year, they had a perfect right to go on the platform, a perfect right to become scrutineers and to take an active part in elections ? I can only say that if that is the position taken by the' Minister of the Interior, the time has come when we should have a Civil Service Act that will do away with such abuses, and afford no occasion for ministers of the Crown to take such a position as that.
Now this Bill takes away the right of appeal before a judge, which is the safeguard of men living in the rural districts. This government would not dare to force such a measure on the older provinces, this government would not dare to force this measure on the province of Ontario. Let them come before the province of Ontario
with such a nefarious measure as this, and they would very soon find reason to regret it. The Conservative party stands for hands off Manitoba, it stands for the rights of minorities, for purity in elections. But we cannot have purity in elections with such a law as this on the statute-book. However, we feel that brighter and better days are dawning for the people of this Dominion. The present government are tottering to their fall, their knees are shaking like Belshazzar's at the feast. All I can say to the opposition is, stand firm on this question and let dissolution come. Let the government go to the country on this question if they dare.
When ?

Whenever they dare. The Minister of Agriculture who boasts down in the province of Quebec, of the little he has accomplished for the farmers, let him go out into the western provinces if he dare, and talk of the measures he has put on the statute-book. Instead of going into the province of Quebec and trying to rouse up the people and telling them to look out for what is coming, he had better go into the west and say to the people of Manitoba that he is going to give them a square deal in this matter. But I am afraid that the Minister of Agriculture is too much of a party man to be willing to give the opposition a square deal in regard to this Bill.
I am afraid he is falling into the views of the men who sit behind him, that they cannot possibly win the next general election unless they bring in some nefarious measure like this which will give them an unfair advantage. I can only say to the men who are fighting this Bill to stand to their guns. It is our duty to stay here and to persist in our present attitude. I say that we are justified in withholding a large portion of the estimates, so that this government may not hold the whip hand over us for the next few weeks or the next few months. We feel that we are justified in taking the stand that we and our friends from the Northwest have taken in regard to this measure, we stand by the convincing statements that we have made, statements that no man who will investigate this question and who will take a reasonable view of it can fail to support, and we confidently believe that it is our duty to stay here until tiie snow flies if necessary, to fight this Bill. In closing, I would ask the government to take this matter into their serious consideration and to give to the western provinces and the unorganized districts of Ontario and Quebec a square deal. If the government will eliminate clause 1 and blot out clause 17 they will find the opposition ready and willing to sit down and discuss with them a measure that will be for the general benefit of the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the objection to the present Manitoba law regarding voters' lists is not so much to the registration as to the revision. In the compilation of voters' lists there are two separate stages : registration and revision. Under ordinary conditions a voters' list is fixed by the "revision, not by the registration, but under the Manitoba law as administered, registration is more important than revision. Names are placed on the preliminary or registration list by the registration clerk, on a statutory declaration being made personally before him by the applicant at a certain time and place. If personal presence is insisted upon in some cases and not in all and especially if it is insisted upon in the case of members of one political party and not in the case of members of the other-a great advantage is thereby given to the favoured persons or party in getting their names on the preliminary lists. An instance has been given and admitted in which three names and declarations were accepted by the registration clerk without the presence of the parties, which names were allowed by the judge at the final revision of the lists notwithstanding opposition based on the wording of the law. The position taken by the registration clerk, as stated by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), was that his duty was merely to accept applications for consideration and decision by ti e revising officer. The revising officer approved the application and added the names to the list although he was satisfied that application had not been made in person to the registration clerk, as required by the statute. Being satisfied of the qualifications of these voters he ruled, as stated by the hon. member for Marquette, that he would not allow the technicality of their failure to appear for registration to debar them from the list According to this precedent and under this ruling of the revising officer the presence of the voter is not an absolutely necessary condition of registration. Given registration clerks appointed by and only responsible to the provincial government, guided by such precedent and ruling, it is only reasonable to believe that the presence of the voters, as required by the statute, was not insisted upon by the registration clerks in the case of Conservative voters as it was in the case of Liberal voters. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Jackson) stated, in addressing this House, that on going to the registration office himself to have his own name placed upon the list, the name was placed upon the list by the registration clerk without any affidavit on his part and he personally saw the registration clerk add the names of a number of other voters without affidavits on their part. We have this indisputable evidence that names have been placed on the lists by the registration clerks without affidavit and again we have Mr. ARMSTRONG.
absolute evidence that they have been placed on the registration list and allowed by the revising officer without the person's presence at the registration booth. These two facts being established, we have not then a compilation of the list as required by the Act. This is an instance where the law is satisfactory but the administration is not satisfactory. In a country where population is scattered and distances great, registration without the presence of Conservatives while the presence of Liberals was insisted upon, would give a tremendous advantage to the Conservatives in getting names on the preliminary list. No provision was made for the printing of the preliminary list. It was posted on the door of the building in which the revision was held and copies could be demanded of the registration clerk, but to get the copy from the registration clerk was quite a different matter from making the demand. Compliance with the demand could at least be delayed so as to render the right of demand of little value. The list as compiled, in many cases, did not give the post office address of the voter. In case of an attempt to have a name struck off the list by the revising officer notice had to be sent to the person whose right was questioned. In case a person whose right to be on the list was questioned-
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman what document he is reading from.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am rending from a document of excellent authority, quite superior to the affidavits that my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) read.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Speaker. May I ask your ruling?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: My ruling as to what.
The hon. Minister of the Interior is reading his speech.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Of course the rule is plain that an hon. member is not permitted to read his speech.
Mr. OLIVER, i take the point of order that my hon. friend raises as a considerable compliment-that the remarks which have been placed before the House have been direct and to the point. I will admit that the remarks that I have been placing before the House are written. They are written for the purpose of enabling me to put before the House the arguments that I desire to place before it in the shortest and most concise form in order to save the time of the House.
Whose are they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When they are placed before the House they will be mine.
Tliey will be presented to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I want to continue if I may.
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the point is pressed, of course the bon. gentleman cannot continue to read.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then I would like to impress upon the attention of the House the eminent fairness with which it is proposed by our friends of the opposition to carry on this debate. I think that is a fair sample of the fairness with which they carry on the business of revising the voters' lists in the province of Manitoba. However, I do not think that the point of order, or the effort that they made, will at all deprive the House of the views that I desire to put before it although it may cost the House a little more time. , As however it seems to be the object of hon. gentlemen to squander the time of the House and the country I presume they are thereby attaining their object. I was proceeding to say, Mr. Speaker
No, to read.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was proceeding to say, Mr. Speaker, that unless it could be shown to the satisfaction of the revising officer that the voter whose name was objected to had been notified at his post office address the revising officer properly and legally refused to strike the name off the list. By the device of not giving the post office address of the voter on the registration list the name was protected from revision by the revising officer, although the revising officer was a judge of the county court.
What list is the minister referring to?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The list as compiled by the registration clerks.
Appointed by the judges?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Appointed by the judges if you like.
But not since they have been appointed by the government. They put the post office address in each case ; that is the superiority of the present system.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have said that the lists as they stand to-day are without post office addresses of a large number of the men whose names are on them.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That has been stated and restated here.
It is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has been stated and restated by hon. members whose word is absolutely good on the question.
Their word may be good, but their facts may be wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, it is a fact or it is not a fact and it is not worth while arguing it. It was stated as a fact by hon. gentlemen who have personal knowledge and their statement was not contradicted.
It was.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg pardon, it was explained very clearly that while the lists as they existed up to a certain time did not contain the post office addresses, names added to the lists after that time did contain the post office addresses. Therefore, the lists as they stand to-day contain names which have not post office addresses and, therefore, are not subject to the same scrutiny in revision as if the post office address were given. That seems to be admitted by gentlemen on both sides. It is also admitted, I think, that the time which elapses between the preparation of the preliminary lists and the revision is not sufficient. It was stated by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that in one case the time allowed between the close of the registration and the opening of the court of revision was three days. Under the law the revising judge is entitled to have the lists in his hands three days before the court of revision opens and the registration clerk not being required to deliver up those lists until two days after the court of registration is closed, five days would be required therefore to fulfil the terms of the land and in this case only three days were allowed.
Who fixed the date of the court of revision?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know.
The judge did.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would appear from the proclamation which the hon. member for Kootenay had here to-day that it was fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
That is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It makes no difference as to that, because the point I am making is that there was absolutely no opportunity for revision in that case.

The hon. gentleman refers to the case at Neepawa. It was the judge who appointed the date for the court of revision there and I stated at the time that I was convinced it was an oversight on the part of the judge. His attention has since been called to it and the judge has postponed the date of the

court of revision for upwards of twenty days.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any way here is an indisputable instance of the allegation that has been made-
But it is not a partisan instance.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Never mind, it is an indisputable instance of the fact that there was not sufficient time allowed between the registration and revision. The allegations we make is that the whole system of administration is such as to prevent adequate revision. *
And the non-partisan officer who had control of that has rectified it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Admitting that, it is not yet established that there has been any rectification in other instances throughout the province which are not quite so glaring.
Does the minister know of any case which has been brought to the attention of a judge where it has not been rectified?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not here to give instances. The friends of my hon. friends have made a law and they have administered it, and when the attention of the country is called to an iniquitous piece of administration of that lawr it is not good enough to say it is rectified in that instance and left as it was in every other instance. The fact that there was such a case is evidence enough that a lawT which can be so administered is not a proper law or that its administration is not proper.
But that is the law which this Act is going to perpetuate, and not only that, but it is the same revising barrister or judge who by this Act is going to administer the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We will come to that presently. We have established that there is not a fair opportunity for revising the lists, and that the lists in the first place are compiled with such lack of scrutiny, supervision and control as to give the advantage of so-called registration to the one party and to cut it off from the other.
Explain how that could be?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I don't object to make a long speech if gentlemen opposite insist on it, but I did intend to be brief. I have already stated how it is. May I go so far as to say that the very fact 'that my hon. friend and his friends are so determined to retain this law affords evidence that there is a great gain to them in doing so.
Hear, hear.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they would be willing to discuss this matter fairly we might believe that they intended to play fair, but do they expect us to believe that in the back township of Manitoba with a registration clerk appointed by a government which, however much it is entitled to credit for energy and executive ability has never yet been accused of impartiality to its opponents, do they expect us to believe that the registration clerks appointed by such a government would give us any fairer play than these gentlemen opposite give us in the House of Commons in the broad light of publicity before the whole Dominion.
Does the minister think that the accidental oversight of a judge in fixing the date for revision in one instance is sufficient ground upon which to argue that the law ought to be entirely changed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not at all admit that there was only one instance. The hon. gentlemen from Manitoba stated numerous instances but I mention only the most glaring one.
And that fell to the ground.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That did not fall to the ground. It is thoroughly established that the date fixed for the court of revision was not a proper date because the same authority that fixed it changed it. As far as I have followed the information given by the members who directly represent Manitoba, the interval between the closing of the court of registration and the holding of the court of revision was in the majority of cases too short to give a fair opportunity to revise the lists. It must be remembered that the constituencies in Manitoba are in some instances very large, that moil communication is not. in all cases frequent and that notification to the voter whose name is on the list must practically be made by post, and unless he has been notified of the sitting of the court of revision by mail addressed to his post office then, when the removal of his name comes up before the court of revision, it cannot be struck off. Given a rural constituency 100 miles in length and given a desire to revise the list in regard to names of men residing in remote parts of the constituency with only a weekly mail, will any one say that an interval of a month between the sitting of the court of registration and of the court of revision is sufficient or more than sufficient ? I say unquestionably it is not. There should be at least a month in many constituencies in Manitoba in order to secure a fair revision.
What proof is required by the judge that people have been notified ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would vary in different cases.
All that is necessary is simply a certificate of the registration of a letter from the office where is was posted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I suppose the judge would take account of the length of time necessary for the letter to reach the person to whom it was addressed and to permit that person to make appearance or to be represented at the court. If the judge does not give consideration to that feature of the case, I think we will have to revise our opinion as to the judgment of the judges. If the man whose name is appealed against is to have an opportunity to appear on his own behalf or to make representations on his own behalf there must be an allowance of time, and I submit that an allowance of a month between the closing of the court of registration and the opening of the court of revision is not more than sufficient time in some constituencies in Manitoba.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) the other night read to the House the times allowed in the diffenent constituencies. and in no case that I remember was more than a month allowed; it seemed to me that it was seldom that a month was allowed, in the large majority of cases it was considerably under a month.

Clause 1 of this Act states that the whole operation shall take place after the issue of the writ which runs for about 28 days. How does he propose to get all the other notices in and then give this month's notice of revision ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend had read the first clause as carefully as he probably has read some other portions of the Bill, he would have seen that the Bill does not confine action in the ordering of the revision to a date subsequent to the issue of the writ.
It permits it and why should it not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and why should it not? If there had not been a revision before that time and a revision was required before the election it could not do anything else, it could only give the time available and no more. But when my hon. friend says that is the only provision in the Bill, he is mistaken, because he will find on reading that it provides after the issue of the writ or at such other time as the Governor in Council may see fit. Therefore the revision is not confined necessarily to that period after the issue of the writ, it is only confined to that period in case there has not been a revision previous to that time and I suppose my hon. friend will admit that even this government is not required to give more than is possible or more than exists.

Does the hon. gentleman think he will be a better judge of the length of time necessary than the board of registration of the province of Manitoba which consists of all the county court judges of that province ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can only say it has been up before the House repeatedly
The court of revision does not decide the date, it is fixed by proclamation based on order in council.
The judges in every case fix the time, hour and place. How else would the people be notified of the time except by proclamation.
The time is fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council by order in council.
It is not.
I beg pardon, I can get the order in council. The Lieutenant Governor in Council are the only part}' having power to fix the time for tiie court of revision and they do so.
If the hon. gentleman went further he would see that is always done on the report of the board of county judges.

So what the hon. member (Mr. Crawford) says is true.
Mr. CRAWFORD The county court judges have no power to fix the time. The power is vested in the Lieutenant Governor in council.
Who in practice have always acted in the representation of the board of judges.
What the hon. member (Mr. Burrows) says is true then ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked if it was not reasonable to suppose that the board of registration, composed of the county court judges, would know better and would be more likely to give adequate time between registration and revision than the Lieutenant Governor in Council. My only answer is that in the instance mentioned here a few minutes ago, whether it was determined by an individual judge or the Lieutenant Governor in Council, sufficient time was not given in a most glaring case. It strikes me as remarkable that this most glaring case should have occurred in the constituency of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie. It will be observed that it did not occur in the constituency of my hon. friend from Marquette or that of my hon. friend from Souris, or even that of my hon. friend from Macdonald^-It occurred in the constituency of Portage la Prairie.
ROCHE That is rather a reflection upon the judge.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentlemen have said repeatedly that the judges fixed the dates for the sittings of the court of revision. The statement has been challenged from this side of the House and in explanation the leader of the opposition replied that the dates were fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council on the report of the judges.
Which has never been departed from.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot accept the explanation. It is not good enough. When there is such a villainous case as that in the local constituency of Beautiful Plains, it is not sufficient to say that the order in council was based upon the report of the judges. I am not questioning the action of the judge but I am questioning the authority which passed the order in council.
Will my hon. friend agree to withdraw this clause if the judges are called upon to substantiate what I have said and do so ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Most undoubtedly not. I do not know whether my hon. friend has made the suggestion simply as a suggestion or to draw attention from the argument. I am rather inclined to the latter view. I say again that under the statute, the sittings of the court of revision are fixed by order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
Upon the report of the judges.
ROCHE (Marquette) The statute does not say that the judges alone shall be the revising barristers, but in practice they are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the House is entitled to rather fairer treatment than it is receiving.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When my hon friend said that this court of revision was appointed by the judges, he should have had better evidence. I now have the authority of the statute for saying- that the dates are fixed by order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council. I have the text of the proclamation fixing the dates by order in council. My hon. friend says that in practice the report of the judges is accepted by the Governor in Council. In reply I say that I think he is going too far in asking the country to believe that the judges of Manitoba-one or all of them-are responsible for the fixing of the date in the Beautiful Plains case.
The best way to find that out is to ask the judges to come down here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If our hon. friends are going to rest their case on a proposition of that kind, they should have come here fortified by a statement from the judges. It is established that the dates of the sittings of the court of revision are fixed by order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council empowered thereto by a statute of the provincial legislature. Let me add that the period between the closing of the court of registration and the opening of the court of revision does not correspond, in the list the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) read, with the areas of the different local constituencies, with their means of communication, or with the opportunities within them of proper notification regarding the sittings of the court of revision. The dates did vary considerably. In some constituencies there were upwards of thirty days, in some there were less than twenty days, and in others they were down to seventeen and fifteeen days. I am not familiar with the actual circumstances, but I say that it is a fair supposition that the difference in the periods between the closing of the court of registration and the opening of the court of revision in the various local constituencies depended rather upon political exigencies, as understood by the provincial government, than upon the merits of the case or a desire to secure a fair revision, and I instance in this connection the case of the constituency of Beautiful Plains. The places at which the courts of revision sit are fixed by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council. They may be convenient or they may not. We have the instance often alluded to of the Lac du Bonnet case where the court was appointed to sit at a place where it was impossible for twenty or thirty voters to get their names on the list. When the court was adjourned so that these men could get their names on the list, the sittings were illegal and the names were not legally inscribed. Although on some occasions permission was given to have a number of registration offices in each local constituency. at which hundreds of names were registered, with or without personal presence, according to or contrary to the law, as the case may be, the court of revision- if I remember rightly the statement of the case made by the hon. member for Marquette-sat in a large majority of instances only one day or a part of a day in each local constituency. It is proposed under this measure that the revision shall take a day or part of a day when the registration took four, five, six, eight and ten days. I would ask the House how it could ever have been expected that a registration which took eight or ten days, could be revised in one day or less and yet have the levision adequate. The evidence is incontrovertible that the court of revision was not intended to revise. In fact it was in-

tended to prevent revision. We have the statement of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie that in his constituency there were 600 names of Conservatives on the list which should not be there as compared with 200 Liberals; and he told the House that it is impossible, under the law, to have these names struck off. If they are ever to be struck off, it must be by mutual agreement between the two parties in the interest of fair play. Just to revert to the point which we were discussing a few minutes ago. The Manitoba Election Act, chapter 52, revised statutes of Manitoba of 1902 with amendments of 1903 and 1904, published by authority, says, in section 21;
The list of electors shall hereafter only be made and revised at such times and in the manner hereinafter provided Annually on or before the first day of May, the Lieutenant Governor shall, by order in council, authorize the issuing of a proclamation setting forth:
i. The date or dates on, the place or places at, and the hours between which courts of revision will be held in the several electoral divisions of the province to consider and decide such applications, and to receive further applications of others to have their names added to the list of electors.
I find nothing there in regard to the authority of the judges to either revise or amend that authority. The ' Manitoba Gazette ' of Saturday, April 25, 1908, contains a proclamation in regard to the revision of the voters' lists, and gives the names and post office addresses of the persons appointed as registration clerks in the several electoral divisions. It appoints the hours at which they shall sit and says :
That, where not otherwise stated, the hours between which registration clerks shall "hit to receive applications for registration and the correction and striking off names of electors, shall be from 9 o'clock a.m. to 12 o'clock noon and from 1 o'clock p.m. till 6 o'clock p.m.
I find nothing, so far, stating that the judges have any authority whatever in this connection.
That is with regard to courts of registration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I have already read with regard to the courts of revision.
Oh, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) does not understand it. He has posted you wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I find in this publication, the same issue of the ' Maritime Gazette,' the following :
A proclamation.
Whereas it has been determined to add to and revise the lists of electors in and for the several electoral divisions in the province of
Manitoba, pursuant to the provisions of the Manitoba Election Act, and it is necessary for the said purpose to constitute the several judges of the county courts in the said province a board of registration:
Now, therefore, we have thought fit and do hereby, pursuant to the powers and authority contained in the Manitoba Election Act, constitute the several judges of the county courts holding office in the province of Manitoba a board of registration for all and singular the premises.
In testimony whereof, we have, &c.
Now, our friends opposite have stated in so many words that the boards of registration composed of county judges, appointed the registration clerks.
Never.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They did not ?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then I hope we have the point fixed
Certainly they did not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very well, that is accepted.
It never was contended otherwise.
It was stated to-night.
7. ROCHE. I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. Who stated it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it was stated by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche).
The member for Marquette stated nothing of the kind. I did not refer to the courts of registration at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When I was alluding to the instances of names which were put upon the lists without the presence of the voters, my hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) rose and said : Who appointed that registration clerk ?
Yes, because it was done under the original Act, the Act of 1903. The hon. minister (Mr. Oliver) is not posted ; that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then, my hon. friend gave the House a most excellent impression in regard to the fairness of this Act, which, whether I am well posted or not, I have, in my ignorance, been fortunate enough to show clearly is not justified. My hon. friend by his statement, whether intentionally or not, conveyed to the House the impression that the registration clerks were appointed by the board of judges.
1. ROCHE. Originally.
So they were at one time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So they were at one time? But they are not now. So, we have that established for the first time in this discussion. It is established that the registration clerks are appointed by His Honour the Lieutenant Governor in Council. They are then partisan appointments.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Do I understand they are not partisan appointments ?

Do I understand the hon. Minister (Mr. Oliver) to say that when the judges appointed the registration clerks they did not appoint Liberals as well as Conservatives ? And, if so, does he claim that tlie Conservatives were partisans but that the Liberals were not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not talking about that at all. What I am asking-if the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. .1. Roche) wants crossfiring in this way-is:	The registration
clerks who, to-day, are appointed by His Honour the lieutenant governor, are they or are they not partisans of the government of the day ?
Mr. BERGERON'. Why should they be ? Mr. OLIVER. Are they or are they not ?
What do you call a partisan ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A man who votes consistently and persistently for one political party.
And is rewarded.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And I say that my hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) will not deny that these registration clerks are partisans of the provincial government.

- And then

?
Mr. OLIVER, Well, now, that point is established-that to these partisan appointees is entrusted the choice as to whether personal registration shall be insisted upon or not.
What about the law that is proposed here ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If that is the case, I ask what is the provision as to personal registration but a provision to keep Grits off and let Tories on ?
What about the law that is proposed here ? Will it not be the same on the other side ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We will come to that

Is the minister (Mr. Oliver) aware that two. of the main cases that have been relied upon on the other side are cases which occurred when these Mr. W. J. ROCHE
registration clerks w7ere appointed by the judges ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that has anything to do with the case. But now we have that preliminary point established .-that the compilation of the preliminary list is absolutely in partisan hands under the interpretation that has been given to the law on the authority of my hon. friend from Marquette, and on the statement of my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. S. J. Jackson) they are given practically a free hand in the compilation of these lists to party advantage. Now, I said before, and,
I beg to repeat, that in instances where it is considered necessary that there should be a number of courts of registration in a single constituency, it is not considered necessary that there should be an equal number, or anything like an equal number, of courts of revision. That is to say that, where names can be put upon the list by the partisan registration officer at his own sweet will, in four, five, six, eight or ten different places
Seventeen.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -these names could only be struck off in one place in the constituency in one day or part of day. I said, and I beg to repeat, that that is not a provision for the revision of the lists, it is a provision to prevent the revision of the lists. The time that is allowed for the revision of the lists is, as I have shown, absolutely inadequate. There are naturally a number of people who have not been able to get their names on before the court of revision and who are anxious to get on. They may be of one political party or the other, or of both ; we will suppose they are of both parties. The court of revision has but one short day to sit. Now, it is natural and proper that'the application of the men who are present to be on the list will be taken up before the applications to strike off are considered, with the result that in practice there is to all intents and purposes no striking off the lists compiled in the way I have described. Do my hon. friends contradict that statement?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then I will refer them to the statement of my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), who informed the House that at a certain date there was a revision in the city of Winnipeg which resulted in the striking of 2,500 names off the list. Nobody questions that it was a proper revision. The city of Winnipeg is a large city and has a very fluctuating population, much more so than any city in eastern Canada. My hon. friend from Souris informed the House that in the year succeeding that revision there had been in one year 25 names struck off. in another year I think 30 names and in another year 30 or 40 names. I think

he managed to total up in three or four years about 100 names that had been found to be improperly on the list in the great city of Winnipeg ; when in the revision immediately before that it was found there were 2,500 names that were improperly on the list. Now, these lists having been compiled as I have described, hon. gentlemen will not suggest that there is any good opportunity to get names off those lists improperly. When in the city of Winnipeg, where every effort is made, if it is made anywhere, to get the lists revised properly, it has only been possible to get a paltry hundred or so off the list in three or four years, the House need not go further for absolute evidence out of the mouth of the member for Souris that there is no such thing as a revision of lists in the province of Manitoba.
In this connection it might not be out of place to refer to the methods employed to secure names for insertion on the lists in the city of Winnipeg, as described by my hon. friend who represents that city. He placed before the House certain sworn statements by certain people, that at a certain day, a certain hour Sand a certain place, and under certain circumstances, some 450 men who, in a large majority of cases were not entitled to be naturalized, and in any case were not entitled to be naturalized as they were, were naturalized by the assistance of the party machinery of the local government in the city of Winnipeg. The affidavit is explicit, it gives time, place, dates and persons. The affidavit is denied by our friends on the other side and is denied by counter affidavits. It is not creditable to the city of Winnipeg, it is not creditable to the party in power there, that their party machine did, as admitted, employ the person who made this affidavit, and which affidavit they declare to be false. They declare that he was a jail bird and that now he is a fugitive from justice. This is the man that their party machine employed. They admitted that he was in their employ, that he is the man they employ to-day to do their work. He is the man who has made this affidavit as to the management of the party machine. We find that these 450 naturalizations took place on the day immediately preceding the day for registration of the voters in the city of Winnipeg. And we find on searching the records here the remarkable fact that there were some 790 naturalizations put through in the city of Winnipeg on that particular day. It is a coincidence of course that the affiuavit of Rudneski accounting for 450 of these should happen to be made on the same date. But it is a coincidence our friends will admit. It is also a coincidence that in the constituency of North Winnipeg, which was considered to be a safe Liberal seat, one of the leading citizens, one of the oldest inhabitants in the city of Winnipeg, 276
a man who had enjoyed the honour of being mayor of the city, in that safe Liberal seat was defeated in the election by the candidate of the Conservative party machine by a large majority, a majority, if I remember right, of about 400 or 450. Those who are acquainted with the political conditions in Manitoba were astonished when they heard how the election had gone. It was indeed a famous victory. It is only a coincidence that the Conservative majority in North Winnipeg was approximately the same as the number of manufactured naturalizations that Mr. Rudneski swears to. But it was a coincidence at any rate.
Now, it is said that this Rudneski is a very improper person, that he has been a jail bird, that he is now a fugitive from justice, and that he committed perjury in making that affidavit. That is a serious charge. It is asserted also that not only did he commit perjury, but that he was suborned to commit perjury, that he was paid for doing it by a cheque to the amount of |25 given to him by a certain gentleman named Walton, who acts in some capacity on behalf of the Liberal party. I submit that the statement on the part of members of the Manitoba government that Rudneski was a jail-bird, that he is now a fugitive from justice, that he is a suborned perjurer, or that Mr Walton suborned that perjury, is not good enough in this case. These gentlemen are charged with the administration of justice in the province of Manitoba. I hope that under their administration perjury has not become so common as to have no attention paid to it or that subornation of perjury should not be dealt with as the Criminal Code provides. If the facts are as these gentlemen have stated-have stated broadly in the newspapers-in the newspapers of their own ownership, as it is even said- their position it seems to me is not enviable. Either the Rudneski affidavit is true or the government of Manitoba is not maintaining the law as the government of Manitoba is charged with the responsibility of doing. The government of Manitoba is winking at perjury, at the subornation of perjury if it does not take every proceeding within its power to bring the men Rudneski and Walton to justice, to lay them by the heels in jail and to see that they are punished to the full extent of the law. That is the only answer they can make to the Rudneski affidavit. It is that or it is nothing. Either Rudneski and Walton should be in jail or the Rudneski affidavit is true. There is no escape from that. Rudneski Is out of the country, it is said. Perhaps he is and perhaps he is not. We do not know whether he is. My hon. friend from Macdonald rather indicated to the House that the government of Manitoba, or at any rate the party machine in Manitoba, had



knowledge of the whereabouts of Rud-neski while they had knowledge of the nature of the affidavits which he had made.
Mr. STAPLES I beg to contradict the hon. gentleman. I never made any such statement. I never said anything of the kind. I am surprised at the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend knew the price that was paid for the cheque ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He says he knew the price that was paid for the cheque. Does he know who paid it ?
Mr. STAPLES Yes, I know who paid it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then my hon. friend knows that somebody got it from Rudneski.
Precisely so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That it was not in the interests of the party machine in Manitoba.
Mr. STAPLES Why not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No reason in the world why not, but it could not have been got by the party machine in Manitoba for its face value unless there had been protection to Rudneski guaranteed by the province of Manitoba. Why should Rudneski give up a $25 cheque for $25 instead of taking it to the bank and getting it cashed ?
The bank was closed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does he know where it was paid ? My hon. friend knows too much about this1 cheque for his own good and so do his friends know too much about it. This is a question of perjury, a matter of seven years' penitentiary if justice is done.
Did this government undertake to prosecute Nixon or Wagner ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This government is not called upon to prosecute Rudneski any more than it was called upon to prosecute Nixon or Wagner. It is the business of the government of Manitoba to prosecute Rudneski.
May I ask the hon. gentleman whose duty it was in Wagner's case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that it makes any difference as to whose duty it was to prosecute Wagner, But, I will say that Wagner was prosecuted. Wagner was convicted, I think, on improper evidence. Our friends who have been shouting in this House and out of it against Wagner, whose prosecution or persecution has been referred to by the hon. gentleman, are not taking any steps against Rudneski. Again I say that either the Rudneski affidavit is true or the government of Manitoba stands convicted of being a government unworthy to govern.

I would like, in reply to the minister, to say that the government of Manitoba are to-day trying to find Rudneski.
Mr. OLIVER My hon. friend had possession of the cheque which he held up in this House.
Do you want to see it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I saw it or what my hon. friend said was it, I am taking his word and it is good enough. He said that the cheque had not been cashed.
Neither it had.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That no more had been paid for it than its face value.
That was right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If it would give evidence of his having been suborned to perjury to the men who are charged with the responsibility of punishing him is it to be supposed that he would give up that cheque unless he got a promise of protection? Rudneski is accused of being a jail-bird, he is accused of being a fugitive from justice, he is accused of being a perjurer, but he is not accused of being such a consummate fool as that. However, we will drop the question of Rudneski.
There is an affidavit placed before the House by my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) of another person who, in so many words, confirmed every statement made by Rudneski. To sum up : The registration clerks are appointed and hold sittings as directed by order in council. The present provision for correcting the overlapping by the returning officer has not been satisfactory in practice, therefore some other method should be provided. In order that the people may freely cast their votes it is necessary that polling divisons should be conveniently arranged.
